teile.einleitung: Without water no plant can live. Plants take up water with their roots and carry it up into the leaves. Some plants even live in water, while others get by for a long time without rain.
wichtigste: Plants take up water with their roots.
Through fine tubes in the stem, the water rises into the leaves.
If a plant gets too little water, it wilts.
A limp cut flower often straightens up again in fresh water.
Cacti can store water for a long time.
Reed and water lily grow beside and in water.
A cucumber consists of well over nine tenths water.

abschnitte.text: Plants take up water from the soil with their **roots**. In the **stem** there are fine tubes. Through them the water rises up into the **leaves**. In the leaves the plant needs the water to make food with sunlight. Part of the water evaporates through tiny openings in the leaves.

If a plant gets too little water, leaves and stem become **limp**. It lets its head hang and **wilts**. If it gets water again in time, its cells fill up again. Then it often straightens up again. You can see this well with a **cut flower** that you put in fresh water.

Some plants live in very dry regions. The **cactus** can **store** water in its thick stem for a long time. Instead of leaves it often has spines, so that less water evaporates. In this way it gets by for a long time without rain. Other plants with thick, fleshy leaves also store water.

Some plants love it wet. The **reed** grows on the shores of lakes and ponds. Its roots stand in wet soil or directly in the water. The **water lily** roots at the bottom of ponds and lakes. Its large leaves **float** on the water surface.

Many plants and their fruits contain a great deal of water. A **cucumber** consists of well over nine tenths water. That is why it is so juicy and crunchy. Watermelons, tomatoes and lettuce also consist mostly of water.

gewusst: On a hot summer day, a large broadleaved tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water through its leaves.
If you put a white flower in coloured water, its petals take on the colour after a while. In this way you can see how the water rises upwards.

teile.einleitung: The walnut tree is a large broadleaved tree with round, hard nuts. In Switzerland the walnut is mostly called the Baumnuss. Its wood is very popular for beautiful furniture.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the walnut is mostly called the Baumnuss.
The green husk of the nut stains the hands brown.
The nut kernel recalls a small brain.
Walnuts ripen in autumn, mainly in September and October.
Crushed leaves smell strong and spicy.
Walnut wood is hard, dark and beautifully grained.
The Romans probably brought the tree across the Alps.

abschnitte.text: The **walnut tree** can grow large and broad and live for many decades. Its leaves are pinnate, so they consist of several single leaflets. If you rub a leaf between your fingers, it **smells strong** and spicy. Many insects do not like this scent. In the past, people therefore liked to plant walnut trees next to farmhouses.

The walnut first sits in a **green fruit husk**. This husk contains a dye that **stains the skin brown**. The colour goes away only slowly. In autumn, mainly in **September and October**, the husk bursts open, and the ripe nuts fall down. Inside lies the hard shell, which is easiest to open with a **nutcracker**.

The **nut kernel** has two halves with many folds and windings. That is why it recalls a small **brain**. Walnut kernels contain a lot of fat and protein. You eat them raw, in muesli or in baking. In Switzerland, for example, people know **walnut bread**, called Baumnussbrot.

The wood of the walnut tree is called **walnut wood**. It is hard, dark and beautifully **grained**. That is why valuable furniture, wooden bowls and panelling are made from it. An old, straight walnut trunk can be worth a lot of money.

The walnut originally comes from areas between the **Balkans** and **Asia**. The **Romans** probably planted it in their provinces north of the Alps. In this way the tree came to Central Europe and to Switzerland. Today it grows here in gardens, in meadows and at the edge of villages.

gewusst: The leaves and roots of the walnut tree give off a substance that makes some other plants grow worse under the tree.
The German name “Walnuss” originally means roughly “foreign nut”, that is, a nut from the south.

teile.einleitung: Rowan berries are small, bright orange-red berries. They grow on the tree called the **rowan**, which is also called the mountain ash. Many birds like to eat them very much in autumn.
wichtigste: Rowan berries grow on the rowan.
The rowan is not related to the ash.
Ripe rowan berries are orange-red and hang in large clusters.
Raw they taste bitter, but cooked they are quite edible.
In May and June the rowan flowers white.
The leaves are pinnate.
In Switzerland the rowan grows from the lowlands up high into the mountains.

abschnitte.text: The tree on which rowan berries grow is called the **rowan**. Despite the name, it is not related to the ash. Its leaves only look similar to it. A leaf consists of many small leaflets, which is called **pinnate**. The rowan is very robust. In Switzerland it grows from the lowlands far up into the **mountains**, where other broadleaved trees are missing.

In May and June the rowan bears large, **white flower clusters**. Later the berries grow from them. In late summer and autumn they turn bright **orange-red**. Many berries hang together in large, heavy **clusters**. That is why you can see them from far away.

Blackbirds, thrushes and many other **birds** like to eat the berries. That is where the German name Vogelbeere, bird berry, comes from. With their droppings the birds spread the **seeds**. In this way new rowans often grow in entirely different places. In the past, **bird catchers** laid rowan berries as bait in their traps.

Raw rowan berries taste **bitter**. Whoever eats many of them can get a **stomach ache**. In **cooking**, the substance that causes the trouble is broken down. That is why you can make jam or jelly from rowan berries. So they are not entirely poisonous, as many children believe.

gewusst: In the Alps the rowan still grows where hardly any other broadleaved trees occur.
The name rowan berry, literally bird berry, recalls that people used to attract birds with the berries.

teile.einleitung: Cinnamon is one of the oldest spices in the world. It is obtained from the bark of cinnamon trees that grow in the tropics. In Switzerland, it smells especially of cinnamon at Christmas time.
wichtigste: Cinnamon is the dried bark of cinnamon trees.
The cinnamon tree is an evergreen tree from tropical Asia.
It belongs to the laurel family.
The most important kinds are Ceylon cinnamon and cassia cinnamon.
The substance cinnamaldehyde gives cinnamon its flavour.
Cassia cinnamon contains a lot of coumarin and should not be eaten in large amounts.

abschnitte.text: The cinnamon tree is an **evergreen tree**, so it bears leathery leaves all year round. It grows in tropical Asia and belongs to the **laurel family**, so it is related to the bay laurel. On plantations the trees are not allowed to grow tall. They are cut back again and again so that many young shoots grow back, whose bark can be harvested.

For cinnamon, the bark of the young shoots is peeled off and the outer layer removed. On drying, the thin inner bark rolls up by itself. This is how the well-known **cinnamon sticks** arise. In Ceylon cinnamon, several thin pieces of bark are pushed into one another, so its sticks look like a cigar with many layers. Ground, they become cinnamon powder.

There are two important kinds. **Ceylon cinnamon** originally comes from Sri Lanka, which used to be called Ceylon. It is regarded as finer and milder. **Cassia cinnamon** comes mainly from China and tastes stronger. It is cheaper and is therefore often used. But cassia cinnamon contains a lot of **coumarin**. In large amounts, this substance can harm the liver, so you should not eat very much of it.

Cinnamon owes its typical flavour mainly to the substance **cinnamaldehyde**. It is found in the essential oil of the bark. Cinnamon flavours sweet things such as apple cake, rice pudding or mulled wine, but in many countries also meat dishes. In Switzerland, **cinnamon stars** are baked at Christmas time from almonds, egg white, sugar and cinnamon and spread with a white glaze.

Cinnamon was known in antiquity and very valuable. For a long time, people in Europe did not know exactly where it came from. Later, European sailors fought over the trade. First the Portuguese controlled the cinnamon trade from Ceylon. From the middle of the 17th century, the **Netherlands** took it over, and later the British. Today cinnamon is grown in many tropical countries.

gewusst: Ceylon cinnamon sticks consist of many wafer-thin layers of bark, cassia sticks mostly of just one thick layer.
The German word Zimt has the same origin as the English “cinnamon”.

teile.einleitung: The **WWF** is one of the largest nature conservation organisations in the world. It was founded in Switzerland in 1961 and has its international headquarters in Gland in the canton of Vaud. **WWF Switzerland** works for nature, animals and climate in its own country.
wichtigste: The international WWF has its headquarters in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
WWF today stands for World Wide Fund for Nature.
The panda logo was drawn in 1961 after the female panda Chi Chi.
In Earth Hour, people all over the world switch off the light for an hour.
WWF Switzerland offers camps and outings for children and young people.

abschnitte.text: The WWF was founded in **1961**, in Switzerland. Its international **headquarters** are today in **Gland** in the canton of Vaud on Lake Geneva. Originally it was called the World Wildlife Fund. Today WWF stands for **World Wide Fund for Nature**. The WWF is represented in many countries with organisations of its own.

The well-known logo shows a black and white **panda**. Its model was **Chi Chi**, a female panda in London Zoo. The logo was drawn after her in 1961. The panda works well as a symbol: it is popular, easy to recognise and was strongly threatened at the time.

Once a year the WWF organises **Earth Hour**. Then people, cities and companies all over the world switch off the light for **one hour**. Famous buildings also stay dark. With this the WWF draws attention to **climate protection**. In Switzerland, many municipalities take part too.

**WWF Switzerland** offers **camps** and outings in nature. Children and young people experience forests, streams and mountains up close there. They get to know animals and plants and learn how to protect them. Besides this, WWF Switzerland works for waters, forests, biodiversity and the climate. It is also one of the organisations that have the right of associations to appeal in Switzerland.

gewusst: One of the largest nature conservation organisations in the world has its headquarters in a small place on Lake Geneva.
The panda logo has been simplified several times over the years, but it has always stayed a panda.

teile.einleitung: A **dry stone wall** is built entirely without mortar. The stones hold together only through clever layering. In its cracks and gaps, many plants and animals live.
wichtigste: A dry stone wall holds without mortar, just through clever layering.
On steep slopes it was used to build terraces for vines and fields.
A retaining wall is built leaning slightly back towards the slope.
Water can drain away through the joints, so it lasts a long time.
Lizards, snakes and wild bees like to live in dry stone walls.
In 2018 the art of dry stone walling was added to the UNESCO list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

abschnitte.text: In a dry stone wall, stones are laid on top of each other so that they support one another. **Only their clever layering** holds them together. Large stones go at the bottom, and the joints are staggered, as in a puzzle. Gaps are filled with small stones. A good **retaining wall** on a slope **leans slightly back towards the slope**, so the earth does not push it over.

In the past, many dry stone walls were built on steep slopes **to create terraces for vines and fields**. This produced flat land that could be worked. In Switzerland the vineyard terraces of **Lavaux** on Lake Geneva are famous and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. There are also many such walls in the Valais and in Ticino. Because **water can drain away through the joints**, no pressure builds up behind the wall, and it often lasts a very long time.

The stones of a dry stone wall **store the sun’s heat**. That is why **lizards and snakes** love these walls, as they need warmth to be active. The **wall lizard** even carries the wall in its name. In the joints of sunny walls, **wild bees** build their nests. Snails, spiders and beetles also find hiding places.

In the cracks grow plants that manage with little soil and water. The **biting stonecrop** has thick leaves in which it **stores water**. Ferns such as wall-rue and small flowers also settle there. That way an old dry stone wall becomes a colourful habitat. In **2018**, the art of dry stone walling was added to the UNESCO list of **Intangible Cultural Heritage**, jointly by several countries, including Switzerland.

gewusst: Some dry stone walls have stood for many centuries.
A dry stone wall can be repaired by resetting individual stones, without tearing down the whole wall.

teile.einleitung: **Clay minerals** are tiny mineral platelets found in almost every soil. They make clay sticky and easy to shape. They are important for plants because they hold on to water and nutrients.
wichtigste: Clay minerals belong to the phyllosilicates.
They form mainly through chemical weathering of feldspars and micas.
Kaolinite is a two-layer mineral and hardly swells at all.
Montmorillonite swells strongly and is the main component of bentonite.
In illite, potassium is firmly built in between the layers.
Their negatively charged surface binds nutrients such as calcium and potassium.
In Switzerland, Opalinus Clay is planned for a deep repository.

abschnitte.text: Clay minerals belong to the group of **phyllosilicates**. They consist of thin layers that lie on top of each other like the pages of a book. The building blocks are mainly silicon, aluminium and oxygen. The individual particles are **tiny, thin platelets**, much smaller than a grain of sand. That is why clay minerals have a huge **specific surface area**: even one gram of clay has a very large surface.

Clay minerals form mainly through **chemical weathering**. Water and acids slowly attack rocks such as granite. In the process, **feldspars** and **micas** are changed. Over a long time, new, very fine minerals are made from them. Depending on the climate and the rock, different clay minerals form.

**Kaolinite** is a **two-layer mineral** and hardly swells. It is used, for example, to make porcelain. **Montmorillonite** can take up a lot of water between its layers and **swells strongly**. It is the main component of **bentonite**, a clay used for sealing. In **illite**, **potassium** sits firmly between the layers and stops it from swelling.

The surfaces of clay minerals are **negatively charged**. That is why they hold on to positively charged particles, called **cations**. These include important nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium. Plant roots can later exchange them again and take them up. How many cations a soil can bind in this way is called the **cation exchange capacity**. Soils rich in clay are therefore often fertile.

**Opalinus Clay** is a clay-rich rock that formed about 175 million years ago. It is very dense and lets hardly any water through. That is why in Switzerland it is planned as the **host rock** for a geological **deep repository** for radioactive waste. In 2022, Nagra proposed the Nördlich Lägern area for this. In the Mont Terri rock laboratory in the Jura, Opalinus Clay has been studied for years.

gewusst: Swelling clay can seal fine cracks by itself again when it takes up water.
The word kaolinite comes from the Chinese place Gaoling, where porcelain clay used to be mined.

teile.einleitung: The **forget-me-not** is a small flower with sky-blue blossoms. It blooms in spring in many gardens. Its name recalls friendship and remembrance.
wichtigste: The flowers of the forget-me-not are mostly light blue.
In the middle sits a small yellow ring.
Each flower has five petals and is only a few millimetres across.
The buds are often pink and turn blue as they open.
The forget-me-not blooms in spring.
The water forget-me-not grows by water.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of the forget-me-not are mostly **light blue**. They are very small, only a few millimetres across. But many flowers stand together in clusters. Each flower has **five petals**. They are arranged around a small **yellow centre**.
The yellow ring in the middle is not just pretty. It shows insects the way to the **nectar**. Bees, flies and butterflies visit the flowers. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower.

The buds of the forget-me-not are often **pink**. As they open, the flowers turn blue. On one plant you can therefore sometimes see both colours at once. In the garden the forget-me-not blooms in **spring**, often together with tulips. After that it fades.
There are different kinds of forget-me-not. The **water forget-me-not** loves wet soil. You find it by streams, ponds and in marshes. Other kinds grow in meadows, in the woods or in the garden.

The name says: forget me not, so **think of me**. That is why the flower is given as a sign of **remembrance** and friendship. In other languages, too, the flower has a similar name, for example “Vergissmeinnicht” in German.

gewusst: In German, the forget-me-not is called “Vergissmeinnicht”, which means exactly the same.
On one flower cluster you can see pink buds and blue flowers at the same time.

teile.einleitung: The tinder fungus is a large, hard fungus that grows on tree trunks. It looks like a horse’s hoof. As early as the Stone Age, people used it to make fire.
wichtigste: The tinder fungus grows on tree trunks, especially on beeches and birches.
It has the shape of a horse’s hoof.
It is as hard as wood and not edible.
A tinder fungus lives for several years.
It makes the wood of the tree soft and rotten.
In the past it was used for making fire.
Even Ötzi had tinder fungus with him over 5,000 years ago.

abschnitte.text: The **tinder fungus** belongs to the **bracket fungi**. It grows sideways on tree trunks, especially often on **beeches and birches**. Its fruiting body has the shape of a **horse’s hoof** and is grey to brown. It is **as hard as wood** and therefore **not edible**. On the underside it has many fine tubes from which it releases tiny spores, with which it spreads.

Unlike many fungi in the forest, the tinder fungus does not disappear after a few days. It **lives for several years**. Every year it forms a new layer underneath. That is why you see grooves on its side, similar to annual rings. Over the years it can become quite large. It grows mainly on weakened or already dead trees.

abschnitte.titel: What it does to the tree
abschnitte.text: Inside the tree, fine fungal threads grow. They break down the wood and **make it soft and rotten**. This is called **white rot**, because the decomposed wood turns pale. An infected tree can break in a storm. For the forest the fungus is nevertheless important: it helps to break down dead wood, and so the nutrients are freed again for new plants.

abschnitte.titel: Making fire as in the past
abschnitte.text: The name comes from **tinder**. This is the name for a material that begins to smoulder from a single spark. From the soft inside of the fungus, tinder was made in the past. With **flint** and a piece of iron or pyrite, people struck sparks that ignited the tinder. **Ötzi**, the man from the ice, had tinder fungus in his equipment over 5,000 years ago.

gewusst: Ötzi was found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps on the border between Austria and Italy.
From the inside of the tinder fungus you can make a soft, leather-like material from which even caps were once made.

teile.einleitung: In winter, life is hard for wild animals in the mountains. It is cold, and food is scarce. Wildlife quiet zones are areas in which animals have peace and are not disturbed by people.
wichtigste: In a wildlife quiet zone, wild animals are to remain undisturbed.
Wildlife quiet zones are especially important in winter.
Every flight in the snow costs an animal a lot of strength.
Wildlife quiet zones are marked with signs and entered on maps.
Snowshoe walkers and ski tourers should stay on marked routes.
Chamois, black grouse and mountain hares, for example, are protected.

abschnitte.titel: What is a wildlife quiet zone?
abschnitte.text: A **wildlife quiet zone** is an area in which wild animals are to find peace. People may not enter it at all or only on certain paths and routes. In Switzerland, the **cantons** and **municipalities** set such zones. Often the rules apply mainly in winter and in spring. Whoever ignores them can be fined.

In winter the animals find little food. Many therefore save energy, move little and lower their metabolism. If an animal is startled, it flees through the deep snow. That costs **a great deal of strength**. If it happens often, the animal is weakened and sometimes cannot survive the winter.

The **chamois** lives in the Swiss mountains and needs peace in winter. The **black grouse** digs itself a cave in the snow and rests in it. If it suddenly flies up, it loses valuable warmth and energy. The **mountain hare** wears a white coat in winter and is well camouflaged. Red deer, ibex and ptarmigan also benefit from wildlife quiet zones.

Wildlife quiet zones are recognised by **signs** in the terrain. You also find them on maps and on the internet. Whoever is out with snowshoes or touring skis stays on **marked routes**. You should avoid forest edges and snow-free places, because animals look for food there. Dogs belong on the lead. The Swiss campaign “Respect your limits” explains these rules.

gewusst: The white winter coat of the mountain hare turns brown again in spring.
In a snow cave it is much warmer for the black grouse than outside in the wind.

teile.einleitung: Eight-armed octopuses are sea animals with eight arms and a soft body without bones. They have three hearts and blue blood, and can change their colour in a flash. Many researchers consider them the cleverest invertebrates.
wichtigste: An octopus has eight arms with many suckers.
It can change its colour and even its skin surface.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
They belong to the molluscs, like snails and mussels.
There are around 300 species of eight-armed octopuses.
When in danger, they squirt out a cloud of dark ink.
Most octopuses live only one to two years.

abschnitte.text: Octopuses have a soft body, called the **mantle**, and eight arms with suckers. Because they have no bones, they can squeeze through tiny gaps. Between the arms lies the mouth with a hard beak, similar to that of a parrot. The smallest species are only a few centimetres in size, while the Giant Pacific octopus can reach several metres with its arms.

An octopus has three hearts. Two of them pump the blood through the gills, and the third supplies the rest of the body. The blood is blue because it contains the substance **haemocyanin**, which contains copper. In us humans, by contrast, iron-containing haemoglobin makes the blood red.

In the skin of octopuses sit thousands of small colour cells called **chromatophores**. With them, an octopus can change its colour in fractions of a second and blend in with the background. Some species even change their skin so that it looks like a stone or an alga. The mimic octopus imitates other animals such as sea snakes or lionfish.

Octopuses have a large nervous system, and a large part of it is in the arms. Each arm can therefore feel and taste to some extent on its own. In experiments, octopuses have opened screw lids on jars and solved small puzzles. Some species even carry coconut shells around with them to hide in.

Octopuses live in all seas, from shallow coasts down to the deep sea. There are none in the Swiss lakes, because they need salt water. They eat mainly crabs, mussels and fish, which they grab with their arms. The common octopus can be found, for example, in the **Mediterranean**.

A female octopus lays thousands of eggs in a den. She guards the eggs for weeks or months, fans fresh water over them and hardly eats during this time. Shortly after the young have hatched, the mother usually dies. The tiny young first drift in the sea as **plankton**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals with a soft body without bones, such as snails, mussels and octopuses.
Colour cells in the skin with which octopuses change their colour.
A copper-containing substance that colours the blood of octopuses blue.
A dark liquid that octopuses squirt out to confuse enemies.

gewusst: An octopus can taste with its suckers what it touches.
The blue-ringed octopus is small, but its venom is very dangerous for humans.
If an octopus loses an arm, a new one can grow back.

teile.einleitung: Trees have to transport water from the roots up to the crown. In conifers, this is done mainly by **tracheids**. These long, dead cells carry water and at the same time make the wood strong.
wichtigste: Tracheids are long, dead cells with pointed ends and pits.
Softwood consists mainly of tracheids.
They carry water and strengthen the wood.
Their walls are made woody by lignin and can withstand pressure.
Vessels, by contrast, have perforated cross walls.
In the bordered pit sits a thickened middle part, the torus.

abschnitte.text: A **tracheid** is a **long, dead cell** with **pointed ends**. When it is fully built, its inside dies off, and only the firm wall is left. This wall is made woody with **lignin** and so can **withstand pressure**. Through small spots in the wall, the **pits**, water flows from one tracheid into the next. In softwood, tracheids make up most of the wood.

Broadleaved trees also have **vessels**. They consist of many cells whose **cross walls are perforated**. This produces long, wide tubes through which water flows quickly. Tracheids, by contrast, are single, narrow cells. The water has to pass from cell to cell through the pits, which is slower, but safer.

In drought or frost, **gas bubbles** can form in the water pipes. An **embolism** like this interrupts the water transport. In a wide vessel, one bubble can block a long tube. In tracheids, **the bubble stays limited to one small cell**. In the **bordered pits** sits a thickened middle part, the **torus**. It can close the pit like a valve so that the air does not spread.

In softwood, tracheids perform **two jobs at once**: **carrying water and providing strength**. In spring the tree forms wide, thin-walled tracheids, the light **earlywood**. In summer, **thick-walled** tracheids with a **narrow lumen** form, the darker **latewood**. Through this alternation, clear **annual rings** can be seen in the wood. From them you can tell the age of a tree.

gewusst: Even the earliest land plants over 400 million years ago had tracheids.
A tracheid in spruce wood is only a few millimetres long, but much longer than it is wide.

teile.einleitung: A weather balloon is a large balloon that carries measuring instruments high into the atmosphere. With weather balloons, weather data are measured far above the clouds. Every day, hundreds of such balloons go up worldwide and help to forecast the weather.
wichtigste: With weather balloons, weather data are measured high up in the atmosphere.
A weather balloon is mostly filled with helium or hydrogen.
It carries a small measuring instrument, the radiosonde.
The sonde measures temperature, air pressure, humidity and wind.
The balloon rises to a height of about 30 kilometres and then bursts.
Worldwide, weather balloons are launched at many stations twice a day at the same time.
In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss regularly sends up weather balloons in Payerne.

abschnitte.text: A **weather balloon** consists of a thin rubber skin filled with a gas lighter than air, mostly **helium** or hydrogen. Below it, a small measuring instrument hangs on a string. At the launch the balloon has a diameter of about one to two metres. It rises into the sky at about five metres per second.

The measuring instrument is called a **radiosonde**, because it sends its data by radio to the ground station. It continuously measures temperature, air pressure and humidity. By GPS, the balloon’s drift is tracked, from which wind direction and wind strength are calculated. In this way a precise picture of the layers of air arises, from the ground up to great height.

The higher the balloon rises, the lower the air pressure around it becomes. That is why it expands more and more and grows several metres wide. At a height of about 30 kilometres, in the **stratosphere**, the skin finally bursts. The sonde sinks to the Earth on a small parachute, often far from the launch site.

The measurements go into **weather models**, with which computers calculate the weather of the next days. Worldwide, the stations launch their balloons at the same time, mostly at midnight and noon universal time. In this way the weather services get a simultaneous picture of the atmosphere over the whole Earth. The data also help to observe climate change at altitude.

In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss** runs an aerological station in Payerne in the canton of Vaud. There, weather balloons with radiosondes go up daily. Whoever finds a sonde that has landed can report it to the weather service.

As early as around 1900, researchers sent balloons with measuring instruments up high. The Frenchman Léon Teisserenc de Bort discovered in this way that above a certain height the temperature does not fall any further, and he found the stratosphere. In 1931 the Swiss physicist **Auguste Piccard** rose into the stratosphere with a balloon and a pressurised cabin as one of the first people. Today, weather balloons are still indispensable despite satellites.

begriffe.erklaerung: a small measuring instrument that sends its data by radio to the ground
the envelope of air that surrounds the Earth
the layer of air above about 10 to 15 kilometres, in which the ozone layer also lies
the weight of the air pressing on a surface

gewusst: At altitude, a radiosonde often measures temperatures of minus 50 degrees and colder.
When it bursts, a weather balloon is often as big as a small house.
Auguste Piccard was the model for the character of Professor Calculus in the Tintin comics.

teile.einleitung: Global food supply means the question of how all people on Earth get enough healthy food. Many international organisations take care of it. Even so, many people still suffer from hunger or malnutrition.
wichtigste: The FAO is the UN organisation for food and agriculture, based in Rome.
The World Food Programme received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.
The UN goal SDG 2 is called “Zero Hunger”.
Hidden hunger means a lack of vitamins and minerals.
Maize, rice and wheat supply most of the food energy from plants.
The self-sufficiency rate shows how much a country produces itself.
The Global Hunger Index compares hunger in different countries.

abschnitte.text: The **FAO** (Food and Agriculture Organization) was founded in **1945** and is based in **Rome**. It collects data on hunger and agriculture and advises states. The **World Food Programme (WFP)** provides food aid in crisis areas. It is the largest humanitarian organisation that distributes food. In **2020** it received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

The UN has adopted 17 **Sustainable Development Goals**, abbreviated SDG. **SDG 1** stands for “No Poverty”, **SDG 2** for “Zero Hunger”. By 2030 it calls for food security, better nutrition and sustainable agriculture. The **Global Hunger Index** shows every year how far countries are from this. It is published by aid organisations such as Welthungerhilfe and sums up values such as undernourishment and child mortality.

Hunger does not mean only eating too few calories. In **hidden hunger**, **micronutrients** such as iron, iodine or vitamin A are lacking. Those affected often feel full but are malnourished all the same. If children lack protein for a long time, a serious illness called **kwashiorkor** can arise. In it, water collects in the body, and the belly looks swollen.

Three cereals supply the largest part of the food energy from plants worldwide: **maize, rice and wheat**. A large share of humanity’s calories comes directly from these plants or via animal feed. If a harvest fails because of drought or war, prices rise worldwide. That is why varied agriculture is important.

The **self-sufficiency rate** states what share of a country’s food consumption comes from its own production. In **Switzerland** it is about half of the calorie requirement. Switzerland imports the rest. The movement **La Via Campesina**, an alliance of small farmers’ organisations, coined the term **food sovereignty** in **1996**. According to it, peoples should determine their own agricultural and food policy themselves.

gewusst: Worldwide, a large part of the food produced is wasted or lost on the way to the plate.
16 October is World Food Day, the date of the founding of the FAO in 1945.

teile.einleitung: Urban gardening means gardening in the city. People grow vegetables, herbs and flowers on roofs, in back yards or on wasteland, often together with others.
wichtigste: Urban gardening means gardening in the city.
Growing is often done communally on wasteland, roofs or in back yards.
On sealed surfaces, people garden in crates, sacks and raised beds.
In Switzerland many city dwellers rent an allotment garden.
The German city of Andernach became known as the “Edible City”.
Soils beside busy roads can contain heavy metals such as lead.

abschnitte.titel: Green in the middle of the city
abschnitte.text: In **urban gardening**, people garden in the city. They grow tomatoes, lettuce, herbs or flowers on unused areas. Often this is done **communally**: neighbours share a garden, swap knowledge and harvest together. That creates green places where people meet. At the same time bees and butterflies find food.

In the city the ground is often **sealed**, that is, covered with concrete or asphalt. That is why, on roofs or car parks, people often garden in **crates, sacks and raised beds**. They bring the soil there and can be moved if needed. A well-known example is the **Prinzessinnengarten** in Berlin-Kreuzberg. It was created on wasteland at Moritzplatz, where gardening was done in mobile crates.

In Switzerland there have long been **allotment gardens**. Many cities rent out plots on shared sites, and in Germany they are called “Schrebergärten” or “Kleingärten”. The German city of **Andernach** on the Rhine took a different path. As the **“Edible City”**, it plants vegetables, herbs and fruit in public spaces, and the population may harvest them.

In **guerrilla gardening**, public spaces such as wasteland or the soil around trees are planted without permission. Often **seed bombs** made of soil, clay and seeds are used. Quite different is **vertical farming**: plants grow in buildings on many levels one above another, often under artificial light. That way a lot can be produced on a small footprint.

Not every city soil is clean. Traffic and old contaminated sites can burden the soil with **heavy metals** such as **lead**. Vegetables right beside busy roads can take up these substances. That is why it is worth having the soil tested before growing, or gardening in crates with fresh soil.

gewusst: Even a balcony can be a small city garden, for example with herbs in pots.
Community gardens are often also places where children learn where vegetables come from.

teile.einleitung: Every plant species has a scientific name, usually of two Latin words. These names apply all over the world. In this way researchers everywhere know exactly which plant is meant.
wichtigste: Scientific names are unambiguous worldwide.
They are Latin or are formed in a Latin way.
A species name consists of the genus name and a species epithet, for example Fagus sylvatica.
Names of plant families end in “-aceae”.
The Asteraceae are the daisy family.
Directly above the species stands the genus.

abschnitte.text: Popular names differ from region to region. The dandelion has many names in German, and in every language it is called something different again. A **scientific name**, on the other hand, designates **the same species** anywhere in the world. The names are **Latin** or are formed in a Latin way, even if they come from Greek or from people’s names. Latin was for a long time the language of science.

The Swedish naturalist **Carl Linnaeus** established naming with **two words** in the 18th century. The first word is the **genus** and is written with a capital letter. The second word is the **species epithet** and is written in lower case. An example is **Fagus sylvatica**, the common beech. In books such names are usually printed slanting, that is, in italics.

The species epithet often describes a characteristic. **alba** means white: Abies alba is the silver fir with its light grey bark. **sylvatica** comes from “silva”, the Latin word for forest. The common beech is one of the most important forest trees in Switzerland. **officinalis** means used in the pharmacy. The common sage, Salvia officinalis, was used as a medicinal plant in the past.

Living things are arranged in **ranks**. Several closely related species form a **genus**, several genera a **family**. From bottom to top the order runs: species, genus, family, order, class. Names of plant families end in **“-aceae”**, for example Rosaceae for the rose family. The **Asteraceae** are the **daisy family** with daisies, dandelion and sunflower.

gewusst: The “flower” of a daisy is actually a head of many tiny single flowers, which is why the family is named after the flower head.
Behind a scientific name there is often an abbreviation for the person who named the species. “L.” stands for Linnaeus.

teile.einleitung: Viticulture means planting vines and making wine from their grapes. In Switzerland there are vineyards in all parts of the country, especially many in the Valais, in Vaud, in Geneva, in Ticino and in German-speaking Switzerland. Every region has its typical grape varieties.
wichtigste: Phylloxera destroyed many vines in Europe in the 19th century.
Since then, vines have been grafted onto resistant American rootstocks.
Chasselas is the most important white variety, and in the Valais its wine is called “Fendant”.
In Ticino, the red variety Merlot shapes viticulture.
In 2022, Pinot Noir was the most widely grown variety in Switzerland.
Sauser is young, just fermenting grape juice.
In Visperterminen, vines grow at over 1,000 metres.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century a tiny insect was brought in from **North America**: **phylloxera**. It damages the roots of European vines, so that many vineyards died. American vines, on the other hand, are resistant. That is why European varieties have been **grafted** onto American **rootstocks** ever since. Grafting means: you join part of one plant to the root of another.

The most important white grape variety in Switzerland is **Chasselas**, called Gutedel in German. Wines from it are called **“Fendant”** in the Valais. In 2022, the red **Pinot Noir**, also called Blauburgunder, took the largest vineyard area with about 3,760 hectares, just ahead of Chasselas. It grows in German-speaking Switzerland, in the Valais and in Neuchâtel.

In **Ticino**, **Merlot** arrived around 1900. Today it is the most important variety there, because it thrives very well in the mild climate south of the Alps. The **Valais** is the largest wine region in Switzerland. A typical Valais speciality is the white **Petite Arvine**, which is grown almost only there. In **Visperterminen**, vines grow at over 1,000 metres above sea level, mainly the variety **Heida**.

In autumn the grapes are harvested. Then they are pressed. In the juice, yeasts begin to turn the sugar into alcohol, which is called **fermentation**. Young grape juice that is just beginning to ferment is called **Sauser** in Switzerland. It tastes sweet, fizzes lightly and already contains a little alcohol. Wine is an alcoholic drink and is meant only for adults.

gewusst: The vine terraces of Lavaux on Lake Geneva have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.
The vineyard of Visperterminen is regarded as one of the highest in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Arve, also called the Swiss stone pine, is a conifer of the high mountains. In Switzerland it grows up to the forest line, for example in the Engadine and in the Valais. It can stand great cold and can become very old.
wichtigste: Arve and Zirbelkiefer are two names for the same tree.
In the Swiss stone pine, five needles always grow together from one spot.
Its cones contain edible little nuts.
The spotted nutcracker hides the little nuts and so helps new Swiss stone pines to grow.
A Swiss stone pine can live to about 1,000 years.
Swiss stone pine wood is known for its fine scent.

abschnitte.text: The **Arve** is mostly called **Zirbelkiefer** or Zirbe in Austria and Germany. It is a kind of pine and grows in the Alps and the Carpathians. In Switzerland you find it mainly at high altitudes, often together with the larch. There it forms the uppermost forests at the **forest line**. The Swiss stone pine grows very slowly but can live to about **1,000 years**.

You can recognise the Swiss stone pine easily by its needles. They always grow in **fives** from one spot, like the fingers of a hand. In most other pines in Switzerland there are only two. The needles are soft and stay on the tree for several years. The Swiss stone pine **stands great cold well** and survives icy winters and short summers in the high mountains.

In the cones of the Swiss stone pine there are **edible little nuts**, also called stone pine nuts. The cones do not open by themselves. The **spotted nutcracker**, a bird of the crow family, hacks them open and hides the little nuts in the ground as a store. It finds many again, but not all. From the forgotten hiding places, young Swiss stone pines grow. In this way the bird helps the tree to spread.

**Swiss stone pine wood** is soft, easy to work and has a fine, spicy **scent** that lasts a long time. That is why in the mountains people liked to line whole rooms with it. An **Arvenstube** is a room whose walls and ceiling are clad with Swiss stone pine wood. Such rooms are well known, for example, from old Engadine houses. Furniture, beds and carvings are also made from Swiss stone pine wood.

gewusst: A single nutcracker can hide many thousands of stone pine nuts in one autumn.
The wood of the Swiss stone pine shows many small knots, which can be seen as dark dots in the wood.

teile.einleitung: Every day, roots bore a little deeper into the hard ground. So that their delicate tip is not damaged in the process, it wears a protective cap: the root cap. It also helps the root to tell down from up.
wichtigste: The root cap is a protective cap at the root tip.
It protects the dividing tissue behind it.
The technical term for the root cap is calyptra.
Its cells release mucilage so that the root slides more easily through the soil.
Statoliths in the root cap indicate the direction of gravity.
Growth in the direction of gravity is called gravitropism.

abschnitte.text: The **root cap** sits like a cap on the tip of every growing root. In technical language it is called the **calyptra**. The word comes from Greek and means covering or veil. Not only the main root but also every growing **lateral root** wears a root cap. A root system therefore has very many of them.

Directly behind the cap lies the **meristem**. There new cells divide constantly, and the root grows longer. This tissue is very sensitive. Without protection it would be damaged by hard grains of soil. The root cap pushes ahead like a shield and keeps the friction off.

The outer cells of the root cap form a **mucilage**. It acts like a **lubricant** between the root and the soil particles. Even so, the outer cells are constantly **scraped off** as the root pushes forward. From inside, **new cells** are formed all the time. In this way the cap always stays about the same size.

In the root cap lie heavy **starch grains**, the **statoliths**. They always sink to the bottom in the cells, like sand in a glass. By this the plant recognises the direction of **gravity**. Roots grow towards the pull of the Earth. This is called **positive gravitropism**, and it used to be called geotropism. If you lay a plant on its side, the root tip bends downwards again after a short time.

gewusst: Charles Darwin already studied in the 19th century how the root tip steers the direction of growth.
The mucilage of the root cap also feeds many soil bacteria around the root.

teile.einleitung: The martagon lily, called “Türkenbund” (Turk’s turban) in German, is a wild lily that grows in light woods and on mountain meadows. Its nodding, pink to purple flowers are reminiscent of a turban.
wichtigste: The martagon lily is a lily and usually grows 30 to 150 centimetres tall.
Its flowers hang downwards, and the petals are rolled far back.
It flowers pink to purplish red with dark spots.
Hawk-moths such as the hummingbird hawk-moth pollinate it, especially in the evening.
One stem can bear up to 20 flowers.
Because of its golden-yellow bulb it used to be called golden root.

abschnitte.text: The German name comes from the special shape of the flower. The petals are strongly **rolled back**. That makes the flower look like a **turban**, a wound headscarf. The stamens then hang freely downwards. The flowers **nod downwards** and hang on long stalks.

The martagon lily mostly flowers **pink to purplish red**. Dark spots sit on the petals. The plant usually grows **30 to 150 centimetres** tall. One stem often bears several flowers, and in sunny places there can be **up to 20**. The leaves stand in tiers around the stem. It flowers in summer.

The martagon lily smells strongest in the **evening** and at night. With this it attracts **hawk-moths**, a group of moths with a very long proboscis. A well-known example is the **hummingbird hawk-moth**. It hovers in the air in front of the flower and collects the nectar. In doing so it carries pollen from flower to flower.

The martagon lily likes cool, **half-shaded places** in light woods. In the mountains it also grows on **mountain meadows** and in tall herb communities. In Switzerland you can find it mainly in the Alps and the Jura. Because it has become rare, it should not be picked or dug up.

Under the ground, the martagon lily has a **golden-yellow bulb**. That is why it used to be called **golden root**. Some people even believed that you could make gold with it. Of course that never worked.

gewusst: The martagon lily belongs to the same genus as the large garden lilies.
A hummingbird hawk-moth can hover in the air in front of a flower like a hummingbird.

teile.einleitung: You can recognise the **weeping willow** at once by its long branches that hang down to the ground. It often stands by ponds, lakes and in parks. It originally comes from China.
wichtigste: The branches of the weeping willow hang down to the ground.
It belongs to the willows.
It originally comes from China.
Its leaves are long and narrow.
It is often planted at the edge of ponds and lakes.
It grows quickly, and a twig in damp soil often forms roots.

abschnitte.text: The weeping willow is a medium-sized tree with a broad crown. Its thin, flexible branches **hang down to the ground** and move even in a light wind. The **leaves** are **long and narrow**, green on top and paler underneath. In spring it comes into leaf early and glows light green. It belongs **to the willows**, like the goat willow or the white willow.

The weeping willow originally comes **from China**. Along trade routes it came west and later to Europe. Its scientific name is **Salix babylonica**, because it used to be wrongly believed to come from Babylon. Many weeping willows in our parks are crosses with other kinds of willow. They put up with winter better here.

Willows love damp soil. That is why weeping willows are often planted **at the edge of ponds and lakes**, where their branches reach down into the water. The weeping willow **grows quickly**. If you stick a willow twig into damp soil, **it often forms roots** and becomes a new tree. Willow wood is rather soft and light.

The hanging branches remind many people of mourning and **farewell**. That is how the tree got its name. In the past, weeping willows were often planted **in cemeteries**. Today you see them mainly in parks and gardens, for example on Swiss lakeside promenades. The weeping willow also often appears in poems and pictures.

gewusst: The bark of willows contains salicin, a substance from which remedies for pain and fever were once obtained.
Willow twigs are so flexible that baskets can be woven from them.

teile.einleitung: Plant cells are surrounded by a firm envelope, the cell wall. It gives the cell shape and support and is the reason why plants can stand upright although they have no skeleton.
wichtigste: The cell wall lies on the outside of the cell membrane of a plant cell.
It gives the cell firmness and a fixed shape.
The most important building material is cellulose, along with pectin and other substances.
The cell wall stops a cell from bursting when it takes up a lot of water.
Neighbouring cells are held together by the middle lamella.
Animal cells have no cell wall, only a cell membrane.
Fungi have cell walls made of chitin.

abschnitte.text: Every plant cell is surrounded by a thin **cell membrane**. Outside it lies the **cell wall**, a stable envelope. It supports the cell and gives it a firm shape. Under the microscope you see the cell walls as fine lines that separate the cells from one another like walls. Animal cells lack this wall, so they are softer and can change their shape more easily.

The most important building material of the cell wall is **cellulose**. These are long fibres made of sugar building blocks, arranged like a coarse net. In between lie other substances such as **pectin**. Between two neighbouring cells lies a thin cementing layer, the **middle lamella**, which glues the cells together. Pectin is known from the kitchen: it is used as a gelling agent when making jam and makes the jam set.

Plant cells take up water. In doing so, the cell contents press from inside against the wall, and this pressure is called **turgor**. The firm cell wall holds against it, which is why the cell does not burst. The pressure makes leaves and young stems firm. If water is lacking, the pressure falls and the plant lets its leaves hang. The cell wall itself is well permeable to water and dissolved substances, and the actual selection is made by the cell membrane.

In some parts of plants, the cell walls are greatly thickened. In **wood**, the substance **lignin** is also deposited, and the walls are said to **lignify**. That is why a tree trunk is so hard and can carry a heavy crown. Many lignified cells are dead in the end, but their firm walls remain as a framework and as tubes for water transport.

It is not only plants that have cell walls. **Fungi** also have a cell wall, but it is made of **chitin** instead of cellulose. Chitin is also found in the shell of insects. Many **bacteria** also have a cell wall, made again of a different substance. Animal cells, and with them the cells of humans, on the other hand, have no cell wall.

gewusst: Paper and cotton consist for the most part of cellulose, that is, of the building material of cell walls.
Cellulose is the most common natural substance from living things on Earth.
Humans cannot digest cellulose, but it helps digestion as dietary fibre.

teile.einleitung: A desert is an area where it hardly rains and so only very few plants grow. Deserts arise through very small amounts of precipitation over a long time. There are hot deserts such as the Sahara, but also icy cold deserts such as Antarctica.
wichtigste: Deserts arise through very small amounts of precipitation over a long time.
In deserts, usually less than 250 millimetres of precipitation fall per year.
The Sahara in North Africa is the largest hot desert on Earth.
The largest desert overall is Antarctica, a cold desert.
Only a small part of the deserts consists of sand dunes, and many are stony or gravel deserts.
Between day and night, the temperature in deserts often varies very strongly.
Plants and animals of the desert have special tricks to get by with little water.

abschnitte.text: A **desert** is an area with so little water that hardly any plants can grow. Usually less than 250 millimetres of rain fall there in a year, whereas in Switzerland it is in many places over 1,000 millimetres. Often, more water also evaporates than falls from the sky. A distinction is made between **hot deserts** and cold deserts.

Many hot deserts lie near the tropics, where sinking, dry air prevents clouds. Others lie in the **rain shadow** of high mountains that catch the rain. Areas far from the sea also get little precipitation, like the Gobi Desert in Asia. Cold ocean currents off the coast keep the Atacama in Chile and the Namib in Africa extremely dry.

The **Sahara** in North Africa, at about 9 million square kilometres, is the largest hot desert, more than 200 times as big as Switzerland. The Atacama in Chile is among the driest places on Earth, and in some spots it does not rain for years. The largest desert of all is **Antarctica**, because hardly any snow falls there. Other large deserts are the Arabian Desert, the Kalahari and the deserts of Australia.

Many people imagine deserts as endless sand dunes. But in the Sahara only about a fifth is covered with sand. Large areas are stony deserts of rock blocks or gravel deserts with small stones. By day it can become over 40 degrees hot, and at night it sometimes cools down to almost zero degrees, because no clouds hold the warmth.

The **dromedary** can get by for days without water and then drink a great deal in a short time. The desert fox, the fennec, loses heat through its large ears. Cacti in America store water in their thick stems and have spines instead of leaves. In an **oasis**, groundwater comes to the surface, and date palms grow there and people live.

With a south wind, **Saharan dust** is sometimes carried as far as Switzerland. Then the sky turns yellowish, and the snow in the Alps turns orange. In many countries, deserts are spreading through overuse and climate change, which is called **desertification**. About 10,000 to 5,000 years ago, by the way, the Sahara was green and full of lakes, giraffes and hippos.

begriffe.erklaerung: water that falls from the sky as rain, snow or hail
a place in the desert with water and plants
a hill of sand that the wind has piled up
the spread of deserts through drought and overuse
the dry side of a mountain range, where hardly any rain falls

gewusst: Antarctica counts as the largest desert on Earth, although it is almost entirely covered with ice.
When it does rain heavily in the desert, dried-up river valleys, the wadis, can turn into raging rivers within minutes.
Some sand dunes in the Sahara are higher than 150 metres.

teile.einleitung: Scavengers are animals that feed on carrion, that is, on dead animals. That sounds disgusting, but it is very important for nature. Scavengers are something like nature’s refuse collection.
wichtigste: Animals that feed on carrion are called scavengers.
Carrion is the flesh of dead animals.
Well-known scavengers are vultures, hyenas and ravens.
Beetles such as the burying beetle and many flies also live on carrion.
Scavengers prevent diseases from spreading from dead animals.
In Switzerland, the bearded vulture, a large scavenger, lives again.
Many scavengers also hunt living prey.

abschnitte.text: A scavenger is an animal that eats dead animals that it has not killed itself. Experts also say **necrophage**, which means corpse eater. Only a few animals eat nothing but carrion, and most eat it alongside other food. Foxes, wild boar and crows, for example, gladly take a dead animal if they find one.

Vultures are the best-known scavengers among the birds. They soar for hours high in the sky and spot dead animals with their sharp eyes. The **bearded vulture** even eats mainly bones, which it drops from above onto rocks so that they break. Ravens, kites and the African marabou stork also regularly look for carrion.

In Africa, **hyenas** are important scavengers, and with their strong jaws they can even crack bones. Hyenas, however, also hunt a great deal themselves. Here, it is mainly small animals that take care of dead mice and birds. The **burying beetle** buries small animal corpses and lays its eggs next to them so that the larvae have food.

Without scavengers, dead animals would lie around for a long time and decay. In the process, bacteria and diseases could spread. Scavengers clear up and make sure that the nutrients return to the **cycle of nature**. In the end, bacteria and fungi break down the last remains, so that the soil becomes fertile.

The bearded vulture had been wiped out in the Alps because it was wrongly thought to be a dangerous predator. Since 1991, young bearded vultures have been released in Switzerland, first in the Swiss National Park. Today several pairs breed again in the Swiss Alps. In summer, more and more **griffon vultures** from France and Spain also come to visit.

begriffe.erklaerung: The body of a dead animal.
The technical word for an animal that eats carrion.
The slow breaking down of dead tissue by bacteria and fungi.
Animals are brought into nature so that they live there again.

gewusst: Vultures often have a bare head so that their feathers do not get dirty while eating.
The stomach of vultures is so acidic that it kills many dangerous germs.
The bearded vulture can swallow whole bones and dissolve them in its stomach.

teile.einleitung: In winter, broadleaved trees look bare. But on their twigs the buds for the next spring are already sitting. These winter buds protect the new leaves and flowers and even give away which tree it is.
wichtigste: The buds for the next year are already formed in the summer before.
In a winter bud there is a fully formed shoot with leaves or flowers.
Bud scales protect the inside from cold and drying out.
From the buds you can recognise the tree species even without leaves.
The ash has black buds, and the beech long, pointed, brown ones.
Flower buds are usually thicker and rounder than leaf buds.

abschnitte.text: A tree forms its buds **already in the summer** of the previous year. In autumn and winter they wait ready on the twig. In every bud there is a small **shoot** with leaves or flowers, folded up tightly. In spring it only has to grow and unfold. That is why trees can turn green so quickly when it gets warm.

Most winter buds are wrapped in **bud scales**. These hard little leaves lie over one another like roof tiles. They protect the delicate inside from cold, drying out and animals. Some buds are also hairy or stuck together with resin. The big buds of the **horse chestnut**, for example, are shiny and sticky.

Every tree species has buds with its own shape and colour. The **ash** has velvety **black** buds, which is rare among our trees. The **beech** has long, thin, pointed and light brown buds, like small spears. In the **oak**, several buds sit close together in a **cluster** at the end of the twig. In this way you can identify trees even in winter.

On fruit trees there are two kinds of buds. **Flower buds** are thicker and rounder, and the flowers are inside them. **Leaf buds** are slimmer. An old custom uses the flower buds: on **4 December**, Saint Barbara’s Day, you cut, for example, cherry twigs and put them in water. In the warm living room these **Barbara branches** open by Christmas.

gewusst: Under a bud you often see a small scar: there a leaf hung in summer.
The bud right at the tip of a twig is called the terminal bud, and the others are called side buds.

teile.einleitung: The Zwetschge is a popular stone fruit that ripens in late summer. It is closely related to the plum. In Switzerland it is known especially from the Zwetschgenwähe, the plum tart.
wichtigste: The skin of a ripe Zwetschge is dark blue to violet.
The white coating is a natural layer of wax.
The flesh is yellowish.
The stone is flat and oblong.
The Zwetschge is closely related to the plum.
Here, Zwetschgen ripen in late summer.
Dried Zwetschgen are called Dörrzwetschgen.

abschnitte.text: The **Zwetschge** is an oblong fruit with a **dark blue to violet** skin. Often there is a **white coating** on it that you can wipe off. This is a **natural layer of wax** that protects the fruit from drying out. The flesh is **yellowish** and juicy. In the middle lies a **flat, oblong stone**, which in ripe fruits can usually be removed easily.

The Zwetschge is closely related to the **plum**. Botanically both belong to the same species, and the Zwetschge is a subspecies of it. Plums are mostly rounder and softer, and their stone comes away less easily. Zwetschge trees, like cherries and apricots, are among the **stone fruit trees** of the rose family. They flower white in spring.

Here, Zwetschgen are ripe in **late summer**, from August to September depending on the variety. Ripe fruits feel slightly soft and come away well from the twig. In Switzerland, Zwetschgen are grown in many orchards. You eat them fresh or make them into cakes, compote and jam.

A classic of Swiss cooking is the **Zwetschgenwähe**, a flat tart with halved Zwetschgen on a base of dough. Dried fruits are called **Dörrzwetschgen**. They keep for a long time and are a sweet store for the winter. A schnapps is also distilled from Zwetschgen, the Zwetschgenwasser. In southern Germany and Austria, people like to bake Zwetschgenknödel, plum dumplings.

gewusst: Dried Zwetschgen contain a lot of fibre and stimulate digestion.
You do not eat the stone of a Zwetschge: in the kernel there are substances that can be harmful in larger amounts.

teile.einleitung: In the 1980s, many people in Switzerland and Germany were greatly worried about the forest. People spoke of “Waldsterben”, forest dieback. The fear led to stricter environmental laws and cleaner air.
wichtigste: At the start of the 1980s, many trees showed thin crowns and yellowed needles.
Air pollution was seen as the main cause.
Sulphur and nitrogen oxides made the rain acidic.
Sulphur dioxide arose mainly from burning coal and heavy heating oil.
For new petrol cars, the catalytic converter became compulsory in Switzerland.
The forest has not died off over large areas.
With the Sanasilva programme, Switzerland observes the tree crowns.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the **1980s** it was noticed that many trees had **thin crowns** and **yellowed needles**. People feared that large parts of the forest could die within a few years. The word **Waldsterben** was on everyone’s lips. Newspapers, television and politics dealt intensively with it.

The main cause was seen as **air pollution**. Exhaust gases from industry, heating and traffic burdened the air heavily. In the burning of sulphurous coal and heavy heating oil, **sulphur dioxide** arises. Together with **nitrogen oxides** from engines, it forms acids with water. This **acid rain** can acidify soils and weaken plants.

Switzerland reacted with stricter laws. With the **Ordinance on Air Pollution Control**, with exhaust filters and low-sulphur fuels, pollutants fell clearly. For new petrol cars, the **catalytic converter** was made compulsory at the end of the 1980s. It converts toxic exhaust gases such as nitrogen oxides into less harmful substances. Above all the sulphur dioxide in the air fell sharply.

The Swiss forest has **not died off over large areas**. In some places it is damaged, but the forecasts of the time were too gloomy. Experts say today that several causes work together: pollutants, drought, pests and storms. But the debate achieved a lot, because the air became cleaner as a result.

Since the 1980s, Switzerland has observed the condition of the forest with the programme **Sanasilva**. The name means roughly “healthy forest”. Experts regularly assess how densely the **crowns of the trees** are covered in leaves. In this way you can see whether the forest is doing better or worse. Today it is mainly heat and **drought** through climate change that cause new worries.

gewusst: The German word “Waldsterben” became so well known that it was partly taken over in France as a foreign word: “le Waldsterben”.
Acid rain harmed not only trees but also lakes, fish and buildings made of sandstone.

teile.einleitung: A meadow is an open area on which mainly grasses and flowers grow. In summer there is humming, chirping and crawling everywhere in it. In Switzerland there are meadows from the Central Plateau up high into the Alps.
wichtigste: A meadow is a grassy area that is mown regularly.
A meadow on which cows graze is called a pasture.
The daisy is a small white flower with a yellow centre that often grows in lawns and meadows.
The grasshopper chirps loudly on the meadow in summer.
The mole digs tunnels under the meadow and makes molehills.
Poor, lightly fertilised meadows are especially rich in species.
Without mowing or grazing, most meadows in Switzerland would turn into forest over time.

abschnitte.text: A **meadow** is an area with grasses and herbs that is mown by people. The mown grass is often dried and stored as hay for the animals in winter. If an area is instead grazed by cows, sheep or horses, it is called a **pasture**. In the mountains, the pastures are called alpine pastures in summer.

On meadows grow many grasses such as cock’s-foot and meadow foxtail. In between flower dandelion, clover, buttercup, oxeye daisies and meadow clary. The **daisy** likes to grow especially in short-mown lawns and closes its flowers at night and in rain. Many meadow plants have deep roots and sprout again quickly after mowing.

In summer you hear **grasshoppers** chirping everywhere, and the males use it to attract the females. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies visit the flowers and pollinate them. Under the ground the **mole** digs long tunnels and pushes the soil up as heaps. There it eats mainly earthworms and insect larvae, and it does not touch plants.

A **fertilised meadow** is heavily fertilised and mown several times a year, and it supplies a lot of fodder. But there only a few strong plant species grow, such as dandelion and ryegrass. A **lean meadow** is hardly fertilised and mown only once or twice. On it, over 50 different plant species can grow, including orchids and gentians.

Meadows and pastures cover a large part of the Swiss farmland and are the basis for milk and cheese. Many species-rich dry meadows and flower meadows have disappeared since 1900. Today the Confederation protects the most valuable ones as **dry meadows** of national importance. Farmers receive payments if they mow meadows late and fertilise little, so that flowers and insects survive.

In most areas of Switzerland, forest would slowly arise without mowing and grazing. First shrubs would come, then young trees. Only through the work of farmers over centuries did the colourful meadows arise. Whoever makes a flower meadow in their own garden helps wild bees and butterflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: a grassy area on which animals such as cows or sheep graze
dried grass that serves as winter food for animals
a lightly fertilised meadow with many different flowers
the transfer of pollen so that seeds can form

gewusst: Grasshoppers hear with ears that sit on their legs or on their body.
A mole can dig many metres of new tunnels in a day.
The daisy flowers almost all year round, even on mild winter days.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes a whole new plant can grow from a single leaf. This is due to an astonishing ability of many plant cells: **totipotency**. Nurseries and laboratories use it to propagate plants.
wichtigste: A totipotent plant cell can give rise to a whole plant.
Specialised cells can dedifferentiate and divide again.
In tissue cultures, a disorganised mass of cells forms, the callus.
Gottlieb Haberlandt predicted in 1902 that this is possible.
Frederick C. Steward showed it in the 1950s with carrot cells.
A lot of cytokinin in relation to auxin encourages the formation of shoots.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Latin: “totus” means whole, “potentia” means ability. A **totipotent** cell can therefore form a **whole plant** with roots, stem and leaves. In plants, many fully grown cells keep this ability. Cells that can form many, but not all, cell types are called **pluripotent**.

In a plant, most cells have a fixed job, for example as a leaf cell or a root cell. They are said to be **differentiated**. Under certain conditions they can give up this specialisation and **become able to divide again**. This is called **dedifferentiation**. That is why a whole new plant can grow from a **leaf cutting** of an **African violet**.

In **tissue culture**, small pieces of plant are placed on a nutrient medium with sugar, salts and plant hormones. There a disorganised mass of cells grows first, the **callus**. With the hormones **cytokinin** and **auxin**, you control what becomes of it. A high ratio of cytokinin to auxin encourages the formation of **shoots**, while a lot of auxin tends to encourage roots. That way, for example, orchids or virus-free potatoes can be propagated in large numbers.

The Austrian botanist **Gottlieb Haberlandt** predicted as early as **1902** that isolated plant cells in culture could develop into whole plants. At that time, however, he did not manage to do it himself. In the **1950s**, the researcher **Frederick C. Steward** showed with cells from the **carrot** that it really works. Complete carrot plants grew from single cells.

gewusst: Plants propagated in this way from parts of a single mother plant are clones, that is, almost identical in their genes.
Haberlandt is regarded as the father of plant tissue culture.

teile.einleitung: In **grafting**, gardeners put a piece of a good variety onto another plant with roots. The two parts grow together. This is how fruit trees, roses and vines in particular are propagated.
wichtigste: The part put on is called the scion, the plant with roots the rootstock.
The cambium of both parts must touch so that they grow together.
In budding, a single bud is put into a T-shaped cut in the bark.
In whip grafting, parts of equal thickness are cut at a slant and joined.
The rootstock M9 gives small apple trees that bear fruit early.
Because of phylloxera, European vines are grafted onto American rootstocks.

abschnitte.text: The **scion** comes from the desired variety, for example a particular apple. The **rootstock** supplies the roots. It influences how strongly the tree grows and how robust it is. For the two parts to grow together, their **cambium** must touch. This is a thin, dividing layer of tissue under the bark.

In **budding**, only a single bud is put into a T-shaped cut in the bark. In German the name comes from the Latin oculus for eye, because the bud is also called an eye. In **whip grafting**, you cut rootstock and scion of equal thickness with slanting cuts of equal length. Then you lay them exactly on top of each other and bind them tightly.

Apple trees are mostly **heterozygous** and are pollinated by other trees. A little tree from a pip therefore differs clearly from the parent variety. A variety such as “Gala” would not be kept that way. That is why varieties are grafted. The rootstock **M9** comes from East Malling in England. It slows growth, so small trees arise that bear fruit early.

In the late 19th century, **phylloxera** was brought into Europe. It destroyed the roots of European vines. American vine roots are largely resistant. Since then, European varieties have been grafted onto **American rootstocks**. This also applies to many vineyards in Switzerland.
The graft union of a fruit tree is placed above the ground. If it lies in the soil, the scion can form roots of its own. Then the influence of the rootstock is lost, for example the weak growth.

gewusst: Several apple varieties can be grafted onto a single tree.
Almost all vines in Europe today stand on American roots.

t1dk6xhi.t: WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF

teile.einleitung: The **WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF** studies snow, avalanches and permafrost. It has its seat in **Davos** in the canton of Graubünden. In winter it publishes the avalanche bulletin for Switzerland.
wichtigste: The SLF has its seat in Davos in the canton of Graubünden.
The avalanche bulletin appears every day in winter at 5 pm.
The European Avalanche Danger Scale has five levels.
Most fatal avalanche accidents happen at level 3, considerable.
The IMIS network supplies data from high-mountain stations.
On the Weissfluhjoch lies the SLF’s long-established test site.

abschnitte.text: The SLF belongs to the **WSL**, the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research. It has its seat in **Davos**. Above Davos, on the **Weissfluhjoch**, lies its long-established test site. The snowpack has been measured there for decades. It is among the oldest snow measuring sites in the high mountains.

In winter the SLF publishes the **avalanche bulletin** every day at **5 pm**. If needed, it is updated in the morning at 8 am. It uses the **European Avalanche Danger Scale** with five levels: low, moderate, considerable, high and very high. Most fatal accidents of snow sports enthusiasts happen at **level 3, considerable**. Then many people are out, and the danger is often underestimated.

In accidents, the **slab avalanche** is the most common kind of avalanche. In it, a connected slab of snow breaks away over an area. It glides off on a weak layer. Often it is triggered by winter sports enthusiasts themselves. To find such layers, the snowpack is examined, for example with the **ram penetrometer**. It is driven into the snow with a falling weight, and its resistance shows hard and soft layers.

For the bulletin, the SLF uses data from the **IMIS** network. This stands for Intercantonal Measurement and Information System. Automatic stations in the high mountains measure snow depth, wind and temperature. The SLF is also involved in the **PERMOS** measuring network, which observes **permafrost** over the long term. Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all year round.

gewusst: At danger levels 4 and 5, fewer fatal accidents happen, because most people then do without tours.
Besides PERMOS for permafrost, Switzerland has the GLAMOS measuring network for glaciers.

teile.einleitung: The tundra is a treeless, cold landscape in the far north. The winter is long and dark, the summer short, and the ground stays frozen at depth all year round.
wichtigste: In the tundra it is too cold and the summer too short for trees.
Mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs grow there.
Under the surface lies permanently frozen ground, the permafrost.
Reindeer move through the tundra in large herds, in North America they are called caribou.
The Arctic fox has a white coat in winter.
In summer in the far north, the sun does not set for days on end.

abschnitte.text: The tundra lies north of the great coniferous forests, the **taiga**. There it is cold for a very long time, and the summer lasts only a few weeks. Trees have too little time to grow. In between lies the **forest tundra**, where only single, low and crooked trees stand. Further north the open tundra begins.

In the tundra only low plants grow that can cope with cold and a short growing season. Typical are **mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs**. Dwarf willows and dwarf birches hardly grow knee-high. Flat on the ground, they are protected from the icy wind. In the short summer the tundra often blooms in many colours.

Under the tundra lies the **permafrost**, ground that stays permanently frozen. In summer only the top layer thaws, the **active layer**. The water cannot drain down into the depths. That is why the ground is often wet despite little precipitation, and there are many **marshes and pools**. On a slope, the wet layer slowly slides downhill, which is called **solifluction**.

The best-known animals are the **reindeer**, which migrate in large herds. In North America they are called **caribou**. The **Arctic fox** has a white coat in winter and is well camouflaged in the snow. Other residents are lemmings, mountain hares and musk oxen. In summer many **migratory birds** come here to breed.

In summer in the far north, the sun does not set for days on end. This is called the **midnight sun**. In winter it is the other way round: then it stays dark for weeks, which is the **polar night**. In the Alps, too, above the tree line there is a similar landscape, called **alpine tundra**.

gewusst: If the permafrost thaws because of warming, houses and roads can sink.
Well-preserved mammoth remains have already been found in the frozen ground of the tundra.

teile.einleitung: Many plants and animals are taken by humans to new areas. Only a small part of them later becomes a problem. The tens rule is a rule of thumb that roughly describes how many introduced species make it through each stage up to an invasive species.
wichtigste: Mark Williamson and Alastair Fitter made the tens rule well known in the 1990s.
According to the rule, about one in ten species gets through each stage.
Of 1,000 introduced species, about 10 become permanently established.
Of 1,000 introduced species, about 1 becomes an invasive pest.
The transition rates lie roughly between 5 and 20 per cent.
In vertebrates the rates are far higher, at about 50 per cent.
The tens rule is a statistical rule of thumb.

abschnitte.text: The **tens rule** comes from **Mark Williamson** and **Alastair Fitter**. They published their analyses in **1996**, building on older observations by Williamson. The rule sums up how many introduced species get from one stage to the next. At each step roughly **one in ten species** makes it.

First a species is **introduced**, for example as a garden plant. If it turns up in nature without staying, it is called **casual**. After that follows **establishment**: the species reproduces permanently without human help. The last stage is the **invasive** species, which causes damage. Only a small part of the species reach this stage.

Of **1,000** introduced species, about 10 per cent turn up in the wild, which is **100**. Of these, in turn, about 10 per cent become established, that is **10** species. Of these, again about one in ten becomes harmful. At the end **1** invasive species is left. As a calculation: 1,000 times 0.1 times 0.1 times 0.1 makes 1.

The ten is only an **average**. Williamson and Fitter gave values for the individual transitions between about **5 and 20 per cent**. So the rule is a **statistical rule of thumb** from many observations.
