For individual groups the rate can differ greatly. **Jeschke and Strayer** found in 2005, for **vertebrates** between Europe and North America, transition rates of about 50 per cent per stage.

In Switzerland, too, there are introduced plants that spread strongly. They are called **invasive neophytes**. Well-known examples are **Himalayan balsam**, **Japanese knotweed** and **Canadian goldenrod**. They crowd out native plants. For some such species, bans apply in Switzerland, and they may, for example, no longer be sold.

gewusst: Many invasive plants originally came as pretty ornamental plants in gardens.
Although only few species become invasive, these few can cause great damage.

teile.einleitung: The Zopf is a plaited bread made of yeast dough with butter and milk. In Switzerland it traditionally belongs to the Sunday breakfast. In Bern it is called Züpfe.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, Zopf is traditionally eaten on Sunday for breakfast.
The Zopf dough contains butter and milk, which are missing in a plain bread.
Yeast makes the dough rise.
The Zopf is plaited from strands of dough.
Before baking, it is brushed with egg so that it shines.
In Bernese German it is called Züpfe.

abschnitte.text: In many Swiss families the **Zopf** belongs to the **Sunday breakfast**. You eat it with butter and jam, with honey or with cheese. It is soft, slightly sweet and has a shiny, golden-brown crust. Because it used to be more expensive than ordinary bread, it was eaten mainly at weekends and on feast days. In Bern it is called **Züpfe**, in other regions simply Zopf.

For a Zopf you need flour, **milk**, **butter**, salt, a little sugar and **yeast**. Butter and milk make the dough soft and tasty, and in a plain bread they are missing. Yeast is a **raising agent**: it consists of tiny fungi that form gas in the warm dough. As a result the dough rises and becomes airy. You knead it well and let it rest for a while.

The Zopf gets its shape because **strands of dough are plaited**. You roll the dough into long strands and lay them over and under one another, often with two strands, sometimes with more. The name comes from a **plaited hairstyle**, which is also called Zopf. Before baking, the Zopf is brushed with **egg**. In this way it gets its beautiful shine and its golden colour.

From a similar sweet yeast dough, the **Grittibänz** is baked in Switzerland for **St Nicholas Day** on 6 December. This is a figure in human shape, often with raisins as eyes. In other countries, too, there are plaited breads, for example the Hefezopf in Germany. Zopf also freezes well and can be made the next day into Fotzelschnitten.

gewusst: A Zopf that is left over from Sunday is often made into Fotzelschnitten, that is, slices of bread fried in egg and milk.
In some regions the Grittibänz is also known under the name Grättimaa.

teile.einleitung: The Scots pine is an undemanding conifer. In Switzerland it is mostly called the Föhre or forest Föhre. You can recognise it easily by its orange-red bark at the top of the trunk.
wichtigste: In the Scots pine, two needles always stand together.
The needles are blue-green, about 4 to 7 cm long and often slightly twisted.
At the top of the trunk the bark is fox-red to orange, and below it is grey and cracked.
In Switzerland the tree is mostly called the Föhre.
It also grows on dry, poor soil.
The Scots pine is a light-demanding tree and needs a lot of sun.
The Pfynwald in the Valais is one of the largest pine forests of the Alps.

abschnitte.text: In the Scots pine, **two needles** always grow together from one spot. At the bottom a small sheath holds them together. The needles are blue-green, about 4 to 7 centimetres long and often **slightly twisted**. The cones are small and cone-shaped. When they are ripe, their scales open and the winged seeds fly away.

At the top of the trunk and on the branches the bark is **fox-red to orange**. At the bottom of the trunk it turns grey, thick and cracked. Older Scots pines lose their lower branches. That is why they often have a **long bare trunk** and an umbrella-like crown at the top. In this way you can recognise them from far away.

The Scots pine is very **undemanding**. It also grows where the soil is dry, sandy or stony. With its roots it can reach deep into the ground. It is a **light-demanding tree**: in the shade of other trees it grows badly. That is why you often find it in places where other trees struggle.

In Switzerland the Scots pine is mostly called the **Föhre** or forest Föhre. A particularly well-known pine forest is the **Pfynwald** in the Valais. It lies between Leuk and Sierre and is one of the largest pine forests of the Alps. In Switzerland, pines also grow in the Jura, on dry slopes and in the Alpine valleys.

gewusst: The Scots pine is one of the most widespread conifers in the world, from Europe far into Asia.
From the resin of pines, people used to obtain turpentine and rosin, which violin players need for their bows.

teile.einleitung: Plants cannot walk. For their seeds to reach new places all the same, many use the wind. With wings, hairs or little parachutes the seeds sail away. This kind of spreading is called wind dispersal.
wichtigste: The technical term for spreading by the wind is anemochory.
Seeds that the wind spreads are usually very light.
Maple fruits are called “Nasenzwicker” in German and spin like a propeller.
Lime fruits hang from a wing-like bract.
Poplars let white seed fluff fly in early summer.
Spruce seeds ripen in cones and have a small wing.
In dry, windy weather the seeds fly furthest.

abschnitte.text: The spreading of seeds by the wind is called **anemochory**. The Greek word “anemos” means wind, and “chorein” means to move on. Such seeds are usually **very light**, so that the wind can lift them and carry them far. They fly best in **dry, windy weather**. Damp seeds are heavier and tend to stay lying.

The fruits of the **maple** have wings. When they fall from the tree, they spin like a propeller and sink slowly. Children split them open and stick them on their nose as a **“Nasenzwicker”**, a nose pincher. The **lime** hangs its round fruits from a narrow **bract** that acts like a wing. The **birch** forms very many tiny fruits with small wings.

Other seeds have fine hairs. The **poplar** lets white seed fluff fly in early summer, which looks like cotton wool or snow. The **dandelion** and the **thistle** have seeds with small **hair parachutes**. The wind carries them away like parachutes. In the dandelion, the ball of many such seeds is called a dandelion clock.

In the **spruce**, the seeds ripen in the **cones**. Each seed has a thin wing. In dry weather the cone scales open, and the seeds sail away. In rain the scales close again. In this way the seeds are released when they can fly well.

Directly under the mother plant it is crowded and shady. There the young plants would have little **room and light**. Further away they find better conditions. In addition, plants can in this way **settle new places**, such as a fresh clearing in the forest or an area of gravel. That is why birches are often seen as the first trees on fallow land.

gewusst: Orchids have seeds so tiny that they float through the air almost like dust.
A single large tree can form many thousands of winged seeds in a year.

teile.einleitung: Tulips are popular spring flowers with large, bright blooms. They grow from a bulb and originally come from Asia.
wichtigste: Tulip bulbs are planted in autumn and flower in spring.
Wild tulips come from the mountains of Central Asia.
A simple tulip has six petals in two circles.
The Netherlands is famous for its huge tulip fields.
Around 1637, a rare tulip bulb in Holland cost as much as a house.
In the Upper Valais grows the rare Grengiols tulip.

abschnitte.text: The tulip grows from a **bulb**. In it the plant stores nutrients for the next year. The bulbs are put into the ground in **autumn**. They need the **cold of winter** to flower in spring. After flowering, the plant draws its strength back into the bulb.

A simple tulip has **six petals**. They stand in two circles of three. Tulips come in very many colours: red, yellow, white, pink, purple and almost black. A **true, pure blue** has still not been bred. Cut tulips **keep growing in the vase**, and their stems get a few centimetres longer.

Wild tulips originally grow in **Asia**, for example in the mountains of Central Asia. In the Ottoman Empire, in what is now Turkey, they were very popular. From there they came to Europe in the 16th century. The name “tulip” comes from an old word for **turban**, because the flower is reminiscent of this headwear.

In Holland in the 17th century, tulips became a real craze. Rare varieties with flame-patterned flowers were in hot demand. Around **1637**, people paid as much for a single especially rare bulb as for a house. Then prices suddenly collapsed. This period is called **tulip mania**. To this day the **Netherlands** is famous for its colourful tulip fields and sells tulips all over the world.
In Switzerland too there is a very special tulip. The **Grengiols tulip** grows only near Grengiols in the **Upper Valais**. It is very rare. That is why it is protected and must not be picked.

gewusst: The flame patterns of the expensive tulips of tulip mania were caused by a plant virus.
Tulips often turn their flowers towards the light and close them again in the evening.

teile.einleitung: A trophic mismatch arises when an animal species needs its food most urgently at exactly the time when it is no longer most plentiful. Climate change can make such shifts in timing stronger.
wichtigste: Mismatch means roughly “not fitting together”.
What is meant is a decoupling in time between the need for food and the supply of food.
The idea comes from the British fisheries biologist David Cushing.
A textbook example is the pied flycatcher in the Netherlands.
Many migratory birds go by day length, plants and insects rather by temperature.
Reindeer in Greenland and wild bees can also be affected.

abschnitte.text: Many animals raise their young when there is the most food. But if predators and prey react differently to changes, the **peak of the food supply** no longer coincides with the time of greatest need. Then, for example, food is missing for the young birds. This decoupling in time is called a **trophic mismatch**.

The **match-mismatch hypothesis** was originally formulated by the British fisheries biologist **David Cushing**. He wanted to explain why some year classes of fish are strong and others weak. What matters, he suggested, is whether the larvae hatch at the time of the **plankton bloom**. Then they find enough food.

A well-studied example is the chain **oak, winter moth caterpillar, great tit**. The budburst of the oak determines when the caterpillars hatch. The tits need many caterpillars at exactly that time for their nestlings. With warming, these dates shift by different amounts. In the Netherlands the **pied flycatcher** became the textbook example: it returns from West Africa when the caterpillar peak may already be over.

abschnitte.titel: Why migratory birds are especially affected
abschnitte.text: Many migratory birds set off according to **day length**, and this does not change with the climate. Plants and insects, on the other hand, react more strongly to **temperature**. Long-distance migrants in winter quarters south of the Sahara cannot sense how early spring begins in Europe. Short-distance migrants can adjust their return more easily.

In West Greenland, plant growth began earlier because of warming. But the calves of the **reindeer** were not born correspondingly earlier and missed the most nutritious food. A mismatch also threatens between **early flowering plants and wild bees**: if plants flower too early, the pollinators are missing, and the bees find less food later.

gewusst: The numbers of the pied flycatcher fell most where the caterpillar peak came especially early.
Some bird species have already moved their breeding season forward somewhat in recent decades.

teile.einleitung: The growing season is the time of year in which plants can grow, flower and form seeds. In the high mountains it is much shorter than on the Central Plateau, and plants have developed special tricks.
wichtigste: The growing season is the time with enough warmth and light for plant growth.
In the alpine zone it lasts only about two to three months.
For every 100 metres of climb, it gets about 0.5 to 0.7 degrees cooler on average.
Almost all high-mountain plants are perennial.
Many form their flower buds as early as the previous year.
First frosts and snowfalls often end the growing season as early as September.

abschnitte.text: Plants need **warmth and light** to grow. The time of year in which both are enough is called the **growing season**. On the Central Plateau it lasts many months. In the high mountains, on the other hand, snow lies for a long time, and frost returns early. In the **alpine zone**, therefore, only about **two to three months** are left for growing, flowering and forming seeds.

With increasing height the air becomes cooler. On average the temperature falls by about **0.5 to 0.7 degrees per 100 metres**. In addition the snow melts later up high. That is why the warm season begins much later at altitude. The **dandelion** on an alpine pasture therefore flowers only weeks after the dandelion in the valley. And as early as **September**, first frosts and snowfalls can end the growing season.

Alpine plants have to be quick. Many form their **flower buds as early as the previous year**, in the late summer before. In spring they only have to open them. In addition, many plants store **sugar and starch** in roots or underground shoots in late summer. With this they can start growing straight after the snow melts.

An annual plant has to germinate, grow, flower and form seeds in a single summer. In the short mountain summer this rarely succeeds. That is why almost all high-mountain plants are **perennial** and live for many years. Because it is uncertain whether enough seeds will ripen, many also reproduce by **runners, bulbils or offshoots**.

After the short summer, the plants rest until the next year. The snow acts like a **warm blanket**. Under it, it is less cold than in the icy air above. With climate change, the growing season is getting longer in many areas, because the snow melts earlier.

gewusst: The alpine snowbell can even push its flower through a thin layer of snow.
Some Alpine plants live for many decades, even though they are only a few centimetres tall.

teile.einleitung: A trophic cascade arises when a predator has an effect across several steps of the food chain. If it eats plant eaters, the plants can increase as a result.
wichtigste: In a trophic cascade, a predator acts indirectly all the way down to the plants.
A well-known example: the return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996.
The main prey of these wolves is elk.
When predators control the system, it is called top-down control.
Even the fear of predators changes the behaviour of prey animals.
In biomanipulation, predatory fish are introduced to make lakes clearer.

abschnitte.text: You can imagine a food chain like a staircase. If something changes at the top, you feel it further down. An example from the meadow: spiders eat grasshoppers, grasshoppers eat grass. If the **spiders** increase, there are fewer or more cautious grasshoppers, and the **grass** increases. This domino effect is called a **trophic cascade**.

In Yellowstone National Park in the USA, wolves were missing for about 70 years. In **1995 and 1996**, wolves from Canada were reintroduced there. Their main prey is **elk**, a large kind of deer. Fewer elk and more cautious behaviour can take pressure off the plants along the banks. How strong this effect is, is still debated among experts today.

Predators do not only act by eating prey. Even their presence changes where and for how long prey animals feed. This is called the **landscape of fear**. Dangerous places are avoided, and plants can grow better there. In Swiss mountain forests, it is expected that wolves keep red deer and roe deer on the move and that in some places fewer **young trees are browsed** as a result.

Ecologists distinguish two kinds of control. In **top-down control**, predators at the top determine the size of the lower levels. In **bottom-up control**, nutrients and plants limit the whole system. The **green world hypothesis** of 1960 says: the world is green because predators keep the plant eaters in check.

Knowledge about cascades is also put to use. In **biomanipulation**, predatory fish such as **pike** are introduced into lakes. They eat small fish that feed on zooplankton. As a result the **zooplankton** grows, which in turn eats algae. The water can become clearer in this way.

gewusst: A famous example from the sea: sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. Where sea otters live, dense kelp forests often grow.
The green world hypothesis comes from the researchers Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin.

teile.einleitung: Among the flowering plants, two large groups are distinguished by the number of seed leaves. Dicotyledons form two seed leaves on germinating. They include, for example, dandelion, bean, rose and oak.
wichtigste: Dicotyledons form two seed leaves on germinating, called cotyledons in technical language.
Their leaves mostly have net-like venation.
The flower parts are often arranged in fours or fives.
A taproot with lateral roots is typical.
A cambium ring allows trees such as beech and oak to grow thicker.
In the modern system, the eudicots largely replace the old group.

abschnitte.text: When a seed germinates, the **seed leaves** appear first. In technical language they are called **cotyledons**. In the **dicotyledons** there are two, which is why the group is also called **dicots**. In the bean you can see the two thick seed leaves well. The other large group are the **monocotyledons** with only one seed leaf, which include grasses, cereals, lilies and orchids.

Dicotyledons often have leaves with **net-like venation**: the leaf veins branch like a net. In monocotyledons they mostly run parallel. In many dicotyledons the flower parts are arranged **in fours or fives**, for example five petals in the rose. Underground they often have a **taproot with lateral roots**, whereas grasses form many fibrous roots of equal thickness.

In the stems of dicotyledons, the vascular bundles lie in a ring. Between the wood part, the **xylem**, and the sieve part, the **phloem**, lies a layer capable of dividing, the **cambium**. It forms new cells every year. In this way trees such as **beech** or **oak** can **grow thicker** every year, and annual rings arise. Most monocotyledons cannot do this.

Today we know from genetic comparisons that the old dicotyledons are not a single natural group. That is why in the modern system they are largely replaced by the **eudicots**, the “true dicotyledons”. They can be recognised by their pollen: the pollen grains have **three germination furrows** and are called **tricolpate**. The great majority of all flowering plants belong to the eudicots.

Very many well-known plants belong to the dicotyledons: **dandelion**, sunflower, rose, apple, bean, potato, stinging nettle and almost all broadleaved trees such as beech, oak and maple. On a Swiss meadow, a large part of the flowers are dicotyledons, whereas the grasses belong to the monocotyledons.

gewusst: Cacti also belong to the dicotyledons, although they often have no true leaves.
The seed leaves often look quite different from the later foliage leaves of the plant.

teile.einleitung: Even hard rocks do not stay the same for ever. Water, ice, warmth and living things slowly break up the rock. This process is called **weathering**.
wichtigste: In frost shattering, water freezes in cracks and bursts the rock apart.
Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes.
In the Alps, frost weathering is especially important.
Water with carbonic acid slowly dissolves limestone.
In biological weathering, roots, for example, burst rocks apart.
At the foot of rock faces, stones collect into scree slopes.
From weathered rock, sand, silt and clay arise for the soil.

abschnitte.text: Water penetrates fine cracks in the rock. When it freezes, ice needs more room than water. The volume increases by about **9 per cent**. The ice pushes the crack apart and bursts the rock. This is called **frost shattering**. In the high mountains of the **Alps** it freezes and thaws very often, so frost weathering is especially important there.

In deserts it is very hot by day and cold at night. Rock expands in heat and contracts in cold. These stresses make the surface flake off over time. This is **temperature weathering**. Together with frost shattering it belongs to **physical weathering**, in which rock is only broken up.

Rainwater takes up **carbon dioxide** from the air and so becomes slightly acidic. This water with **carbonic acid** slowly dissolves limestone. In this way, for example, **caves** and karren arise, which are grooves in limestone mountains. In Switzerland such forms are found, for example, in the Jura and in the limestone Alps.
Plants and animals also weather rock. Growing **roots** push cracks open and so burst rocks apart. **Lichens** attack the rock surface. This is called **biological weathering**.

Through weathering, stones break out of rock faces and fall down. At the foot of the wall they collect into a **scree slope**. Over time the rock breaks down into ever smaller grains: **sand**, **silt** and **clay**. Together with **humus** from dead plants, they form the soil.

gewusst: Without weathering there would be no soil in which plants could grow.
Large stalactite caves were formed by water that dissolved limestone over a very long time.

teile.einleitung: Dutch elm disease is a tree disease that has killed millions of elms in Europe. It is caused by a fungus that small beetles carry from tree to tree.
wichtigste: Dutch elm disease is caused by sac fungi of the genus Ophiostoma.
Elm bark beetles transmit the fungal spores from sick to healthy trees.
The fungus blocks the water pipes in the wood, and the leaves wilt.
The first big wave began around 1920 in Europe.
In the 1960s a more aggressive form came from North America.
In Switzerland the wych elm is the most common kind of elm.

abschnitte.text: Dutch elm disease is caused by **sac fungi** of the genus **Ophiostoma**. They penetrate the wood of the elms. The tree tries to stop the fungus and seals off its **conducting channels**. As a result, no more water reaches the crown. The leaves wilt and turn brown. Many infected trees die within a short time.

The fungus is carried from tree to tree by **elm bark beetles**. They breed under the bark of sick or dead elms. The young beetles take **fungal spores** with them. When they later feed on healthy elms, they infect them. That is how the disease spreads quickly.

People often speak of **Dutch elm disease**, although it did not come from the Netherlands. In the 1920s, however, Dutch researchers found out that a fungus causes the disease. They were **Bea Schwarz** and **Christine Buisman**. That is where the name comes from.

Shortly after the First World War, the first sick elms were noticed in France and the Netherlands. Around **1920** the first big wave began in Europe. In the **1960s**, a new, much **more aggressive fungus** reached Great Britain with timber deliveries from Canada. This second wave killed millions of elms in Europe. In many landscapes, large, old elms almost completely disappeared.

Three kinds of elm are native to Switzerland. The most widespread is the **wych elm**, which grows in damp, cool ravine and slope forests. Less common are the **field elm** and the **European white elm**. You can recognise elms by their fruits: the seed sits in the middle of a **round, flat wing**. That way the wind carries the fruits far away.

gewusst: Young elms often only become sick when they are bigger. That is why there are still many young elms, but only a few old ones.
Researchers are breeding elms that are less susceptible to the disease.

teile.einleitung: Sugar cane is a very tall grass from warm countries. In its stem it stores sweet sap from which sugar is made. Worldwide, most of the sugar comes from sugar cane.
wichtigste: Sugar cane is grown in the tropics and subtropics.
It is a grass and grows about 3 to 6 metres tall.
It stores the sugar in the stem.
Brazil harvests the most sugar cane worldwide.
In Brazil, ethanol is also made from it as fuel.
In processing, bagasse and molasses are left over.
Noble cane was originally bred in New Guinea.

abschnitte.text: Sugar cane belongs to the **grass family**, like wheat or maize. It grows about **3 to 6 metres** tall and has thick stems divided into sections, similar to bamboo. Sugar cane needs a lot of warmth, sun and water. That is why it grows only in the **tropics and subtropics**. After harvesting, it sprouts again from the rootstocks, so you can harvest for several years.

The plant stores the sugar in the **stem**. After harvesting, the stems are chopped up and pressed. The sweet juice is cleaned and boiled down until **sugar crystals** form. What is left is a dark, thick syrup, the **molasses**. It is used, for example, as animal feed or made into rum. Brown cane sugar still contains some molasses.

After pressing, a fibrous residue is left, the **bagasse**. In many sugar factories it is burned to produce electricity and heat for the factory. You can also make paper or disposable tableware from it. In **Brazil**, **ethanol** is obtained from sugar cane juice in large amounts, a kind of alcohol that is used as **car fuel**.

**Noble cane** was originally bred in **New Guinea**. From there it reached South-East Asia and India, where people learned early on to make solid sugar. Via Persia and the Arab world it came to the Mediterranean region. Today **Brazil** harvests the most sugar cane worldwide, followed by India.

After the arrival of Europeans in America, huge **sugar cane plantations** arose in the Caribbean and in Brazil. The hard work had to be done mainly by people who had been taken from Africa and **enslaved**. In this way sugar became a widespread luxury food in Europe. This history is among the dark sides of world trade.

gewusst: The word sugar originally comes from Sanskrit, an ancient language of India.
Measured by harvest quantity, sugar cane is the largest field crop in the world.

teile.einleitung: Plants reveal a lot about their site. Indicator values are numbers that state under what conditions a plant species mostly grows. For the Swiss flora, the ETH botanist Elias Landolt set such values.
wichtigste: An indicator value shows under what conditions a plant mostly grows.
Elias Landolt of ETH Zurich set indicator values for the Swiss plants.
The moisture number F describes soil moisture.
The reaction number R describes how acidic or limy the soil is.
The light number L describes how bright the site is.
In the “Flora indicativa” the values run from 1 to 5.

abschnitte.text: **Indicator values** state where a plant species mostly occurs. For example: damp or dry, acidic or limy, bright or shady. If you know the plants on an area, you can in this way draw conclusions about the **site**. The **stinging nettle**, for example, grows lushly where there is a lot of nitrogen in the soil. It therefore has a high **nutrient number**.

abschnitte.titel: Elias Landolt and the Swiss flora
abschnitte.text: The Swiss botanist **Elias Landolt** (1926 to 2013) worked at **ETH Zurich**. In **1977** he published ecological indicator values for the Swiss flora. In **2010** a greatly expanded new edition appeared under the title **“Flora indicativa”**. The Swiss indicator values divide the values into **five levels from 1 to 5**, partly with half steps. The indicator values according to **Ellenberg** in Germany, on the other hand, mostly run from 1 to 9.

The **moisture number F** states how dry or wet the soil is at the typical site. A low value means dry, a high one wet. The **reaction number R** describes the acid content. Low values show acidic soils, high values basic, often limy soils. The **light number L** shows whether a species grows more in the **shade** or in bright, open places. In addition there are further numbers, for example for nutrients or temperature.

To describe an area, you note the species and their indicator values. Then you calculate the **mean**. An example: four species have the moisture numbers 2, 3, 4 and 3. You add the values and divide by the number of species: (2 + 3 + 4 + 3) ÷ 4 = 12 ÷ 4 = **3**. So the area is **moderately damp**. In this way you can also compare different meadows well with one another.

gewusst: With indicator values you can also follow how a meadow changes over many years, for example through fertiliser.
Elias Landolt was professor of geobotany at ETH Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Many plants carry fine hairs on their leaves and stems. In scientific language these little hairs are called **trichomes**. In the mountains especially, they are an important protection against cold, sun and drought.
wichtigste: Trichomes are fine hairs on leaves and stems.
The edelweiss is covered with dense, white woolly hairs.
Densely hairy parts look silvery, because air between the hairs reflects the light.
The hairs keep a calm, damp layer of air at the leaf and so protect against drying out.
Light-coloured hairs block some of the UV rays.
On cold nights they hold in heat like a jumper.

abschnitte.text: **Trichomes** are outgrowths of the outermost layer of cells of a plant, the epidermis. They can be single-celled or multicellular, short or long, simple or branched. Some are **glandular hairs** that produce scented substances, as in thyme. Others are **stinging hairs**, as in the stinging nettle. Many plants, however, simply carry dense, soft **woolly hairs**.

Densely hairy plant parts often look **silvery or white**. This is not due to a pigment. **Air between the hairs** reflects the light, much as with snow. The best-known example is the **edelweiss**. The white, hairy **star-shaped rays** around its flower heads are not petals, but **bracts**. They act like a shield and **attract insects**.

In the Alps the sun is strong, especially the **UV radiation**. Light-coloured hairs **block some of the UV rays**, much like a sun hat. In addition, wind often blows and dries out leaves. A dense covering of hair **keeps a calm, damp layer of air** right at the leaf. That way less water evaporates.

On mountain nights it often gets very cold, even in summer. The hairs hold on to air and **so hold in heat like a jumper**. The **pasqueflower** flowers as early as spring, when it is still cold. It wears a furry coat of hairs and is therefore also called the **fur anemone**. Many other Alpine plants are also noticeably hairy.

gewusst: The edelweiss is a symbolic plant of the Alps and a well-known emblem in Switzerland.
The hairs of the stinging nettle break off when touched like tiny glass needles and squirt their burning sap into the skin.

teile.einleitung: A lake is divided into different zones from the shore to the middle. Depending on the depth of the water and the light, quite different plants grow there, and this is called lake zonation.
wichtigste: From the land to the deep water follow carr woodland, reed bed, floating-leaf zone and submerged zone.
The shore zone in which light reaches the bottom is called the littoral.
The dark, deep lake bed is called the profundal.
The open water in the middle of the lake is called the open-water zone or pelagial.
Water plants grow only as deep as enough light gets to.
In summer, warm water, the epilimnion, lies above cold deep water.

abschnitte.text: At the edge of many lakes grows a wet **carr woodland**. It is often shaped by the **black alder**, which tolerates ground that is sometimes flooded. Then follows the **reed bed** with reed and bulrush, which stand in shallow water. Further out begins the **floating-leaf zone**. There the leaves of water lilies and yellow water lilies lie on the surface of the water.

In the **submerged zone**, plants live completely under water, for example **pondweeds** and waterweed. In clear lakes, a zone with **stoneworts** often follows even further down. They manage with very little light and form dense lawns. Their name in German comes from the whorled branches, which are reminiscent of a candelabra.

Plants need light for **photosynthesis**. With increasing depth, the light is swallowed up by the water. At some point it is no longer enough, and plants stop growing. That is why the shore zone in which light reaches the bottom is called the **littoral**. All the water plants grow here. The clearer a lake is, the deeper this zone reaches.

The deep lake bed, where hardly any light gets, is called the **profundal**. No plants grow there, but bacteria and worms break down dead matter that sinks down from above. The open water in the middle of the lake is called the **open-water zone** or **pelagial**. It has no contact with the shore or the bottom. Here live mainly **plankton** and fish.

In summer the sun warms the surface water. This warm water, the **epilimnion**, then lies on the cold deep water, the **hypolimnion**. In between, the temperature changes quickly. In autumn the surface cools down, and the water of the lake mixes again.

gewusst: With its rhizomes, reed can colonise large areas and protects the bank from waves.
Water is heaviest at about 4 degrees. That is why the bottom of deep lakes often has about this temperature all year round.

teile.einleitung: The goat’s-beard is a yellow meadow flower that looks a little like the dandelion. Its flower is open only in the morning. After flowering it forms a huge seed head like a dandelion clock.
wichtigste: The flower of the goat’s-beard is yellow.
By midday the flower closes again.
The fruiting head is a large, ball-shaped seed head like a dandelion clock.
The seeds fly away on the wind with a parachute of fine hairs.
The leaves are long and narrow like grass.
White milky sap flows in the stem.
It usually grows about 30 to 70 centimetres tall.

abschnitte.text: The **goat’s-beard** has a **yellow flower** that looks a little like the **dandelion**. It usually grows about 30 to 70 centimetres tall and stands clearly visible among the grasses. Its **leaves** are long and narrow. Without a flower, the plant is therefore easily mistaken for **grass**. If you break off the stem, **white milky sap** comes out, as in the dandelion.

The flower of the goat’s-beard is open for only **a few hours** a day. In the morning it opens, and already around **midday** it closes again. Whoever wants to see the flower in bloom has to go to the meadow early. Because of this habit it is also called **Morgenstern**, morning star, in German.
In the name sits the **billy goat**. After flowering, the withered flowers stick out of the green sheath. This recalls the **beard** of a billy goat. That is where the name goat’s-beard comes from.

After flowering, the goat’s-beard forms a **large, ball-shaped seed head**. It is much bigger than that of the dandelion. Each seed has a **parachute** of fine hairs. With it, it flies away on the **wind** and lands in a new place. In this way the goat’s-beard spreads.

gewusst: Like the dandelion, the goat’s-beard belongs to the daisy family.
In the seed head of the goat’s-beard, the fine hairs of the parachutes are interwoven like a small net.

teile.einleitung: The World Climate Council is a body of the United Nations that sums up the state of research on climate change. It is known above all for its scientific reports on climate change. In English it is called the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, IPCC for short.
wichtigste: The World Climate Council is called the IPCC in English.
It was founded in 1988 by two organisations of the United Nations.
Its seat is in Geneva in Switzerland.
It is known for scientific reports on the state of climate change.
The IPCC does not do research itself but evaluates thousands of studies.
Six major assessment reports have appeared so far, the latest in 2021 to 2023.
In 2007 the IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: The **IPCC** was founded in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations Environment Programme. Almost all states in the world are members. Its task is to inform governments neutrally about climate change. In doing so it does not give rules but shows facts and possible paths.

The IPCC carries out no research of its own and measures no temperatures. Instead, hundreds of experts from all over the world read and assess thousands of published studies. They work on a voluntary basis and sum up the state of knowledge in **assessment reports**. The drafts are checked and commented on by many more experts and governments.

**Working Group I** studies the scientific basis, that is, how the climate is changing and why. Working Group II deals with the consequences for people and nature and with adaptation. Working Group III studies how the emission of greenhouse gases can be reduced. At the end, a **synthesis report** sums up the most important results.

The first assessment report appeared in 1990, the sixth in the years 2021 to 2023. In it, it says that humans have unequivocally warmed the climate. In 2018 a widely noted **special report** appeared on the consequences of warming by 1.5 degrees. The reports form the basis for the international climate negotiations and the Paris Agreement.

The secretariat of the IPCC is in **Geneva**. The Bernese climate researcher **Thomas Stocker** led Working Group I as co-chair from 2008 to 2015. Under his leadership the scientific part of the fifth assessment report of 2013 was produced. Many other researchers from Swiss universities also contribute to the reports.

In 2007 the IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize together with the former US vice president Al Gore. What was honoured was the work of spreading knowledge about human-made climate change. The summaries for policymakers are adopted by the governments sentence by sentence. This makes them a particularly reliable basis for politics.

begriffe.erklaerung: English abbreviation for the World Climate Council
a large report that sums up what science knows about a subject
an organisation in which almost all states of the world work together, abbreviated UN
long-term change of the climate on Earth

gewusst: A single assessment report runs to several thousand pages.
Experts from over a hundred countries contribute to the reports.
The summaries are sometimes negotiated sentence by sentence at meetings with government representatives until deep into the night.

teile.einleitung: The silver fir is one of the tallest trees in our forests. It has soft, flat needles and a light grey bark. That is where its name comes from.
wichtigste: The silver fir often grows 30 to 50 metres tall.
It gets its name from the light grey, almost whitish bark.
Its needles are flat, blunt at the tip and do not prick.
The needles stand flat to the left and right like a comb.
The cones break up on the tree, and only the spindle stays standing.
A deep taproot holds it firmly in the ground in a storm.
Old silver firs often have a flat crown like a stork’s nest.

abschnitte.text: The **silver fir** is among the tallest trees in our forests. It often grows **30 to 50 metres** tall. It gets its name from its **light grey**, almost whitish bark. In old silver firs the top hardly grows any more. The crown becomes **flat** at the top and looks like a **stork’s nest**.

The needles of the silver fir are **flat** and blunt or slightly notched at the tip. That is why they **do not prick**. They stand like a **comb** flat on both sides of the twig. They are said to be **parted**. On the underside they have two light stripes. By this you can easily tell the silver fir from the spruce, whose needles are pointed and stand all around.

The cones of the silver fir stand **upright** on the twigs. They do not fall down as a whole. When they are ripe, they **break up** on the tree into single scales. The seeds fly away. Only the thin central axis, the **spindle**, stays on the twig. That is why you hardly ever find whole cones under silver firs.

The silver fir forms a strong **taproot** that goes deep into the ground. So it usually stands firm in a **storm**. It also tolerates a lot of **shade**. Young silver firs can wait a long time under big trees until they get more light. In Switzerland it grows, for example, in the Jura, on the Central Plateau and in the Pre-Alps.

**Roe deer** like to eat the buds and shoots of young silver firs. If a young tree is nibbled again and again, it hardly grows in height. That is why young silver firs are sometimes protected with **fences** or guards. In this way they can grow up into big trees.

gewusst: The spruce is often called the “Rottanne” in German, which means red fir, but it is not a fir at all. The silver fir is a true fir.
Because the cones break up on the tree, the fir cones you find in the forest are mostly spruce cones.

teile.einleitung: Forest ecology studies how trees, plants, animals, fungi and soil live together in the forest. A forest is a finely balanced system in which every living thing has its role. In Switzerland, forest covers about 32 per cent of the country and protects many mountain valleys from natural hazards.
wichtigste: The forest covers about 32 per cent of the area of Switzerland.
The most common tree species in the Swiss forest is the spruce.
Early bloomers such as the wood anemone use the light in the beech forest before the trees come into leaf.
A large part of the mountain forest protects against avalanches, rockfall and landslides.
In 1876 the first federal forest law for the high mountains came into force.
After heat and drought, the spruce bark beetle attacks mainly weakened spruces.
In the selection forest, for example in the Emmental, trees of all ages stand side by side on small areas.

abschnitte.text: **Ecology** studies the relationships between living things and their environment. In the forest, plants as producers make food with sunlight. Plant eaters such as deer and caterpillars eat the plants, and predators such as the fox and the tawny owl hunt the plant eaters. **Decomposers** such as fungi, bacteria and earthworms turn dead material back into nutrients.

abschnitte.titel: The year in the beech forest
abschnitte.text: In spring, before the beeches put out their leaves, a lot of light falls on the forest floor. **Early bloomers** such as the wood anemone, wild garlic and lungwort use this short time. They have stored nutrients in bulbs or rootstocks and flower quickly. As soon as the canopy closes, it gets so dark on the ground that their parts above ground soon disappear.

The **spruce** is the most common tree species in the Swiss forest, followed by beech and fir. At low altitudes mainly beech, oak and mixed forests grow. Further up in the Alps spruces dominate, and near the forest line larches and Swiss stone pines grow. The **forest line** in the Swiss Alps usually lies between about 1,800 and 2,300 metres above sea level.

In the 19th century many mountain forests were cut down, and serious floods followed. That is why in 1876 the first federal **forest law** for the high mountains came into force, and in 1902 it was extended to the whole of Switzerland. Since then the forest area may not be reduced. Today about half of the Swiss forest protects villages, roads and railway lines from avalanches, rockfall and landslides as **protective forest**.

The **spruce bark beetle** is a small bark beetle that bores in under the bark of spruces. Healthy spruces fend it off with resin, but trees weakened by heat, drought or storms cannot. Then the beetles multiply in huge numbers and can make whole stands die. Because of climate change, foresters at low altitudes increasingly rely on tree species such as oak, fir and Douglas fir.

In the **selection forest**, young and old trees grow side by side on small areas, often firs, spruces and beeches. Only single large trees are ever felled, and the forest stays permanently closed. This form of forestry is common in the Emmental and in the Jura. For biodiversity, **deadwood** is also important, because thousands of beetle, fungus and bird species live from dead trees.

begriffe.erklaerung: community of plants, animals and fungi with their environment
a plant that flowers in early spring before the trees have leaves
a living thing that breaks down dead plants and animals
dead trees and branches that stay lying or standing in the forest
a forest in which trees of all ages grow side by side

gewusst: A female spruce bark beetle eats a tunnel under the bark that looks like lines in a book, which is why in German it is called the book printer.
About a fifth of all forest species depend on deadwood.
The forest law of 1876 is among the earliest environmental protection laws in the world.

teile.einleitung: The meadow bellflower is a delicate flower with blue-violet blossoms. Its flowers look like small bells, which is where its name comes from. It flowers in early summer in many meadows.
wichtigste: The flower looks like a small bell.
It is mostly light blue-violet, rarely white.
The edge of the flower is divided into five pointed lobes.
“Campanula” means little bell in Latin.
Small wild bees sometimes spend the night in the bells.
It flowers from about May to July.
It belongs to the bellflower family.

abschnitte.text: The flower of the **bellflower** has the shape of a small **bell**. That is where its name comes from. The Latin name **Campanula** also means “little bell”, because “campana” is Latin for bell. The bell ends in **five pointed lobes**. In the meadow bellflower they are wide open, so that the flower looks almost like a star.

The **meadow bellflower** flowers light **blue-violet**. Rarely there are also white flowers. It has a **thin, delicate stem**. That is why the flowers sway even in a light wind. It flowers in early summer and summer, from about **May to July**.

Bellflowers are popular with **insects**. Some small **wild bees**, for example **scissor bees**, spend the night or rainy spells in the bells. There they are protected. Some wild bees even collect their pollen only from bellflowers. That is why meadows with bellflowers are very important for them.

The meadow bellflower belongs to the **bellflower family**. Many of its relatives also have bell-shaped flowers. In Switzerland grow numerous kinds of bellflower, from the meadows in the valley up high into the Alps. Meadows that are not mown too often and not heavily fertilised are especially rich in bellflowers.

gewusst: The bellflowers form a large genus with several hundred species.
In many bellflowers the pollen ripens earlier than the stigma of the same flower. In this way the flower is mostly pollinated with pollen from other flowers.

teile.einleitung: Grapes are sweet fruits that grow on vines. You can eat them fresh, press them into juice or dry them into raisins. In Switzerland, vines grow mainly on sunny slopes.
wichtigste: Grapes are mostly green or blue.
A bunch consists of many single berries.
Dried grapes are called raisins.
The grape harvest is called Wümmet in many parts of German-speaking Switzerland.
Vines like to grow on sunny slopes.
There are bred varieties without seeds.
Glucose, called Traubenzucker or grape sugar in German, takes its name from grapes.

abschnitte.text: A **bunch of grapes** consists of many single **berries**. They sit on small stalks. There are light, **green** grapes and dark, **blue** grapes. The dark ones often look almost black. Varieties have also been bred that have **no seeds or almost none**. They are especially popular for eating.

Grapes grow on **vines**, which are climbing plants. Vines need a lot of **sun and warmth**. On slopes they get especially much sunlight. That is why in Switzerland they are gladly planted on **sunny slopes**, for example in the Valais or on Lake Geneva. In **Lavaux**, the vine terraces climb steeply up from Lake Geneva. Since 2007 they have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The grapes ripen in **autumn**. Then the grape harvest begins. In many parts of German-speaking Switzerland it is called the **Wümmet**. Often many people help to cut the grapes by hand. They are laid carefully in crates so that the berries are not crushed.

For **grape juice**, fresh grapes are pressed. It is sweet and can be light or dark. If you dry grapes in the sun or in the oven, they become small, wrinkled and very sweet. Then they are called **raisins**. You eat them in muesli, in cake or just as they are.

Sweet grapes contain a lot of **glucose**, which in German is called Traubenzucker, grape sugar. That is why this sugar bears their name. Glucose gives the body energy quickly. You can also buy it as small tablets, for example for sport or long hikes.

gewusst: Vines have been grown for thousands of years.
Grapes do not ripen any further after harvesting. That is why they are harvested only when they are fully ripe.

teile.einleitung: The sugar beet is a field crop from which sugar is made. It is also grown in Switzerland and processed in two sugar factories. In autumn you often see the harvested beets in large heaps at the edge of the field.
wichtigste: Sugar is made from the sugar beet.
The sugar is in the thick beet that grows in the ground.
Inside, the sugar beet is white.
It is harvested in autumn.
The Swiss sugar factories are in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.
A large beet weighs about 1 kilogram.
The residues after the sugar extraction are called beet pulp and are feed for cows.

abschnitte.text: At the top the sugar beet has a bush of **green leaves**. In the **ground** grows a thick, white beet that can weigh about **1 kilogram**. In it the plant stores sugar, which it makes in the leaves with the help of sunlight. The beet is **white inside**. It is closely related to beetroot and chard, which also belong to the same plant species.

Sugar beets are sown in spring and harvested in **autumn**. Big machines cut off the leaves and lift the beets from the ground. After that they often lie in **large heaps at the edge of the field** until lorries or trains take them to the factory. The time in which the factories process beets day and night is called the **campaign**.

In Switzerland there are two sugar factories: in **Aarberg** in the canton of Bern and in **Frauenfeld** in the canton of Thurgau. There the beets are washed and cut into fine strips. With hot water, the sugar is dissolved out. The sugar juice is cleaned and boiled down until **sugar crystals** form. In this way white sugar arises that is exactly the same as sugar from sugar cane.

What is left after the sugar has been dissolved out is the **beet pulp**. It is dried or pressed and fed to **cows**. The dark syrup that is left over in production, the molasses, is also used as feed or for other purposes. In this way almost the whole beet is used.

For a long time, sugar was obtained only from sugar cane from far-off countries. In the year 1747, the German chemist **Andreas Sigismund Marggraf** discovered that beets contain the same sugar. Around 1800 the first beet sugar factory arose. Through breeding, the sugar content of the beets was greatly increased. Today the sugar beet is the most important sugar plant in Europe.

gewusst: A sugar beet consists of about 15 to 20 per cent sugar, and the rest is mainly water and fibres.
Sugar from beets and sugar from sugar cane can be told apart neither by sight nor by taste.

teile.einleitung: In almost every product there is water that you cannot see: it was needed for growing or making it. This hidden water is called **virtual water**. Whoever buys goods therefore also uses water indirectly.
wichtigste: The term virtual water was coined by the British geographer John Anthony Allan.
Arjen Hoekstra developed the water footprint from it.
Blue water comes from rivers, lakes and groundwater.
Grey water is the water that would be needed to dilute pollutants.
Beef has an especially large water footprint.
A large part of the Swiss water footprint arises abroad.

abschnitte.text: The British geographer **John Anthony Allan** coined the term virtual water in the 1990s. He described that along with goods, the water hidden in them is traded too. For this he received the **Stockholm Water Prize** in 2008. The Dutch researcher **Arjen Hoekstra** introduced the **water footprint** around 2002. With it, you add up the virtual water for people, companies or whole countries.

The water footprint has three parts. **Green water** is rainwater that plants take up in the field. **Blue water** is taken from rivers, lakes and groundwater, for example for irrigation. It is then missing for other users. **Grey water** is a calculated quantity for pollution: the amount that would be needed to dilute pollutants to below the limit values.

For one kilogram of **beef**, about 15,000 litres of water are estimated on a worldwide average, mainly for feed crops. Vegetables and cereals are far below that. In a **cup of coffee** there are, by estimate, about 130 litres of water. Most of it is rainwater on the plantations. Such figures are estimates and depend strongly on where the crop is grown.

Switzerland imports many foods, textiles and raw materials. That is why the larger part of its water footprint arises **abroad**. If the goods come from dry regions, this can make **water scarcity** worse there. For cotton or rice from dry regions, the share of blue water is especially high.

gewusst: In a single cup of coffee there are about 130 litres of virtual water.
Switzerland is a country rich in water, but through imports it uses a lot of water in other countries.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, certain environmental organisations may lodge an appeal against building projects. This is called the **right of associations to appeal**. In this way nature, which cannot defend itself, gets a voice in court.
wichtigste: The right of associations to appeal was first anchored in the Nature and Cultural Heritage Act (NCHA).
The Environmental Protection Act (EPA) also regulates it, in Art. 55.
The Federal Council determines which organisations have the right to appeal.
The organisation must be active throughout Switzerland and pursue non-profit aims.
Since 2007, organisations that lose bear the costs of the proceedings.
In 2008, voters clearly rejected an initiative to restrict it severely.

abschnitte.text: With many building projects, nobody who stands up for nature and landscape is personally affected. Without an appeal, no court would check whether **environmental law** had been applied correctly. The right of associations to appeal makes this check possible. Supporters see in it an important protection of nature. Critics say it can delay building projects.

The right was first anchored in **Art. 12** of the **Nature and Cultural Heritage Act** (NCHA). Later **Art. 55** of the **Environmental Protection Act** (EPA) was added. It applies to facilities that need an **environmental impact assessment** (EIA). This is a careful check of how much a project burdens the environment.

Not every association may lodge an appeal. The organisation must be active **throughout Switzerland** and pursue purely **non-profit aims**. Since the revision of 2007, the environment must also have been part of its statutory purpose for at least **ten years**. The **Federal Council** names the eligible organisations in an ordinance. These include, for example, Pro Natura, WWF Switzerland and the Foundation for Landscape Protection.

With the revision of 2007, the rules were tightened. If an organisation loses, it bears the **costs of the proceedings** like other parties. A popular initiative then wanted to restrict the right severely. On 30 November 2008, about two thirds of voters and all the cantons rejected it. The right of associations to appeal remained.

gewusst: Local nature conservation clubs may not lodge an association appeal, even if they are very committed to their area.
The initiative of 2008 was not accepted in a single canton.

teile.einleitung: The primeval forest of Derborence in the Valais is among the last true primeval forests in Switzerland. Two rockslides shaped the remote valley and protected the forest from use by people for a long time.
wichtigste: Derborence lies in the municipality of Conthey in the Valais, below the Diablerets.
Rockslides in 1714 and 1749 buried alpine pastures and made access difficult.
This created the Lac de Derborence.
The forest is a fir and spruce primeval forest with mighty silver firs.
Charles Ferdinand Ramuz made Derborence known with a novel of 1934.
The landscape has been listed in the federal inventory BLN since 1977.

abschnitte.text: Derborence lies in the municipal area of **Conthey** in the canton of **Valais**, below the mountain massif of the **Diablerets**. The valley is remote and surrounded by high rock walls. Here grows one of the last **primeval forests** in Switzerland. A primeval forest is a forest that has never been used for forestry.

In **1714 and 1749**, huge masses of rock fell from the Diablerets into the valley. The **rockslides** buried alpine pastures and made the valley hard to reach. The rubble also dammed up the Derbonne stream. This created the **Lac de Derborence**, which is slowly silting up. Because the forest was so remote, it stayed untouched.

In the primeval forest grow mainly **silver firs** and **spruces**. Some silver firs are very large and several centuries old. Old trees die naturally here and stay lying or standing. That means there is a lot of **deadwood**. Fungi, beetles and many other living things live in it. A typical resident is the rare **three-toed woodpecker**, which looks for bark beetle larvae in dying conifers.

True primeval forests are very rare in Central Europe. They show what a forest looks like entirely **without management**: with trees of every age, gaps and a lot of deadwood. Researchers can observe here how a forest renews itself. That is why Derborence is protected. The landscape has been listed since **1977** in the **Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments (BLN)**.

The French-speaking Swiss writer **Charles Ferdinand Ramuz** made the valley famous. In his novel **“Derborence”** of 1934 he tells the story of a herdsman who survives the rockslide and returns from the rocks weeks later. The novel was **made into a film in 1985**.

gewusst: Ramuz is shown on the former Swiss 200-franc note.
The Lac de Derborence is getting smaller and smaller over time, because streams carry gravel and sand into it.

teile.einleitung: The Zurich Herbaria are one of the large plant collections of Switzerland. The University of Zurich and ETH Zurich run their collections of dried plants together. Researchers from all over the world use the specimens.
wichtigste: The Zurich Herbaria belong to the University of Zurich and ETH Zurich.
They are entered with the abbreviations Z and ZT in the Index Herbariorum.
They are located by the Botanical Garden on Zollikerstrasse.
The collection comprises millions of specimens.
A holotype is the specimen to which the name of a plant species is bound.
Old specimens today also serve for genetic analyses.
New specimens are usually protected from pest insects by deep freezing.

abschnitte.text: A **herbarium** is a collection of pressed and dried plants. Each plant is glued onto a sheet of paper and given a label: where and when was it found, and who collected it? Such a sheet is called a **herbarium specimen**. Early herbaria were called **Hortus siccus** in Latin, which means “dry garden”.

In Zurich, the **University of Zurich** and **ETH Zurich** run their plant collections together as the **Zurich Herbaria**. They are located by the **Botanical Garden on Zollikerstrasse**. The collection comprises **several million specimens** from Switzerland and from all over the world. This makes it one of the largest herbaria in Switzerland.

Every large herbarium in the world has an abbreviation. These abbreviations are listed in the **Index Herbariorum**, an international directory. The herbarium of the university has the abbreviation **Z**, that of ETH the abbreviation **ZT**. With these abbreviations, researchers can state exactly in scientific papers where a particular specimen is kept.

When a plant species is scientifically described for the first time, a specimen is fixed as the standard. This specimen is called the **holotype**, and the name of the species is bound to it. Such type specimens are especially valuable. Today researchers use old specimens not only to identify plants but also for **genetic analyses**. In this way you can, for example, study how species have changed.

Dried plants are delicate. Small **pest insects** can eat them. That is why new or borrowed specimens are today mostly treated by **deep freezing** before they enter the collection. The cold kills any insects without using poison. Many specimens are also photographed and made available digitally.

gewusst: Well-kept herbarium specimens can last several hundred years and still remain useful for research.
Herbarium specimens are lent between herbaria all over the world, much like books in a library.

teile.einleitung: The water cycle describes the path that water takes from the sea through the clouds and back to the Earth. In doing so, the water constantly changes between liquid, gas and solid. This cycle is driven by the Sun.
wichtigste: The water cycle is the path of water from the sea through the clouds back to the Earth.
The Sun makes water evaporate from seas, lakes and plants.
Up high, the water vapour cools and forms clouds.
Rain arises when water evaporates, forms clouds and falls again as precipitation.
Through rivers and groundwater, the water returns to the sea.
The water on Earth has been the same for billions of years, and it is only turned over again and again.
Because of its many springs, Switzerland is called the water tower of Europe.

abschnitte.text: The Sun warms the seas, lakes, rivers and the ground. In doing so, liquid water turns into invisible **water vapour** and rises with the warm air. Plants also give off a lot of water vapour through their leaves. But the largest part is supplied by the oceans, because they cover most of the Earth.

The higher the air rises, the colder it becomes. Cold air can hold less water vapour, so tiny droplets or ice crystals form. This process is called **condensation**. Billions of these droplets together we see as a cloud.

In the cloud, the droplets collide and become larger and heavier. When they are too heavy, they fall to the Earth as **precipitation**. Depending on the temperature, it comes as rain, snow, soft hail or hail. On average, a water molecule stays in the air for only about a week to ten days.

Part of the rain runs off through streams and rivers, and another part seeps into the ground. The water that seeps in collects as **groundwater** in layers of gravel and sand. In Switzerland, about 80 per cent of drinking water comes from groundwater and springs. Snow and glaciers often store water for months or years before it flows on.

In the Swiss Alps rise large rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhône, the Inn and the Ticino. Their water flows into the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea and the Adriatic. That is why Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**. About six per cent of Europe’s fresh water reserves lie in Switzerland, in lakes, glaciers and underground.

About 97 per cent of the water on Earth is salt water in the seas. Only about three per cent is fresh water, and most of that is locked up in the ice of the polar caps and glaciers. So only a small fraction can be used directly by people. That is why it is important to keep waters clean and not to waste water.

begriffe.erklaerung: the change from liquid water to water vapour
the change from water vapour to liquid droplets
water that falls from clouds to the Earth, such as rain or snow
water that collects underground in soil and rock

gewusst: The water you drink today may once have been drunk by a dinosaur.
A raindrop falls to the Earth at up to about 30 kilometres per hour.
A drop of water from the Rhine at Basel is on its way to the North Sea, while a drop from the Rhône flows into the Mediterranean.

teile.einleitung: The Paris Agreement is a worldwide treaty to protect the climate. Almost all the countries of the world have committed in it to limiting global warming. It was adopted in December 2015 at the climate conference in Paris.
wichtigste: The Paris Agreement was adopted on 12 December 2015.
Its central aim is to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees.
The countries are also to make an effort to limit the warming to 1.5 degrees.
Each country decides for itself how strongly it cuts its greenhouse gases.
Every five years, countries are to review and tighten their climate targets.
The agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016.
Switzerland ratified the agreement in 2017 and wants to release net zero greenhouse gases by 2050.

abschnitte.text: The **Paris Agreement**, often called the Paris climate accord, is a treaty under international law. It was negotiated at the 21st **UN climate conference** in Paris, also called COP21. It builds on the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change of 1992. It followed the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, which contained obligations for only some of the countries.

Global warming is to stay well below 2 degrees compared with the time before industrialisation. If possible it is even to be limited to **1.5 degrees**. In the second half of the century, the world is not to release more greenhouse gases than forests and other stores can take up. In addition, countries are to be better able to adapt to the consequences of climate change.

Unlike earlier treaties, the agreement does not set a fixed number for each country. Every state submits its own climate plan, the **nationally determined contribution**. Every five years it is checked whether the world is on course, and the plans are meant to become more ambitious. Rich countries support poorer countries with money for climate protection and adaptation.

Almost all the states on Earth have joined the agreement. The USA has announced its withdrawal twice, most recently in 2025, after rejoining in 2021. The climate conferences take place every year in changing places. There it is negotiated how the aims of the agreement are to be reached.

Switzerland ratified the agreement in 2017. It wants to halve its greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 1990. In June 2023 voters accepted the **Climate and Innovation Act**. It states that Switzerland is to reach **net zero** by 2050.

The agreement is seen as a milestone, because for the first time almost the whole world agreed on a common climate goal. Critics complain that there are no penalties if a country misses its targets. Experts calculate that the climate plans so far are not yet enough to keep to 1.5 degrees. Even so, the agreement has speeded up the expansion of solar and wind energy worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A treaty between several states
To confirm a treaty officially so that it applies to your own country
Not releasing more greenhouse gases than are removed from the air again
The annual climate conference of the United Nations, from the English Conference of the Parties

gewusst: When it was adopted in Paris, the delegates cheered and hugged each other, and many had tears in their eyes.
The agreement came into force faster than expected, only just under a year after the conference.
The signatures of many states were collected on Earth Day, 22 April 2016, in New York.

teile.einleitung: A bulb is a special part of a plant that stores food underground. From bulbs grow many spring flowers such as tulip, daffodil and hyacinth. The onion and garlic are also bulbs.
wichtigste: A bulb stores food for the spring.
Its layers consist of thick leaves.
Tulip, daffodil and hyacinth grow from bulbs.
Garlic consists of several small cloves.
Flower bulbs are put into the ground with the tip upwards.
When cutting onions, the eyes often water.

abschnitte.text: Botanically, a **bulb** is an underground, strongly shortened shoot. At the bottom sits a flat **basal plate** on which the roots grow. Above it lie many **thick leaves**, the **bulb scales**. They form the layers that you see when you cut up an onion. On the outside, dry, thin skins protect the bulb.

In the thick scales the plant stores **food for the spring**. In this way it can sprout early in the year, even before the trees have leaves and cast shade. After flowering, the green leaves collect new nutrients and fill the bulb up again. If you leave a **tulip bulb** in the ground, **it sprouts again the next spring**. That is why you should not cut off the leaves straight after flowering.

Many spring flowers grow from bulbs: the **tulip**, the yellow **daffodil**, also called **narcissus**, the scented **hyacinth** with its dense clusters of flowers, and the snowdrop. In autumn you put the bulbs into the ground **with the tip upwards**. The shoot grows from the tip, and the roots form at the bottom.

The **onion** and **garlic** are also bulbs. Garlic consists of several small **cloves** that together form a bulb. When you cut an onion, substances are released that have to do with sulphur. They rise into the air and irritate the eyes, which is why **the eyes often water**. A sharp knife and cold water help a little.

gewusst: In the Netherlands in the 17th century, tulip bulbs were at times so sought after that very high prices were paid for single bulbs.
From every garlic clove, a whole new bulb of garlic can grow again in the garden.

teile.einleitung: The onion skin slide is a classic experiment in biology lessons. With a thin skin from an onion, you can see real plant cells under the microscope. You need only a few aids for it.
wichtigste: You use the thin skin on the inside of an onion scale.
You peel the skin off with tweezers.
On the slide you first put a drop of water.
You lower the cover glass at a slant from the side so that no air bubbles form.
The cells look oblong, like bricks.
With methylene blue the cell nuclei can be stained blue.
Chloroplasts are missing, because onion scales grow without light.

abschnitte.text: You cut an onion open and take one of the thick **onion scales**. On its inside lies a wafer-thin, transparent **skin**. It consists of only a single layer of cells and is therefore ideal for microscopy. With a knife you score a small square and carefully peel the skin off with **tweezers**.

First you put a **drop of water** on the **slide**, the little glass plate on which you lay the specimen. Then you lay the skin flat in the drop without it folding. Now you place the **cover glass** with one edge down and **lower it at a slant from the side**. In this way the air can escape and no air bubbles form. Such a specimen of fresh material in water is called a **wet mount**.

Under the microscope you see many **oblong cells** that lie close together **like bricks** in a wall. The **cell walls** can be made out well as fine lines. In each cell lies a small, round **cell nucleus**. Most of the cell is filled by a large sap space, the **vacuole**. It is best to start with the lowest magnification.

The cell nuclei are hard to see without colour. If you put a drop of **methylene blue** at the edge of the cover glass, the dye is drawn in under the glass. After that the **cell nuclei** appear clearly **blue**. Green **chloroplasts** cannot be seen in the onion skin. The onion scales grow **without light** inside the bulb and carry out no photosynthesis, so they need no chloroplasts.

gewusst: In a red onion the sap in the vacuoles is coloured, so you can see the cells well even without staining.
As early as the 17th century, Robert Hooke observed small chambers in cork and called them cells.

teile.einleitung: In a forest kindergarten, children spend the morning not in a room but outdoors in the forest. There they play, learn and eat. This happens in almost any weather.
wichtigste: The children are almost always outdoors in the forest.
They go out in almost any weather, only not in a storm or thunderstorm.
Weatherproof clothes and good shoes are very important.
The first forest kindergarten arose in the 1950s in Denmark.
Branches, stones, cones and leaves are the toys.
You never eat unknown berries and mushrooms.
After the forest, you check the body for ticks.

abschnitte.text: A **forest kindergarten** is a kindergarten that takes place in the forest. The children meet in the morning and walk together to their spot in the forest. There they play, make things, sing and discover. The idea arose in the **1950s in Denmark**. Later there were many forest kindergartens in Germany and in Switzerland too.

The forest kindergarten also takes place outdoors in **rain, snow or cold**. That is why the children need **weatherproof clothes**, good shoes and often several layers. In this way they stay warm and dry. Only in a **storm or thunderstorm** do they stay away from the forest for safety, because then branches can fall.

In the forest there is a lot of **play material**: branches, stones, cones, moss and leaves. From these the children build huts, figures or little bridges. They get to know animals and plants and notice how the forest changes over the year. They become skilful at climbing and balancing.

abschnitte.titel: The fixed spot and the Znüni
abschnitte.text: Many forest kindergartens have a **fixed spot**, for example a **forest sofa** made of logs as a circle to sit in. A **tarpaulin** protects against rain. There the children eat their **Znüni**, the mid-morning snack. Because there is no tap in the forest, you bring a water canister and wash your hands with it.

In the forest, clear rules apply. Some **berries and mushrooms** are poisonous, so you eat nothing that you do not know for sure. **Ticks** can get onto the skin from grass and bushes. That is why after the forest day you check the whole body carefully. The children also learn to stay within sight and calling distance of the group.

gewusst: In a forest kindergarten, children often spend more time outdoors than most adults in a whole week.
Many forest kindergartens have a trailer or a hut for very cold days, in which you can warm up.

teile.einleitung: Every cell is filled with a kind of gel, the cytoplasm. In it float the small parts of the cell, the organelles, and many processes of life take place here. The word is also spelt cytoplasm with a C.
wichtigste: Cytoplasm is the cell contents inside the cell membrane, without the cell nucleus.
It consists for the most part of water.
The liquid basic substance is called cytosol.
Ribosomes in the cytoplasm make proteins.
The cytoskeleton of protein threads gives support.
In waterweed you can observe cytoplasmic streaming.
In fully grown plant cells, the cytoplasm usually lies as a thin layer at the edge.

abschnitte.text: The **cytoplasm** is the whole **cell contents inside the cell membrane**, without the cell nucleus. It consists **for the most part of water**, in which many substances are dissolved, for example sugars, salts and proteins. The liquid basic substance is called **cytosol**. In it lie the **organelles**, the small working parts of the cell, similar to organs in a body.

Many organelles are spread through the cytoplasm. Tiny **ribosomes** make **proteins** following the blueprint from the cell nucleus. The **endoplasmic reticulum** is a network of channels. The **Golgi apparatus** packs substances into small vesicles and sends them to where they are needed. The **mitochondria** gain energy from nutrients, and in plant cells **chloroplasts** carry out photosynthesis.

The cytoplasm is not simply a soup. A network of fine protein threads runs through it, the **cytoskeleton**. It gives the cell support and shape, like a framework. It also serves as a rail network on which organelles and vesicles are transported through the cell. During cell division it helps to distribute the genetic material correctly to the two new cells.

In many plant cells, the cytoplasm flows constantly. This movement is called **cytoplasmic streaming**. You can observe it well in the little leaves of **waterweed**, a water plant: under the microscope the green chloroplasts slowly move in a circle. In fully grown plant cells, a large **vacuole** fills the interior, so the cytoplasm usually lies only **as a thin layer at the edge**.

gewusst: The name comes from Greek: “kytos” means vessel or cell, “plasma” means something formed.
Many important steps in the breakdown of sugar to gain energy begin directly in the cytosol.

teile.einleitung: The **Venus flytrap** is a plant that catches animals. With its leaves it snaps shut in a flash. In this way it gets nutrients that are lacking in the soil.
wichtigste: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant.
It catches mainly insects and spiders.
Its trap leaves snap shut in less than a second.
Usually the sensory hairs have to be touched twice.
In the wild it grows only in North Carolina and South Carolina in the USA.
After a catch, the trap stays closed for several days.

abschnitte.text: The Venus flytrap belongs to the **carnivorous plants**. Its trap leaves consist of two halves that look like an open mouth. Along the edge sit long **bristles** like teeth. When the trap is closed, they interlock like a grille. In this way the prey cannot escape.

On the inside of the trap sit fine **sensory hairs**. Usually the trap closes only when these are touched **twice** in quick succession. That way it does not snap shut because of a raindrop. The trap closes in a fraction of a second. This is among the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

After a catch, the trap stays closed for **several days**. During this time the plant releases digestive juices and dissolves the soft parts of the prey. Then the trap opens again. Only hard remains are left.

In the wild, the Venus flytrap grows only in a small area in **North Carolina** and **South Carolina** in the USA. There it grows in wet bogs that are **poor in nutrients**. The soil contains hardly any nitrogen. The caught animals supply it with this important nutrient. It still needs light, because like other plants it carries out photosynthesis.

gewusst: The Venus flytrap can close its trap only a few times, after which the trap leaf dies and new ones grow.
It does not get its food only from insects: like every green plant, it makes sugar itself with sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Vanilla is a popular spice obtained from the fruits of an orchid. Because growing it takes a lot of manual work, real vanilla is among the most expensive spices in the world.
wichtigste: Vanilla is an orchid and grows as a climbing plant.
It originally comes from Mexico, and the Aztecs already used it.
Today Madagascar produces the most vanilla.
Each flower is open for only about one day.
Outside its homeland, every flower has to be pollinated by hand.
The most important flavour substance is vanillin.

abschnitte.text: Vanilla belongs to the **orchids**. It grows as a **liana** and climbs up trees or support posts with **aerial roots**.
