On plantations the plants are kept at a reachable height so that the flowers and fruits are easy to get at. Each **vanilla flower** opens on only a single day. If it is not pollinated then, it wilts and forms no fruit.

Vanilla originally comes from **Mexico**. The **Aztecs** already flavoured their cocoa drink with it. Spanish conquerors brought it to Europe in the 16th century. Today it is grown in many tropical countries. The most real vanilla is supplied by the island of **Madagascar** in the Indian Ocean. A cyclone there can make prices rise sharply worldwide.

In the home of vanilla, the flowers are pollinated mainly by certain **bees**. Elsewhere these animals are missing. For a long time, vanilla therefore bore hardly any fruit outside Mexico. In **1841**, the twelve-year-old **Edmond Albius** invented a simple method of pollinating the flowers by hand with a small stick. He was an enslaved boy on the island of **Réunion**. His method is still used today.

The fruit of vanilla is a long, green **capsule** that is called a pod. Fresh, it hardly smells. Only during **fermentation**, treatment with heat and drying over several weeks, is the most important flavour substance, **vanillin**, produced. The pod turns dark brown in the process. The tiny **black dots** in real vanilla ice cream are the seeds from the fruit. Today vanillin is also made artificially, because real vanilla is very expensive.

The island of **Réunion** used to be called **Île Bourbon**. The well-known **Bourbon vanilla** is named after it. Today the name is used for vanilla from the region in the Indian Ocean, including from Madagascar.

gewusst: After saffron, vanilla is regarded as one of the most expensive spices in the world.
A single vanilla pod contains thousands of tiny seeds.

teile.einleitung: A volcano is a mountain from which hot rock can emerge. Deep inside the Earth, rock melts into magma, which forces its way to the surface. Volcanoes can destroy whole landscapes, but they also create fertile soils and new islands.
wichtigste: A volcano is a mountain from which hot rock can emerge.
Molten rock is called magma inside the Earth and lava at the surface.
Most volcanoes lie where tectonic plates meet or drift apart.
Around the Pacific lies the Pacific Ring of Fire with very many volcanoes.
Etna in Sicily is the highest active volcano in Europe.
In AD 79, Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii.
In Switzerland there are no active volcanoes.

abschnitte.text: A **volcano** arises where **magma** from inside the Earth pushes up to the surface. Under the volcano the magma often collects in a magma chamber. If the pressure rises, the volcano erupts and spits out **lava**, ash and gases. Lava is about 700 to 1,200 degrees hot and solidifies into rock as it cools.

Most volcanoes lie at the edges of the tectonic plates. Around the Pacific so many volcanoes line up that people speak of the **Pacific Ring of Fire**, for example in Japan, Indonesia and Chile. In Iceland two plates drift apart, which is why the island is very volcanic. Other volcanoes, as in Hawaii, lie above a hot spot in the Earth’s mantle, a hotspot.

**Shield volcanoes** such as Mauna Loa in Hawaii are flat and broad, because their runny lava flows far. **Stratovolcanoes** such as Vesuvius, Etna or Fuji are steep and built up from layers of lava and ash. Their thick lava often blocks the vent, which is why they often erupt explosively. In this, clouds of glowing gas can race down the slopes at great speed.

In AD 79, Vesuvius buried the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash. The eruption of Tambora in Indonesia in 1815 cooled the climate worldwide. It was followed in 1816 by the “year without a summer”, which also led to failed harvests and hunger in Switzerland. In 2010 the ash cloud of Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland brought air traffic in Europe to a standstill for days.

In Switzerland there are no active volcanoes. Very close by, in the German **Hegau** near Schaffhausen, however, stand extinct volcanoes such as the Hohentwiel. They were active many millions of years ago. Swiss researchers study volcanoes worldwide, and the ash of distant eruptions can blow as far as across the Alps.

Volcanic ash weathers into very fertile soils, which is why many people live on volcanoes despite the danger. In Iceland, geothermal heat is used to heat houses and generate electricity. Pumice and basalt are used as building material. **Volcanologists** monitor active volcanoes with instruments in order to predict eruptions early.

begriffe.erklaerung: molten rock deep under the ground
magma that has emerged at the Earth’s surface
funnel-shaped opening at the top of the volcano
huge plates of rock of which the Earth’s crust is made and which move slowly
an expert who studies volcanoes

gewusst: On Earth there are about 1,500 volcanoes that count as potentially active, and most of those under the sea are not even counted.
The largest known volcano in the solar system is Olympus Mons on Mars, which is more than twice as high as Mount Everest.
Stromboli in Italy has been erupting almost constantly in small explosions for over 2,000 years.

teile.einleitung: A pasture is a meadow on which animals eat the grass directly from the ground. In Switzerland you often see cows, sheep, goats and horses on pastures. By the way, the German word Weide also means a tree, the willow.
wichtigste: On a pasture, the animals eat the grass themselves.
Cows, sheep, goats and horses are typical grazing animals.
A pasture fence keeps the animals on the pasture.
In an electric fence a weak current flows.
A fenced pasture for horses is called a paddock.
Cow pats fertilise the pasture.
Cows, sheep and goats are ruminants.

abschnitte.text: A **pasture** is a meadow on which animals feed. The farmer does not have to mow the grass, because the animals get their **food themselves**. When animals eat grass on the pasture, we say they **graze**. On a meadow, on the other hand, the grass is mown and brought into the barn as hay or grass.

In Switzerland you see mainly **cows** and **sheep** on pastures. Goats and horses also like to eat grass. Cows, sheep and goats are **ruminants**. They first chew the grass roughly and swallow it. Later they bring it back up from the stomach and chew it again in peace.

A **pasture fence** keeps the animals on the pasture. In this way they do not run onto the road or into the neighbouring field. On many fences a **weak current** flows. If an animal touches this **electric fence**, it feels a short, light shock. After that it keeps its distance. A fenced pasture for horses is called a **paddock**.

Cows leave **cow pats** on the pasture. That is their dung. It contains many nutrients and so **fertilises** the soil. In a cow pat also live many beetles and worms that break it down. In this way the nutrients return to the soil, and the grass grows again.

In summer, many farmers take their animals up to the **alp**. There they graze on **alpine pastures** high in the mountains. This time is called **summering**. In autumn the animals return to the valley, often in a decorated **descent from the alp**. Alpine pastures keep the landscape open and are a habitat for many flowers.

gewusst: A large part of the area used for farming in Switzerland is grassland for meadows and pastures.
A cow eats many kilograms of grass a day and chews it again for several hours.

teile.einleitung: Under the forest floor lies a huge web of fine fungal threads. It connects the roots of many trees with one another. This network is jokingly called the “Wood Wide Web”, after the “World Wide Web” of the internet. How much the trees above exchange is disputed in research.
wichtigste: The “Wood Wide Web” is a network of mycorrhizal fungi that connects trees.
Experts speak of a common mycorrhizal network.
In 1997 the term appeared on the cover of the journal Nature.
The researcher Suzanne Simard used marked carbon to show an exchange between birches and Douglas firs.
Peter Wohlleben made the subject well known in 2015 with his book “The Hidden Life of Trees”.
In 2023, researchers criticised that the evidence for deliberate help from mother trees is weak.

abschnitte.text: Many trees live together with fungi. The fine fungal threads, the **hyphae**, wrap around the roots or grow into them. This partnership is called **mycorrhiza**. The fungus fetches water and mineral salts from the soil and gives them to the tree. In return it gets **sugar** from the tree. So both have an advantage.

A single fungus can be connected to the roots of **several plants**, even of different tree species. In this way a **common mycorrhizal network** arises, in English the “Common Mycorrhizal Network”. It is the scientific basis of the catchphrase “Wood Wide Web”. That such networks exist is undisputed.

The Canadian forest ecologist **Suzanne Simard** marked trees with special **carbon isotopes**. For example, you let a tree take up carbon dioxide with carbon-13 and then measure whether the isotope turns up in neighbouring plants. Simard found carbon that had got from **birches to Douglas firs**. The journal **Nature** reported on it in 1997 and headlined it “The Wood-Wide Web”.

abschnitte.titel: The yellow bird’s-nest as a free rider
abschnitte.text: The **yellow bird’s-nest**, called Fichtenspargel in German, is a forest plant without **chlorophyll**. So it cannot carry out photosynthesis. Instead it taps into the fungal network. It gets sugar through mycorrhizal fungi that are connected to trees at the same time. In this way it lives indirectly from the trees around it.

In his book **“The Hidden Life of Trees”** of 2015, Peter Wohlleben describes how trees are connected through fungal webs. Some of his accounts are regarded in research as **simplified**. In 2023, a review by **Justine Karst** and colleagues showed that many field studies do not support the widespread claims. Above all, the evidence that **mother trees** deliberately supply their young is weak.

gewusst: Most land plants live together with mycorrhizal fungi.
Many edible fungi such as the porcini are mycorrhizal fungi and therefore grow only near certain trees.

teile.einleitung: How does the water get from the roots to the top of a tall tree, without any pump? The answer is the **transpiration pull**. The evaporation of water at the leaves constantly draws new water upwards.
wichtigste: The transpiration pull arises mainly at the cell walls of the mesophyll in the leaf.
The plant gives off over 90 per cent of the water it takes in again.
Most of it leaves the leaf through the stomata.
Warm, dry, sunny and windy weather increases transpiration.
The cooling from evaporation cools the leaf.
With a potometer you can measure the water uptake of a shoot.

abschnitte.text: Inside a leaf lies the **mesophyll**, a tissue made of many cells with air spaces between them. At the damp **cell walls** of the mesophyll, water evaporates into these air spaces. The water vapour then flows out **through the stomata**. Where water evaporates, new water is drawn up from the pipes. This creates a pull that reaches all the way down to the roots.

Water molecules hold tightly together, which is called **cohesion**. That is why the water in the fine pipes of the wood forms a continuous **column of water**. If a part is drawn away at the top, the rest follows like a chain. In the root, the **water potential** is lower than in the damp soil. That is why water flows from the soil into the root. More than **90 per cent** of the water taken up is given off again by the plant into the air.

Transpiration is strongest in **warm, dry, sunny and windy** weather. Dry air takes up a lot of water vapour. **Wind** removes the damp layer of air that lies directly above the leaf, the so-called **boundary layer**. Then even more water can evaporate. In very dry conditions, the plant closes its stomata to save water.

When water evaporates, **evaporative cooling** occurs, much as with sweating. It **cools the leaf** on hot days. That is why it is especially pleasant in the shade of large trees. In lessons, transpiration can be measured with a **potometer**. A cut shoot is placed in a tube of water, and you can see how fast the water level drops.

gewusst: A large broadleaved tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water on a hot summer day.
Thanks to the transpiration pull, water also reaches the tops of giant redwoods, which grow to over 100 metres.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss forest is protected by a law of its own: the **Federal Act on Forests**, in short the Forest Act. It makes sure that the forest is kept and is accessible to everyone.
wichtigste: The Forest Act was passed on 4 October 1991 and came into force in 1993.
It replaced the old Forest Police Act.
The forest area of Switzerland is to be kept.
Clearing is in principle forbidden.
Everyone may enter the forest freely.
The cantons are mainly responsible for enforcement.
At federal level, the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) is responsible for the forest.

abschnitte.text: The present **Forest Act** was passed on **4 October 1991** and came into force in **1993**. It replaced the old **Forest Police Act**. A core of the law is **forest conservation**: the forest is to be kept in its area and its spatial distribution. It protects against natural hazards, supplies timber and is an important habitat.

**Clearing** is the permanent conversion of forest into other land, for example into building land. Clearing is in principle **forbidden**. An exception needs a permit for important reasons. Also important: what counts as forest is what is actually covered with trees and fulfils forest functions. That is why forest that has grown by itself on an abandoned pasture is also in principle **protected**.

Everyone may **enter the forest freely**, even if it belongs to a private person. The forest is meant to be accessible to the public. But you may not drive into the forest or on forest roads with **private motor vehicles**. In principle this is allowed only for forestry work. There are special rules for exceptions.

The **Confederation** sets out the principles. The **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)** is responsible. It prepares the groundwork and supports projects in the forest. Enforcement is mainly carried out by the **cantons** with their own forestry services. They approve, for example, timber felling, that is, the cutting down of trees.

gewusst: In Switzerland you may also enter a private forest without asking the owner.
If a pasture is no longer used and becomes overgrown, it can become legally protected forest.

teile.einleitung: Cow parsley is one of the first large flowers that bloom on the meadows in spring. Its many small white flowers form umbrellas. In May, whole meadows can look white from it.
wichtigste: Cow parsley has many small white flowers.
The flowers sit in an umbrella that is called an umbel.
The stem is hollow inside and grooved outside.
The leaves are finely pinnate like a fern.
It grows especially often on heavily fertilised meadows.
It can grow up to about 1.5 metres tall.
It looks like poisonous plants such as hemlock, so it is not eaten.

abschnitte.text: **Cow parsley** has many small **white flowers**. They sit on stalks that all start from one point. In this way an **umbrella** arises, which is called an **umbel**. Plants with such umbrellas of flowers are called **umbellifers**. In May, some meadows look entirely white because of cow parsley.

The stem of cow parsley is **hollow** inside like a tube and **grooved** outside. The leaves are **finely pinnate**. They recall the fronds of a **fern**. Cow parsley often grows hip-high and can reach about **1.5 metres**.

Cow parsley flowers **early in the year**, from April and above all in **May**. So it comes before many other meadow flowers. It loves meadows with a lot of **fertiliser**. There it grows quickly and becomes very common. Many insects such as beetles and flies visit its open flowers.

Cow parsley looks like some very **poisonous umbellifers**, for example **hemlock**. For non-experts it is hard to tell these plants apart for sure. That is why a simple rule applies: **white umbrella flowers from the meadow are not picked or eaten.** Other wild plants should also be eaten only if an experienced person has identified them for certain.

gewusst: Cow parsley is related to carrot, parsley and fennel, which also belong to the umbellifers.
When many meadows flower white in spring, it is often a sign of heavily fertilised soils.

teile.einleitung: The bank is the strip of land right by the water, for example by a stream. Here water and land meet, and that is why especially many plants and animals live there.
wichtigste: The stream bank is the edge where stream and land meet.
Willows and alders like to grow on the bank, because they like wet soil.
Stinging nettles also like the damp, nutrient-rich soil.
Kingfisher, grey heron and dipper look for their food here.
The beaver is living again on many streams and rivers in Switzerland.
Rubbish never belongs on the bank, you always take it with you.

abschnitte.text: On the bank the ground is often damp or even wet. Not all trees like that. **Willows** and **alders**, however, feel at home here. You often see them in a row along streams. Their roots hold the earth in place. That way the bank is not so easily washed away in a flood.

Many plants grow on a stream bank. A well-known one is the **stinging nettle**. It likes damp, nutrient-rich soil. Its fine **stinging hairs** burn on the skin when you touch them. For the caterpillars of many butterflies, however, the nettle is an important food plant. In addition there are grasses, sedges and flowers.

The **kingfisher** is blue and orange. It sits still on a branch above the water. If it sees a small fish, it plunges in in a flash. The **grey heron** has long legs and stands calmly in the shallow water. Then it strikes with its pointed beak. The **dipper** can even dive under and look for insect larvae on the bed of the stream.

The **beaver** is a large rodent. With its strong teeth it gnaws down trees on the bank. From branches it builds **dams** and lodges. That way it dams up the water and creates new ponds in which other animals live. In Switzerland the beaver had once disappeared. Today it lives again on many streams and rivers.

A natural bank is a valuable habitat. In Switzerland many streams used to be straightened and lined with walls. Today some are being made **more natural again** so that animals and plants can return. Everyone can help: **rubbish** never belongs on the bank, because it harms animals and pollutes the water.

gewusst: The dipper is the only songbird here that can walk and dive under water.
A kingfisher dives into the water so fast that you can hardly see it.

teile.einleitung: If someone has eaten something poisonous, every minute counts. In Switzerland, **Tox Info Suisse**, the national poisons information centre, helps then. Its emergency number is **145**.
wichtigste: Tox Info Suisse is Switzerland’s poisons emergency line, with the number 145.
The number can be reached around the clock.
If someone is unconscious, call the ambulance number 144 straight away.
Never make someone vomit yourself.
Take a piece of the plant with you so that experts can identify it.
Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: **Tox Info Suisse** is based in **Zurich** and can be reached **around the clock**, every day of the year. The calls are answered by **doctors and medical experts**. They say whether a poisoning is dangerous and what to do. Often they can reassure you, because many poisonings are harmless. If necessary, they send the people affected to a doctor or to hospital.

If a poisoned child is **unconscious**, has difficulty breathing or has convulsions, you call **144** straight away, the number for the ambulance. Then an ambulance comes as quickly as possible. The number 145 is for questions and advice, the number 144 for acute emergencies. If in doubt, it is never wrong to get help.

abschnitte.titel: What to do with poisonous plants
abschnitte.text: If a younger brother or sister has eaten a poisonous berry, you first get **an adult**. You should **never make someone vomit yourself**, because that can do more harm than good. When you call, the expert will want to know **what, how much and when** something was eaten. The child’s age and weight are also important. If you go to the doctor, you take **a piece of the plant** with you so that it can be identified.

For **unknown berries** in the forest, there is a simple rule: **never eat them without an adult**. Many poisonous berries look pretty, for example those of deadly nightshade or mezereon. If **plant sap gets into the eye**, you rinse the eye straight away and thoroughly **with water**. Medicines, cleaning products and mushrooms are also among the common reasons for a call. It is best to keep such things out of the reach of children.

gewusst: Many calls to Tox Info Suisse concern small children who have put something in their mouth.
Many calls can be settled with advice over the phone, without a visit to the doctor being necessary.

teile.einleitung: **Peat** is a dark, soft mass that forms in bogs. It consists of plant remains that have not fully decomposed. Peat grows very slowly and preserves traces from past millennia.
wichtigste: Peat consists of incompletely decomposed plant remains.
It forms because oxygen is lacking in the wet bog and the water is acidic.
A layer of peat in a raised bog grows only about 1 millimetre per year.
Light, slightly decomposed peat from the upper layers is called white peat.
In the past dried peat was a fuel, today it is mainly found in potting compost.
Over millions of years, peat can turn into coal.

abschnitte.text: In a **bog** the ground is constantly wet. Dead plants, above all **peat mosses**, sink into the water. There **oxygen is lacking** and the water is **acidic**. Bacteria and fungi, which otherwise break down plant remains, can hardly work as a result. The remains are only **incompletely decomposed** and pile up. That is how peat forms over a long time.

A layer of peat in a **raised bog** grows only about **1 millimetre per year**. So one metre of peat takes about a thousand years. The upper, young layers are light and only slightly decomposed. They are called **white peat**. Further down lies older, more strongly decomposed and darker **black peat**.

Because hardly anything rots in peat, things are preserved for **thousands of years**. Researchers find **pollen** in it, that is, flower dust, as well as wood and sometimes objects from earlier times. **Pollen analysis** examines the pollen from different layers of peat. That way you can tell which trees and plants used to grow in an area. The climate of past times can also be estimated this way.

In the past, peat was cut, dried and used **as a fuel for heating**. Today peat is mainly used for **potting and garden compost**, because it stores water well. Since peat extraction destroys bogs and harms the climate, there is more and more **peat-free compost**. If peat lies under pressure and heat for millions of years, it can turn into **lignite** and later **hard coal**.

gewusst: One metre of peat can contain about a thousand years of plant history.
Bogs store a great deal of carbon, even though they cover only a small part of the land surface.

teile.einleitung: In **vertical farming**, plants do not grow in a field but on floors one above another in buildings. Light, warmth, water and nutrients are controlled exactly. This saves space but needs a lot of energy.
wichtigste: Vertical farming is growing plants on floors lying one above another in buildings.
Many plants use hydroponics, that is, growing without soil in a nutrient solution.
Aquaponics combines fish farming and plant growing in one cycle.
LED lamps give mainly red and blue light.
The biggest disadvantage is the high energy use.
Leafy vegetables and herbs are especially suitable.
The idea became well known around the year 2000 through Dickson Despommier.

abschnitte.text: In a vertical farm, growing areas in halls or high-rise buildings are **stacked**. Light, temperature and nutrients are fully controlled. Because weather and seasons play no part, you can harvest all year round. Together with the many floors, this gives a much higher **yield per area of ground** than in a field.

Many vertical farms work with **hydroponics**. The roots stand in a **nutrient solution**, which supplies all the nutrients in a cycle. Evaporated water is caught and reused. That is why vertical farming often needs much less water than growing outdoors. In **aquaponics**, fish are added too: bacteria turn their waste into nutrients for the plants, and the plants clean the water.

Instead of sunlight, the plants use **LED lamps**. They give mainly **red and blue light**. The green leaf pigment chlorophyll absorbs these colours especially well, while green light is reflected more. That is why many plants glow violet-pink.

**Leafy vegetables** such as lettuce and **herbs** are especially suitable. They grow quickly, stay small and are eaten almost entirely. Staple foods such as cereals would be far too expensive indoors. In a field, cereals need a lot of space but hardly any electricity.

The biggest disadvantage is the high **energy use** for light and air conditioning. This makes the products expensive. Whether the climate balance is good depends strongly on the source of the electricity. The idea was made known around the year 2000 by **Dickson Despommier**, a professor at Columbia University in New York. With students he developed the concept of farms in skyscrapers.

gewusst: In a vertical farm, weather and seasons play no part, so you can harvest all year round.
Many vertical farms glow violet because green light is missing.

teile.einleitung: The World Biodiversity Council is an international body that sums up the state of knowledge about the diversity of life. It is meant to help politicians make good decisions to protect nature. Its English abbreviation is IPBES.
wichtigste: IPBES stands in full for Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services.
It was founded in April 2012 in Panama City.
The secretariat is based on the UN campus in Bonn.
It is often compared with the World Climate Council IPCC.
The first thematic report of 2016 dealt with pollinators.
The report of 2019 names the change in land and sea use as the most important driver.
According to the report of 2023, over 37,000 alien species have become established worldwide.

abschnitte.titel: What is the World Biodiversity Council?
abschnitte.text: **Biodiversity** means the diversity of life: species, habitats and the differences within a species. The **World Biodiversity Council** assesses the state of knowledge on this. It is an **interface** between science and politics. It does not carry out research of its own but sums up existing studies in **reports**. It may not decide binding rules.

The council was founded in **April 2012** in **Panama City** by over 90 governments. Its **secretariat** is on the **UN campus in Bonn**. Other UN organisations for environment and climate are based there too. Switzerland is a member of IPBES.

abschnitte.titel: The comparison with the World Climate Council
abschnitte.text: The World Biodiversity Council is often compared with the **World Climate Council IPCC**. Both sum up the state of knowledge in reports. Experts from many countries write these reports. The **summaries** are then adopted jointly by the governments.

The first thematic report appeared in **2016**. It dealt with **pollinators** such as bees and their importance for food production. Many crops depend on pollination. The large **global report of 2019** names five direct drivers of species loss: change in land and sea use, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species. On land and in fresh water, **land-use change** has the greatest influence.

In **2023** a report on **invasive species** appeared. These are alien species that spread and cause damage. The report counts over **37,000** established alien species spread by humans. About 3,500 of them count as **invasive** and harmful. They threaten native plants and animals.

gewusst: The global report of 2019 estimates that about a million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction.
Besides scientific studies, IPBES also draws on the knowledge of indigenous peoples and local communities.

teile.einleitung: When we think of bees, we usually mean the honey bee. But there are many more bees: the wild bees. In Switzerland about 600 species live, and they are important pollinators for flowers, fruit trees and vegetables.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, about 600 species of wild bee are known.
Most wild bees live alone, not in a colony.
Many species dig their nests in the ground.
Wild bees collect nectar and pollen but supply no honey for the beekeeper.
Bumblebees also belong to the wild bees.
Many species have become rare and need protection.

abschnitte.text: The honey bee is only one single species. Besides it, there are about **600 wild bee species** in Switzerland. Some are only a few millimetres small, others big and strong. The furry **bumblebees** are also wild bees. Many species look more like small flies or wasps, so they hardly stand out.

Most wild bees live **solitary**, that is, alone. Each female builds her own nest and makes small chambers in it. Into each chamber go a store of pollen and nectar and an egg. The larva eats the store and grows up in it. Only a few species, such as the bumblebees, live in a colony with a queen.

abschnitte.titel: Nests in the ground, in wood and in stems
abschnitte.text: Many species nest **in the ground**. The **mining bees** dig small tunnels in sandy, open places, and in front of the entrance there is often a small heap of soil. The **red mason bee** uses cracks in walls and hollow stems. The **wool carder bee** scrapes fine hairs off plants and lines its nest with them. The big, blue-black **carpenter bee** gnaws tunnels in rotten, dead wood.

Like the honey bee, wild bees collect **nectar and pollen**. But they do not lay in large stores of honey that a beekeeper could harvest. Instead, they are hard-working **pollinators**. Some species fly even in cool weather, others visit only certain flowers. That is why they complement the honey bee very well.

Wild bees need two things: **food** and **nesting places**. A meadow with many different **wild flowers** offers food from spring into autumn. Open, sandy places, deadwood and hollow plant stems serve as nests. A **bee hotel** helps some species that nest in tubes. Whoever does without poison in the garden also protects the bees.

gewusst: Male bees have no sting, so they cannot sting at all.
Some wild bees collect pollen from only a single group of plants. If this plant is missing, the bee cannot live there.
The violet carpenter bee is among the largest bees in Europe.

teile.einleitung: A tornado is a rapidly rotating column of air that reaches from a thunderstorm cloud down to the ground. It is one of the most violent weather phenomena on Earth. Inside it, the winds can blow faster than in any other storm.
wichtigste: A tornado is a rapidly rotating column of air.
It reaches from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground.
The strongest tornadoes reach wind speeds of over 400 kilometres per hour.
Most tornadoes occur in the USA, especially in the so-called Tornado Alley.
A tornado over a lake or the sea is called a waterspout.
The strength is given on the Fujita scale.
Weak tornadoes also occur occasionally in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **tornado** is a rotating column of air that is connected to a thunderstorm cloud and touches the ground. You often see a grey **funnel** or trunk hanging down from the cloud. It becomes visible through water droplets, dust and debris. A tornado is usually only a few dozen to a few hundred metres wide.

Tornadoes usually form in very strong thunderstorms, often in so-called **supercells**. In these, warm, damp air near the ground meets cooler, drier air higher up. If the wind direction changes strongly with height, the air in the thunderstorm begins to rotate. This rotation can extend downwards and turn into a tornado.

The strength of a tornado is measured by the damage it does, using the **Fujita scale**, today in the USA with the extended version EF0 to EF5. A weak tornado blows tiles off roofs, a very strong one can destroy houses completely. Most tornadoes last only a few minutes. Some strong tornadoes, however, travel for over an hour and for dozens of kilometres.

Tornadoes are most common in the United States, where over a thousand are counted per year. Especially affected is **Tornado Alley** in the Great Plains, for example in Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas. There, damp air from the Gulf of Mexico meets dry air from the Rocky Mountains. In Europe, too, there are hundreds of tornadoes every year, but most are weak.

In Switzerland tornadoes are rare, but they do occur. They are mostly weak whirlwinds that last only a short time. Over lakes such as Lake Geneva or Lake Maggiore, **waterspouts** are occasionally seen. But not every storm damage comes from a tornado, and often strong downdrafts from thunderstorms are the cause.

Weather services watch thunderstorms with **radar** and can therefore warn of rotating storm cells. In the USA, sirens wail when there is a danger of tornadoes, and many houses have a storm shelter. If you are caught by a tornado, it is best to find a cellar or a windowless room in the middle of the house. A car, on the other hand, offers hardly any protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very strong, long-lived thunderstorm with a rotating updraft
A tornado over a body of water
A scale used to classify the strength of a tornado by the damage it causes
A trunk-shaped cloud that hangs down from a thunderstorm

gewusst: A tornado can whirl cars and even houses through the air.
In the USA there are researchers who follow tornadoes with special vehicles, and they are called storm chasers.
Tornadoes in the northern hemisphere mostly rotate anticlockwise.

teile.einleitung: Some plants live in places where it hardly rains and the sun burns. Such plants are called xerophytes. They have developed many tricks to save water, to store it or to find it deep in the ground.
wichtigste: A xerophyte is a plant adapted to dryness.
The Greek word “xeros” means dry.
The spines of cacti are modified leaves.
CAM plants open their stomata at night.
Dense hairs and sunken stomata reduce evaporation.
Some desert plants reach deep groundwater with long taproots.
In the Valais there are dry rocky steppes with many such plants.

abschnitte.text: The word **xerophyte** comes from the Greek “xeros” for dry. Xerophytes are plants that are adapted to **dryness**. Plants lose water mainly through the **stomata**, which are tiny pores in the leaves. That is why many adaptations start exactly there. Other plants store water in thick leaves or stems, and these are called **succulents**.

In **cacti**, the leaves are modified into **spines** that hardly evaporate any water. Photosynthesis is taken over by the green stem. Other plants have **dense hairs**. They slow the wind at the leaf surface and keep a damp layer of air. Light-coloured hairs also reflect sunlight. Some grasses **roll up their leaves**, so that the stomata lie protected inside. In others the stomata sit in small **pits**, where damp air stays put.

Many desert plants have a special metabolism, **CAM metabolism**. They open their stomata **at night**, when it is cool and little water evaporates. Then they take up carbon dioxide and store it as malic acid. By day the stomata stay closed. The stored carbon dioxide is then used for photosynthesis.

Some desert plants send long **taproots** many metres deep. In this way they reach **groundwater** that lies far below the surface. Especially remarkable are the **resurrection plants**. They can **dry out** almost completely and then look dead. After rain they take up water again and turn green within hours.

There are also very dry places in Switzerland. The **Valais** is surrounded by high mountains that keep off the rain. On its sunny slopes, **steppe-like dry grasslands** and rocky steppes therefore thrive. Many plants adapted to drought grow there. The **houseleek**, too, with its thick rosettes of leaves on rocks and walls, stores water in its leaves.

gewusst: With the false rose of Jericho you can watch how the dry ball opens again in water and turns green.
A large cactus can store so much water that it survives long dry spells.

teile.einleitung: In winter it is cold and dark, and the ground is often frozen. Plants can then hardly grow. They get through this time in winter dormancy and save their strength for spring.
wichtigste: In winter dormancy, trees hardly grow and save strength.
Broadleaved trees shed their leaves in autumn.
Annual summer flowers spend the winter only as seeds.
In many meadow plants, the roots survive in the soil.
A blanket of snow protects small plants from hard frost.
Winter wheat is sown in autumn and spends the winter in the field.

abschnitte.text: In winter, broadleaved trees **rest** and hardly grow. As early as autumn they shed their **leaves**. Through the leaves, a lot of water would otherwise evaporate. But from the frozen ground the roots could not supply any water. The new shoots wait well protected in the **buds** for spring. Only when it gets warmer do the trees grow on.

abschnitte.titel: Spending the winter as seeds or roots
abschnitte.text: **Annual** summer flowers die off completely in autumn. Only their **seeds** survive the winter and germinate in spring. In many **meadow plants** the green dies off, but the **roots** in the soil live on. Other plants store nutrients in **bulbs** or **tubers**, like the tulip. In spring they sprout anew from them.

In snow there is a great deal of **air**. That is why a blanket of snow acts like a **warm blanket**. Under it, it gets much less cold than on the surface. Small plants on the ground are in this way protected from hard frost. Without snow, they are more likely to freeze in great cold.

abschnitte.titel: Winter dormancy in field and garden
abschnitte.text: **Winter wheat** is sown in autumn. It germinates and grows a little, rests in winter and grows on in spring. In **late winter**, gardeners often prune the fruit trees. The tree is resting and has no leaves, so you can see the branches well. **Geraniums** cannot stand frost. You keep them through the winter **light, cool and frost-free** and put them out again in spring.

gewusst: Animals such as the squirrel also rest in winter: they sleep a lot but wake up in between and eat.
Winter wheat needs a period of cold so that it forms ears well the next year.

teile.einleitung: Wild animals travel to find food, new territories or spawning waters. Roads, railway lines and settlements often block their way. Wildlife corridors are links over which animals get safely from one habitat to another.
wichtigste: A wildlife corridor connects two habitats for wild animals.
Motorways are fenced and heavily used, so they are almost impossible for roe deer and red deer to cross.
Wildlife bridges, also called green bridges, lead animals over the motorway.
Toads and frogs cross roads through small tunnels with guide fences.
Hedges and fences guide the animals to the crossing.
Wildlife corridors also help to prevent wildlife accidents.

abschnitte.text: Many animals do not stay in the same place all their lives. Young animals look for a territory of their own, others move to feeding places. The **lynx**, for example, lives in large territories in the forest. Young lynxes have to travel far until they find a free place. A **wildlife corridor** is the route that connects these habitats.

**Motorways** are a big obstacle. They are fenced and heavily used. The fences do keep the animals off the carriageway, but they also block their routes. **Dense building** also interrupts corridors: if villages grow together, no passage stays free. In Switzerland there are about 300 supra-regional wildlife corridors, and many of them are impaired.

A **wildlife bridge** or **green bridge** is covered with soil, grass and shrubs. For the animals it feels like natural terrain, so they accept the bridge. **Hedges and fences** nearby guide the animals to the crossing. For **toads and frogs**, small tunnels are built under the road. Guide fences lead the animals there, and so they reach their spawning waters safely.

If animals use safe crossings, fewer of them run onto the carriageway. This means fewer **wildlife accidents**, and that also protects drivers. In addition, groups of animals from different areas can meet again. To keep corridors free, they are taken into account in the **spatial planning** of the Confederation, cantons and municipalities.

gewusst: Wildlife bridges are used not only by deer but also by foxes, badgers and many small animals.
In spring, volunteers in many places help to carry toads safely across the road in buckets.

teile.einleitung: A forest is a large area on which many trees grow close together. It is a habitat for countless animals, plants and fungi. In Switzerland, about a third of the country is covered with forest.
wichtigste: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest (as of 2025).
A forest is divided into storeys, from the moss layer to the treetops.
In the forest, moss often grows as a green, soft cushion on stones and tree trunks.
The stag wears a large set of antlers, which it sheds every year.
The woodpecker knocks holes in tree trunks with its beak.
In the forest you may make a fire only at a fireplace.
In Switzerland everyone may enter the forest freely.

abschnitte.text: A **forest** is an area densely covered with trees and with a climate of its own. In the forest it is cooler and damper in summer than in the open field. A distinction is made between **broadleaved forest**, coniferous forest and mixed forest. In Switzerland the spruce is the most common tree, and the beech the most common broadleaved tree.

Right at the bottom lies the moss layer with mosses, fungi and lichens. Above it follows the **herb layer** with ferns, grasses and flowers such as the wood anemone. The shrub layer is formed by shrubs such as hazel and elder and by young trees. At the very top spreads the tree layer with the crowns of the big trees.

The **red deer** wears a large set of antlers, which it sheds every late winter and grows anew. Roe deer, fox, badger, wild boar and squirrel also live in the Swiss forest. The **woodpecker** hammers holes in tree trunks to find insects and to build nesting holes. In old woodpecker holes, tits, bats or edible dormice later live.

Mosses form soft, green cushions on stones, tree trunks and the ground. They soak up water like a sponge and release it slowly again. Fungi, earthworms, woodlice and bacteria break down leaves and dead wood into fertile soil. Many fungi are connected underground with the tree roots and swap nutrients with them.

abschnitte.titel: What do we need the forest for?
abschnitte.text: The forest supplies **timber** for building and heating and produces oxygen. It filters rainwater and stores it, which is why water from forest areas is especially clean. In the mountains, about half of the forest protects villages and roads from avalanches and rockfall. The forest is also a popular place for walks, games and recreation.

In Switzerland you may enter the forest freely, which is even written in the law. You may make a fire only at an official **fireplace**, and in dry weather a fire ban often applies. You take litter home with you again, and dogs belong on the lead in the breeding and birthing season. Staying on the paths protects plants and animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: a forest in which broadleaved and coniferous trees grow together
bony growth on the head of deer that grows anew every year
the storey of the forest with flowers, ferns and grasses
a forest that protects people and buildings from avalanches, rockfall and debris flows

gewusst: The forest area of Switzerland is growing, especially in the Alps, because many alpine pastures are no longer used.
A great spotted woodpecker can strike with its beak up to about 20 times a second.
Trees in the forest are connected with one another through fungal threads in the soil, which is sometimes called the “wood wide web”.

teile.einleitung: Plants grow because their cells divide. From one cell, two arise, and from two, four. So that every new cell gets everything it needs, cell division runs in precisely ordered steps.
wichtigste: Before division, the genetic material is doubled.
In mitosis, two daughter nuclei with the same genetic information arise.
At the start of mitosis, the nuclear envelope breaks down.
In metaphase, the chromosomes lie in the middle of the cell.
In anaphase, the chromosome halves are pulled to the poles.
The spindle apparatus pulls the chromosomes apart.
Plant cells form a cell plate in the middle as a new dividing wall.

abschnitte.text: A plant grows as its cells divide and then stretch. The cells divide especially often in the **tips of root and shoot**. There lie **meristems** in which new cells arise constantly. In this way the plant grows longer. In injuries, too, cell divisions help to close wounds.

Before a cell divides, it has to **double its genetic material**. In this the **DNA** is copied exactly. Only in this way does each daughter cell get the complete genetic information. The nuclear division in which two daughter nuclei with the **same genetic information** arise is called **mitosis**. Both daughter cells receive the same genes.

At the start the DNA condenses into **chromosomes**, and the **nuclear envelope breaks down**. In **metaphase**, the chromosomes line up in one plane in the middle of the cell. There they can be seen especially well. In **anaphase**, the two halves of each chromosome separate and are pulled to the opposite **poles**. At the end a new envelope forms around each daughter nucleus.

The chromosomes do not move by themselves. The **spindle apparatus** consists of fine **protein tubes**. It attaches to the chromosomes and pulls their halves apart. For it to reach the chromosomes, the nuclear envelope has to disappear beforehand. After the division, the spindle apparatus is broken down again.

After the nuclear division, the rest of the cell is divided too. In **plant cells**, a **cell plate** forms in the middle of the cell. It grows from the inside outwards until it reaches the old cell wall. From it arises the new **dividing wall** between the daughter cells. **Animal cells** have no firm cell wall and instead pinch in from outside.

gewusst: In an onion root tip you can see cells in different phases of mitosis under the microscope.
The word mitosis comes from the Greek word for thread, because the chromosomes look like threads under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: Whoever hikes high up in the Alps notices that at some point the forest ends. This line is called the forest line. Above it, only single trees, shrubs, grass and flowers grow.
wichtigste: The forest line is the upper limit of the closed forest.
A little higher lies the tree line, up to which single upright trees still grow.
In the northern Swiss Alps the forest line lies at about 1,800 metres.
In the central Alps, for example in the Valais and the Engadine, it lies at around 2,300 metres.
Above all the lack of warmth in summer limits tree growth.
Between forest and open pastures lies the battle zone with crooked, single trees.
In many places the forest is slowly growing higher up today.

abschnitte.text: The **forest line** is the height above which no closed forest grows. The trees there no longer stand close enough together to form a forest. A little further up lies the **tree line**. Up to there, single upright trees still grow. Between the two lines lies a transition zone.

Trees need a certain minimum warmth in the growing season to form new wood. Further up, the summer is too short and too cool. As a **rule of thumb**: the forest line lies roughly where the warmest month reaches an average of about 10 °C. Wind, snow and frost also make life hard for the trees.

In the damper and cooler **northern Alps** the forest ends at about 1,800 metres. In the **central Alps**, for example in the Valais and the Engadine, it climbs to about 2,300 metres. There the mountain massifs are large and high, and the summers are warmer and sunnier. That is why the forest can grow higher there.

In the transition area the trees stand singly and often look stunted. It is called the **battle zone**, because the trees fight against cold, wind, snow and **frost desiccation**. Frost desiccation means: in winter the needles lose water by evaporation, but no new water comes from the frozen ground. Many trees grow here low, crooked or only on one side. Often the **dwarf mountain pine** forms dense, creeping scrub, because its flexible branches do not break under the snow.

In many areas of the Alps, the forest line is slowly moving upwards today. One reason is **warmer summers**. Another reason is that many **alpine pastures** are used less. Where cows no longer graze, young trees can grow up. This process takes a long time but can be measured.

gewusst: The natural forest line in the Alps was often higher in the past than today, because people cleared forest for alpine pastures over centuries.
The dwarf mountain pine is a low-lying form of the mountain pine and can lie under the snow for months without breaking.

teile.einleitung: Root pressure is a force with which the root presses water from below into the plant. It arises because the root collects minerals and water flows in after them. It becomes visible, for example, when small drops hang on leaf edges in the morning.
wichtigste: Root pressure is the pressure that presses water up from the root.
It arises through osmosis in the root.
The root cells actively pump minerals into the inside of the root, and water flows in after them.
Root pressure is important mainly at night and in spring.
It shows in guttation, when plants release drops of water at the leaf edges.
Cut vines “bleed” in spring because of root pressure.
For tall trees, root pressure alone is not enough, and there the transpiration pull is more important.

abschnitte.text: **Root pressure** is an overpressure that arises in the water pipes of the root. It pushes the water from below into the stem. Together with the pull of the evaporating leaves, it makes sure that water rises in the plant. The pressure is usually only about one to two bar.

The cells of the root take up minerals from the soil and carry them, using energy, into the central cylinder. There, more substances are then dissolved than in the soil. Through **osmosis**, water always flows to where more substances are dissolved. A sealing layer of cells, the **endodermis**, stops the water from flowing back again.

In the early morning, glittering drops often hang on the edge of lady’s mantle leaves or on grass tips. This is mostly not dew but water that the plant itself releases through special openings. This process is called **guttation**. It happens mainly in damp, warm nights, when hardly any water evaporates and root pressure presses the water out.

If you cut a vine or a birch in spring, sap drips from the wound. Winegrowers say that the vine “weeps” or **bleeds**. At this time the plants do not yet have leaves that could evaporate water. Root pressure fills the pipes with water and dissolved sugars before the leaves come out.

A pressure of one to two bar can push water up only a few metres at most. Tall trees such as firs or giant sequoias therefore bring their water up mainly with the **transpiration pull**. Some plants, for example many conifers, show hardly any root pressure. Even so, it helps to remove air bubbles from the pipes at night and to fill them again.

Researchers cut a plant off just above the ground and put a tube on the stump. After a while, water rises in it, pressed up by the root. With a pressure gauge, you can determine how strong the root pressure is. The English researcher Stephen Hales studied the sap flow of vines as early as the 18th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: water moving through a thin skin to where more substances are dissolved
the release of drops of water at the leaf edges
a dense layer of cells in the root that controls the flow of water
the pulling force created by evaporation at the leaves

gewusst: From a tapped birch you can obtain several litres of birch sap a day in spring.
Many people take guttation drops for dew, although they come from the plant itself.
Without root pressure, vines would not weep in spring.

teile.einleitung: The **giant water lily Victoria** has the largest floating leaves of all water plants. Its scientific name is Victoria amazonica. It grows in calm waters in the Amazon region.
wichtigste: The giant water lily grows in the Amazon region in South America.
Its round leaves can grow about 3 metres across.
It was named in 1837 after the English Queen Victoria.
The flower opens in the evening, and in the first night it is white.
In the second night it is pink to red.
The underside of the leaf and the stalks are full of spines.
Air chambers keep the leaves above water.

abschnitte.text: The giant water lily grows in calm waters in tropical **South America**, above all in the **Amazon region**. It is warm there all year round. It roots in the muddy bottom. Its leaves and flowers float on the water surface. The name recalls the English **Queen Victoria**: in 1837 the plant was named after her, just when she had become queen.

The round leaves can grow about **3 metres** across. Their edge is bent upwards, so they look like big baking trays. Under the leaf run thick veins. Between them lie **air chambers**. That is why the leaves are light and float. The underside and the stalks are full of sharp **spines**. They protect the plant from fish and other animals.

The leaves are built very sturdily. If the weight is well spread, a large leaf can even carry a **small child**. In the past, children were put for fun on a board laid on the leaf. The construction of the leaf veins is also said to have inspired the builders of large glasshouses.

The flower opens **in the evening** at sunset. In the first night it is **white** and has a strong scent. In this way it attracts **beetles**, which bring pollen with them. After pollination the flower turns **pink to red** in the second night. The colour shows that the flower has already been visited.

gewusst: A single leaf of the giant water lily is wider than a bed is long.
In some botanical gardens, including in Switzerland, you can see the giant water lily in warm glasshouses.

teile.einleitung: The Wildnispark Zürich lies in the Sihl valley south of the city of Zurich. It consists of two parts: the natural forest Sihlwald and the Langenberg wildlife park. Here you can experience wild nature and native animals up close.
wichtigste: The Wildnispark Zürich consists of the Sihlwald and the Langenberg wildlife park.
The Langenberg lies in the municipality of Langnau am Albis.
The Langenberg was founded in 1869 and is regarded as the oldest wildlife park in Switzerland.
The Sihlwald was the first nature experience park in Switzerland.
In the Sihlwald, no timber has been used since the year 2000.
The Sihlwald has belonged to the city of Zurich since the Middle Ages.

abschnitte.titel: Two parts in the Sihl valley
abschnitte.text: The Wildnispark Zürich lies between the Albis and the Zimmerberg. Through the valley flows the **Sihl**, which gave the Sihlwald its name. It joins the Limmat in the city of Zurich. The park includes the large natural forest **Sihlwald** and the **Langenberg wildlife park** in Langnau am Albis. You can reach both easily by train through the Sihl valley.

The Sihlwald is one of the largest continuous **mixed beech forests** on the Swiss Central Plateau. In the past it supplied the city of Zurich with building and firewood. Since the year 2000, no timber has been felled here. Fallen trees stay lying. This **deadwood** is food and home for fungi, beetles and woodpeckers. In this way a wild forest arises again little by little.

The Sihlwald was the first area in Switzerland to receive the label **nature experience park**. Such a park lies close to a city. In its **core zone**, nature may develop freely, and people stay on the paths. All around lies a transition zone in which you can experience nature and learn a lot about it. Meanwhile there is a second such park with the Jorat near Lausanne.

The Langenberg was founded in **1869** and is regarded as the **oldest wildlife park in Switzerland**. Here live animals that are native to Europe or used to be. You can see **bears, wolves, lynxes and elks**, as well as deer and wild boar. The enclosures are large and designed close to nature. Entry to the wildlife park is free.

gewusst: In the Sihlwald, trees are simply allowed to grow old and fall over, as in a primeval forest.
Elks used to live in the area of present-day Switzerland too, but today they are extinct there.

teile.einleitung: On the fine roots of a plant grow tiny little hairs, the root hairs. You can hardly see them, but they are very important. Through them the plant takes up most of its water and nutrients.
wichtigste: Root hairs take up water and minerals from the soil.
Each root hair consists of a single protruding cell.
The many root hairs enlarge the surface of the root greatly.
They are found just behind the root tip.
A root hair lives only a few days.
Water gets into the root hairs by osmosis.

abschnitte.text: The main job of root hairs is to take up **water and minerals**. They are in close contact with the soil particles. A single root hair is a tube-shaped **outgrowth of a single cell** of the root skin. So it is only one cell that has grown long outwards. On a **cress seedling** you can see them with the naked eye as a fine, white fuzz. This is not mould.

A plant has **thousands** of root hairs. Together they enlarge the absorbing **surface** of the root many times over. In this way the plant can reach much more water. You can imagine it like a terry towel: the many small loops soak up more water than a smooth cloth.

Root hairs grow in the **root hair zone**. It lies just behind the growing **root tip**. Older parts of the root no longer have root hairs. Root hairs are **short-lived** and die after **a few days**. But because the root keeps growing all the time, new ones keep arising at the front.

In the cell sap of the root hairs, more substances are dissolved than in the soil water. That is why water flows into the cells by itself. This process is called **osmosis**. When **transplanting**, many of the delicate root hairs tear off. Until new ones have grown, the plant can take up less water. That is why it often lets its leaves hang afterwards and needs enough water.

gewusst: Root hairs are often thinner than a human hair.
Whoever leaves as much soil as possible on the roots when transplanting protects the fine root hairs.

teile.einleitung: The trophic state describes how many nutrients a lake contains and how much biomass, mainly algae, it produces. It helps experts to assess the condition of a body of water.
wichtigste: The trophic state shows the nutrient supply and productivity of a body of water.
The levels from poor to rich are: oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic.
Brown, acidic bog lakes with many humic substances are called dystrophic.
Important measurements are phosphorus, chlorophyll a and Secchi depth.
In eutrophic lakes, oxygen is often lacking in the deep water in summer.
The Swiss researcher Richard Vollenweider shaped water protection worldwide.

abschnitte.text: Experts divide lakes into **trophic levels**. “Oligo” means little, “meso” middling, “eu” good and “hyper” excessive. An **oligotrophic** lake is poor in nutrients, clear and rich in oxygen, like many mountain lakes. A **eutrophic** lake has many nutrients and many algae. A special form is **dystrophic** bog lakes, whose water is brown and acidic because of humic substances.

Above all, the content of **phosphorus** is important, because in many lakes it limits the growth of algae. The amount of algae is estimated from the concentration of **chlorophyll a**, which is found in all algae. A simple measurement is the **Secchi depth**: a white disc is lowered into the water until it can no longer be seen. The more algae, the cloudier the water and the smaller the Secchi depth.

abschnitte.titel: Lack of oxygen in the depths
abschnitte.text: In summer warm water lies on top and cold water below, and the deep water is called the **hypolimnion**. Dead algae sink down and are broken down there. This uses up oxygen, and hardly any fresh supply comes from above. Without oxygen, **phosphate from the sediment** is also released. This internal fertilising can keep a lake rich in nutrients for a long time.

Around the middle of the 20th century, many Swiss lakes were over-fertilised, for example by sewage and detergents. The Swiss researcher **Richard Vollenweider** showed how the input of phosphorus and the renewal of the water determine the trophic state of a lake. Sewage treatment plants and the ban on phosphate in detergents from 1986 helped a great deal. Some lakes in the canton of Lucerne are still artificially aerated today.

A well-known example is the **Burgundy blood alga**, a cyanobacterium. It sometimes turns nutrient-rich lakes such as Lake Murten reddish. Its name recalls the legend of the blood of the Burgundians after the **Battle of Murten** in 1476.

gewusst: Many Swiss lakes are much cleaner today than 50 years ago.
Too few nutrients are not ideal for fish either: in very clear lakes, some fish species grow more slowly.

teile.einleitung: Turgor is the internal pressure in a plant cell. It arises when the vacuole takes up water and presses the contents of the cell against the cell wall.
wichtigste: Turgor is the pressure of the cell sap against the cell wall.
It arises through osmosis: the vacuole takes up water.
The cell wall pushes back with wall pressure and prevents bursting.
If turgor falls because of lack of water, the plant wilts.
Changes in turgor open stomata and move the leaves of the sensitive plant.
In elongation growth, turgor stretches the cell wall.

abschnitte.text: A plant cell has a large **vacuole** full of cell sap. Salts and sugars are dissolved in it. Because of this, water flows into the vacuole by **osmosis**. It expands and presses the cell contents, the **protoplast**, against the cell wall. This internal pressure is called **turgor**. You can compare it to an inflated balloon in a rigid box.

The elastic **cell wall** pushes back with an equal force. This counter-pressure is called **wall pressure**. As soon as the two are equal, the cell takes up no more water. That is why plant cells do not burst in pure water. Animal cells, such as **red blood cells**, have no cell wall and can burst in pure water.

Herbaceous plants have little **supporting tissue** and no wood. Their stability depends strongly on cells filled to bursting. If water is lacking, the vacuoles lose volume, and turgor falls. Then leaves and stems hang down limply, and the plant **wilts**. If it gets water in time, it straightens up again.

Plants also use turgor for movements. The **stomata** of the leaves are surrounded by two **guard cells**. When these take up potassium ions and with them water, their turgor rises. Because of their unevenly thick walls, they curve apart, and the opening opens. In the **sensitive plant**, cells in the leaf joints quickly lose water after a touch, and the leaflets fold together.

Turgor also plays a role in **elongation growth**. Plant hormones such as **auxin** loosen the cell wall. Turgor then pushes it apart, and the cell becomes bigger. That is how young shoots and roots grow in length.

gewusst: The turgor in plant cells is often higher than the air pressure in a car tyre.
If you put plant cells in strong salt water, they lose water and the protoplast comes away from the wall. This is called plasmolysis.

teile.einleitung: The vacuole is a space in the cell filled with liquid. In plant cells it is especially large and has many jobs: it stores substances, keeps the cell firm and protects against animals that eat the plant.
wichtigste: The vacuole is surrounded by a membrane, the tonoplast.
It is filled with cell sap, mainly water with dissolved substances.
In fully grown plant cells it can take up to about 90 per cent of the volume.
The pressure of the filled vacuole is called turgor and makes leaves firm.
If water is lacking, the vacuoles shrink and the plant wilts.
In the vacuole are stored pigments such as anthocyanins as well as bitter and poisonous substances.

abschnitte.text: The **vacuole** is a little sac in the cell that is filled with **cell sap**. This consists mainly of water in which salts, sugars, pigments and other substances are dissolved. A membrane of its own, the **tonoplast**, surrounds the vacuole. It regulates which substances get in and out.

Young plant cells have many **small vacuoles**. As they grow, they take up water and **fuse** into one large **central vacuole**. In fully grown cells it often fills most of the cell, up to about **90 per cent** of the volume. The remaining cytoplasm and the cell nucleus are then pushed to the edge. Animal cells usually have only small vacuoles.

The filled vacuole presses the cell contents against the cell wall. This internal pressure is called **turgor**. It makes parts of the plant that are not woody, such as leaves and young stems, firm. If a plant gets too little water, the **vacuoles shrink**, and the pressure falls. The leaves lose their tension and hang down limply, and the plant wilts.

Many pigments of flowers, fruits and leaves are dissolved in the cell sap. An example is the **anthocyanins**. They give **red cabbage** its colour. Anthocyanins change their colour depending on the **acidity**: in an acidic environment they become reddish, in a basic one bluish to greenish. That is why red cabbage juice can be used as a simple acid test.

The vacuole also serves as a **store**. Plants keep sugars, salts and waste substances in it. Many plants also store **bitter and poisonous substances** there. Animals that feed on the plant are put off by this. That is how the plant protects itself, even though it cannot run away.

gewusst: Whether red cabbage comes to the plate reddish or bluish depends on whether you add acid such as vinegar or apple when cooking.
The word “vacuole” comes from the Latin “vacuus”, which means “empty”, although it is not empty at all.

teile.einleitung: In the woods, in the garden and in the town you can hear many **bird voices**. Every bird species sings or calls in its own way. Whoever listens carefully can recognise birds by their voice.
wichtigste: In spring many birds sing, especially early in the morning.
Male birds sing to show their territory and to attract females.
The woodpecker drums on wood with its beak.
Owls call mainly at night.
The blackbird often sings in the evening from roofs.
Pigeons coo deeply.
With recordings and apps you can learn bird voices.

abschnitte.text: In spring many birds sing already at **dawn** in the early morning. Then it is still quiet, and the song carries far. This bird concert is also called the **dawn chorus**. It is worth getting up early once and listening. In summer and autumn it then becomes quieter again.

Mostly it is the **males** that sing. With their song they show other birds: this **territory** is taken. At the same time they attract **females**. Besides song there are short **calls**. With them, birds warn of enemies, for example, or keep in touch with one another.

The **male blackbird** is black and has a yellow beak. It likes to sing in the evening from high places such as roofs, very melodiously and loudly. **Pigeons** make a deep cooing that you often hear in towns. **Owls** are active at night. That is why you hear their calls mainly in the dark.

The **woodpecker** has a special way of making itself noticed. It knocks very fast on wood with its beak. With this **drumming** it marks its territory. Often it picks a branch that sounds especially loud for this.

There are **recordings** and **apps** with bird voices. Whoever listens often soon recognises the birds by their song. Outdoors you are best entirely **quiet**. Noise drowns out the song and scares the birds away. In Switzerland, for example, the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach offers many bird voices to listen to.

gewusst: Many birds are easier to hear than to see, because they sit well hidden in the foliage.
A woodpecker drums so fast that you can hardly count the individual blows.

teile.einleitung: The UNESCO Entlebuch Biosphere lies in the canton of Lucerne between Bern and Lucerne. It is known for its moorland landscapes and shows how nature protection and the economy can go together.
wichtigste: UNESCO recognised the Entlebuch as a biosphere reserve in 2001.
Beforehand, the population had approved the project in votes.
A large part of the area consists of raised bogs and fens.
The region includes the holiday resort of Sörenberg and the limestone wall of the Schrattenflue.
Biosphere reserves belong to the UNESCO programme “Man and the Biosphere”.
They are divided into core zone, buffer zone and development zone.

abschnitte.text: A **biosphere reserve** is not an area from which people are shut out. People live and work here. They are to **preserve nature** and at the same time carry on farming, trade and tourism **sustainably**. Areas like this belong to the UNESCO programme “Man and the Biosphere”. The Entlebuch was recognised in **2001**, after the population had said yes in votes.

A biosphere reserve is divided into **three zones**. In the **core zone**, nature has priority. The **buffer zone** protects the cultural landscape that has grown up, such as alpine pastures and bogs. In the **development zone** lie villages, farms and businesses, and farming is done sustainably here. That way protection fits the needs of the local people.

The Entlebuch is one of the areas of Switzerland **richest in bogs**. A large part of the area consists of **raised bogs and fens**. Bogs form where the ground is constantly wet and dead plants hardly rot. They store a lot of water and carbon. Rare plants such as sundew and many dragonflies live here.

A striking mountain is the **Schrattenflue**. It consists of **limestone**. Rainwater has washed deep grooves and gaps into it, which are called **karren** (limestone pavement). The best-known holiday resort is **Sörenberg** in the municipality of Flühli. From there a railway leads up the **Brienzer Rothorn**, the highest point of the canton of Lucerne.

The region even gave its name to a breed of dog. The **Entlebucher Mountain Dog** is the smallest of the four Swiss mountain dogs. It comes from the Entlebuch and used to help farmers drive cattle. Cheese, wood and other products from the region are also sold under the name of the biosphere.

gewusst: The Entlebuch was the first UNESCO biosphere reserve in Switzerland under the new rules of UNESCO.
From above, the karren fields of the Schrattenflue look like a giant labyrinth of stone.

teile.einleitung: In early summer, white tufts of cotton wool shine in many Swiss bogs. They belong to cottongrass. This plant looks like a grass but is actually a sedge and grows almost only on wet ground.
wichtigste: The white tufts of cotton wool are long hairs on the fruits.
The wind carries the fruits with the woolly hairs far away.
Cottongrass belongs to the sedge family, like the sedges.
The hare’s-tail cottongrass has only one woolly tuft per stem.
The common cottongrass bears several hanging tufts.
Cottongrass indicates wet, acidic bog soil.

abschnitte.text: Cottongrass flowers early in the year, and the flowers are small and inconspicuous. After that, long, white **bristles** grow on the fruits. Together they form the striking **woolly tufts** that can be seen well in **early summer**. The hairs act like a parachute. In this way the **wind** carries the fruits far over the bog.

Although it is called that, cottongrass is not a true grass. Like the **sedges**, it belongs to the **sedge family**. These plants often have three-sided stems and like to grow in damp places. True grasses such as wheat or meadow grasses, on the other hand, have round, hollow stalks with nodes.

The **hare’s-tail cottongrass** grows in dense tussocks, the **clumps**, in raised bogs. It bears only **one** woolly tuft on each stem. The **common cottongrass** forms **several** nodding tufts on one stem. It often grows in wet **fens**. In the Alps there is also Scheuchzer’s cottongrass, named after the Zurich naturalist Johann Jakob Scheuchzer.

Cottongrass grows almost only on **wet and acidic** soils. Where you see it, there is mostly a **bog**. Bogs are rare habitats and store a lot of water. In Switzerland, bogs have been protected in the **Federal Constitution** since a popular vote in 1987. In the past, people sometimes collected the soft hairs of cottongrass and used them, for example, as **filling for cushions**.

gewusst: A field of cottongrass in the wind looks as if it had snowed in the middle of summer.
The bog protection vote of 1987 is also called the Rothenthurm initiative, after a bog in the canton of Schwyz.

teile.einleitung: Lemon balm is a popular herb from the garden. Its leaves smell fresh of lemon, although it has nothing to do with the lemon tree. It is used for tea, drinks and desserts.
wichtigste: The leaves of lemon balm smell of lemon.
The plant belongs to the mint family and is related to mint.
It is not related to the lemon tree.
The word “Melisse” comes from Greek and means honey bee.
The small flowers are white.
It is perennial and sprouts again in spring.

abschnitte.titel: A herb with a scent of lemon
abschnitte.text: **Lemon balm** is a bushy plant with light green, toothed leaves. If you rub a leaf, it smells strongly **of lemon**. The scent comes from **essential oils** in the leaves. But the plant is **not related** to the lemon tree, and only the scent is similar. It originally comes from the Mediterranean region and western Asia and is grown today in many gardens.

Lemon balm belongs to the **mint family**. To this family belong also mint, sage and thyme. Its leaves look like those of **mint**, and like it, it has a square stem and leaves growing opposite each other. In summer, small **white flowers** appear. The plant is **perennial**: in winter the upper parts die off, and in spring it sprouts again.

The word **“Melisse”** comes from Greek and means **honey bee**. The name fits well: the flowers supply a lot of nectar and are gladly visited by bees. Whoever has lemon balm in the garden is therefore doing the insects a good turn.

From the leaves, **lemon balm tea** is made. It is traditionally drunk **in the evening**, because it is regarded as calming and relaxing. In summer, fresh leaves are added to **cold drinks** such as iced tea, syrup or water. The fresh taste also goes well in salads and desserts. It is best to use the leaves fresh, because part of the scent is lost in drying.

gewusst: Lemon balm can spread strongly in the garden, because it forms many seeds.
As early as the Middle Ages, lemon balm was grown in monastery gardens.

teile.einleitung: For plants to form seeds, pollen has to get from one flower to another. Many flowers leave this to insects. Other plants trust in the wind. This is called wind pollination.
wichtigste: In wind pollination, the wind carries the pollen from flower to flower.
Grasses such as rye, but also maize, birch, hazel and conifers, are pollinated by the wind.
Their flowers are mostly inconspicuous, because they do not have to attract animals.
They form huge amounts of pollen, because most of it is lost.
The pollen is light, small and dry.
MeteoSwiss measures the pollen count and makes pollen forecasts.

abschnitte.text: In **wind pollination**, the wind carries the pollen from one plant to the next. Typical examples are **grasses** such as **rye**. Many trees also use the wind, such as **birch**, **hazel**, **alder**, **spruce** and **pine**. But the wind spreads the pollen at random. Only a tiny part lands on a suitable **stigma**, that is, the part of the flower that takes up the pollen.

The wind does not react to colours or scents. That is why wind-pollinated plants save on colourful **petals**, scent and nectar. Their flowers are mostly small, greenish or brownish. In return the pollen is **light, small and dry** and floats well in the air. Insect-pollinated flowers, on the other hand, often have sticky pollen that clings to the bodies of the animals.

Because so much pollen is lost, these plants form **huge amounts** of it. In spring the pollen of **spruces and pines** sometimes turns puddles and cars yellow. In **maize** the male flower heads sit as a **tassel** at the top. The pollen trickles with the wind onto the female **cobs** further down, on the plant itself and on neighbouring plants.

**Hazels** and **alders** flower very early in the year, before their leaves come out. This has an advantage: without foliage, the wind can carry the pollen unhindered through the branches. Leaves would slow it down and catch it. The hanging catkins of the hazel can often be seen as early as January or February.

Some people react to pollen with **hay fever**: the nose runs, and the eyes itch. In spring the **birch** is one of the most important triggers in Switzerland, and it flowers mainly in March and April. Later in the year the grasses follow. **MeteoSwiss** runs a national pollen monitoring network and reports daily how much pollen is in the air.

gewusst: The technical term for wind pollination is anemophily, from the Greek word “anemos” for wind.
Pollen grains are so small that you can only really make them out under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: A forest is not the same everywhere. Depending on height, soil and climate, different trees and plants grow together. Such a typical community is called a **forest community**.
wichtigste: Heinz Ellenberg and Frank Klötzli described the forest communities of Switzerland in 1972.
Their numbers are still used in forestry practice today.
On the Central Plateau, beech would naturally dominate in most places.
Larch and Swiss stone pine forests grow in the upper subalpine zone.
Downy oak forests grow on dry, warm limestone slopes.
Grey alders shape the floodplain forests along mountain rivers.
The altitudinal zones are called colline, submontane, montane and subalpine.

abschnitte.text: In 1972 the German **Heinz Ellenberg** and the Swiss **Frank Klötzli** published the work “Forest communities and forest sites of Switzerland”. In it they described **71 forest communities** and gave them numbers. These numbers are still used in forestry practice today. In this way foresters know which trees grow well naturally in a place.
