In Swiss forestry practice, vegetation is divided into **altitudinal zones**. From bottom to top they are called **colline**, **submontane**, **montane** and **subalpine**. In the subalpine zone lies the forest line. Above it follow the alpine and nival zones, where no forest grows any more.

On the **Central Plateau**, in the submontane and lower montane zones, the **common beech** would naturally dominate in most places. Under today’s climate it is very competitive there. Many spruce forests on the Central Plateau were planted. On acidic, nutrient-poor soils grows the **woodrush beech forest**. It is named after the white woodrush, a grass with delicate panicles that indicates acidic soils.

In the upper subalpine zone of the **Engadine** and the **Valais** grow **larch and Swiss stone pine forests**. They put up with cold winters and short summers. The Swiss stone pine reaches the forest line there. Along mountain rivers that regularly burst their banks, the **grey alder** shapes the floodplain forest. It copes well with flooding and gravel and grows quickly. In shady, damp gorges grows the **maple and ash ravine forest** with sycamore, ash and elm.

On dry, warm rocky slopes on limestone, for example in the Valais or at the southern foot of the Jura, grows the **downy oak forest**. It is light and rich in warmth-loving plants. On dry, limestone-rich slopes you also find the **winter heath pine forest**. It is named after the winter heath, a dwarf shrub that flowers pink already in late winter.

gewusst: Foresters in Switzerland still use the numbers from a book of 1972 for forest communities.
Without people, a large part of the Swiss Central Plateau would be covered with beech forest.

teile.einleitung: The environmental impact assessment, EIA for short, clarifies whether a large construction project complies with environmental regulations. It takes place before building begins, so that damage can already be avoided during planning.
wichtigste: The EIA is anchored in Article 10a of the Environmental Protection Act (EPA).
The details are regulated by the EIA Ordinance of 1988.
An EIA is needed for installations that can significantly burden the environment.
The developer prepares the environmental impact report (EIR).
The environmental protection agency of the canton or the federal government assesses the report.
For cross-border effects, the Espoo Convention of 1991 applies.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the EIA is anchored in the **Environmental Protection Act**. Article 10a requires an assessment for installations that can **significantly burden** the environment. The details are regulated by the **EIA Ordinance** of 1988. Its annex states which installations need an EIA. These include, for example, national roads, large power stations, landfill sites and large shopping centres.

Anyone who wants to build such a project must prepare an **environmental impact report**, EIR for short. In it the **applicant** sets out how the project affects the environment. Areas such as **air, noise, water, soil and nature** are examined. The report also shows which measures can reduce the burdens.

The report is assessed by the **environmental protection agency**. Depending on the procedure, this is the agency of the canton or the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)**. The agency gives an assessment. The decision, however, is made by the responsible **decision-making authority**, which takes this assessment into account. The EIA is not a procedure of its own but part of the **permit procedure**, such as the building permit or plan approval.

The great advantage of the EIA: it takes place **before building**. Environmental problems can be solved more easily and more cheaply in planning than later. This corresponds to the **precautionary principle** of the Environmental Protection Act. Burdens are to be limited early, not only once damage has occurred.

Some projects have effects beyond the national border, for example a large power station on a border river. For this there is the **Espoo Convention** of the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) of 1991. It obliges states to **inform and consult** neighbouring countries. Switzerland is a party to this convention.

gewusst: For projects that require an EIA, certain nationwide environmental organisations can lodge an appeal. This is called the right of associations to appeal.
Espoo is a city in Finland where the convention was signed.

teile.einleitung: Duckweeds are tiny plants that float freely on the water surface. In summer they can cover a whole pond with a green carpet. Among their relatives is the smallest flowering plant in the world.
wichtigste: Duckweeds float freely on the water surface.
A single frond is only a few millimetres across.
They are also called Entengrütze or Entenflott, that is, duck groats or duck float.
They have no real stem and no real leaves, but flat fronds.
Under each frond of the lesser duckweed hangs a fine root.
New fronds grow out sideways and break off.
The rootless watermeal is regarded as the smallest flowering plant in the world.

abschnitte.text: **Duckweeds** are tiny plants that **float** freely on the water. A frond of the **lesser duckweed** is only a few millimetres across, about the size of a pinhead to a lentil. Duckweeds have no real stem and no real leaves. They consist of small, flat **fronds**. Under each frond hangs a thin **root** in the water.

Because **ducks** like to eat them, duckweeds are also called **Entengrütze** in German, or Entenflott. Fish and other water animals also use them as food. Duckweeds contain a lot of protein. You find them in calm, nutrient-rich ponds, pools and ditches.

Duckweeds mostly reproduce without flowers. From one frond, **new fronds grow out sideways**. They separate and float on. In this way they reproduce **very quickly** in summer. Soon they cover the pond like a **green carpet**.

A dense cover of duckweed lets hardly any **light** through. Plants under water then get little light and grow worse. That is why a pond under a dense duckweed carpet can become dark and low in oxygen. At the same time, duckweeds take up many nutrients from the water.

A relative of the duckweeds is the **rootless watermeal**. It is only about a millimetre across and has no root at all. It is regarded as the **smallest flowering plant in the world**. Its flowers are so tiny that you can only see them with a magnifying glass.

gewusst: In some countries of Asia, rootless watermeal is eaten as a vegetable.
Under good conditions, the number of duckweeds can double within a few days.

teile.einleitung: In worm composting, small worms turn kitchen waste into valuable soil. This even works in a box on the balcony or in the flat. In the end, worm castings arise, a very good fertiliser for plants.
wichtigste: The technical term for composting with worms is vermicomposting.
The product is called worm castings and is a high-quality fertiliser.
The most commonly used is the compost worm Eisenia fetida.
Compost worms naturally live in the topmost litter layer.
The material must be damp, because worms breathe through their skin.
Meat and bones do not belong in the worm box.
Worm compost does not get hot, so weed seeds are not reliably killed.

abschnitte.text: In **vermicomposting**, worms eat organic waste. The term comes from the Latin word **vermis** for worm. Together with many tiny **microorganisms**, the worms break down the material. They excrete nutrient-rich crumbs. From this arise **worm castings**, a high-quality, crumbly fertiliser for the garden and potted plants.

In worm boxes, mostly the **compost worm** is used, with the scientific name **Eisenia fetida**. It naturally lives in the **topmost litter layer**, where leaves, manure and other remains rot. It does not dig deep, vertical tunnels. The compost worm reproduces quickly and eats large amounts. Deep-digging species such as the **common earthworm** are not suitable for the box.

Worms have **no lungs**. They breathe through their **skin**, and it has to be damp for this. That is why the material in the worm box must always be **damp** but not wet. **Plant-based kitchen waste** such as vegetable and fruit scraps and a little paper or cardboard are well suited. **Meat and bones** do not belong in it. They rot easily and attract vermin.

When the worm castings are ripe, you have to separate the worms from them. The easiest way is to put **fresh food on one side** of the box. The worms follow the food and move there. The other side is then almost free of worms and can be taken out. One disadvantage: worm compost does **not get hot** like a large garden compost heap. That is why **weed seeds** and disease germs are not reliably killed.

gewusst: A compost worm can eat a large part of its own weight in a day.
With proper care, a worm box hardly smells, or rather smells of forest soil.

teile.einleitung: Xylella fastidiosa is a tiny bacterium that clogs plants from the inside. It is regarded as one of the most dangerous plant pathogens in the world. In Italy it has made millions of olive trees die, which is why it is also closely monitored in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Xylella fastidiosa is a bacterium.
It lives in the water-carrying vessels of the plant, the xylem.
In Europe, the meadow spittlebug above all transmits the pathogen.
From 2013, millions of olive trees died in Apulia in Italy.
In America the bacterium causes Pierce's disease in vines.
In Switzerland it is a priority quarantine organism with a duty to report.
“fastidiosa” means demanding or fussy.

abschnitte.text: **Xylella fastidiosa** is a bacterium. It lives in the **xylem**, that is, in the channels that bring water from the roots to the leaves. There it multiplies and **clogs** the channels. The plant can then no longer transport water. The leaves turn brown, and the plant dries up. The bacterium can attack hundreds of different plant species.

The bacterium is transmitted by insects that suck **xylem sap**. In Europe the **meadow spittlebug** is the most important carrier. When sucking, it takes up the bacteria. If it then sucks on another plant, it transmits the pathogen. Over long distances the bacterium usually arrives with **infected plants** from trade.

In the Italian region of **Apulia**, the bacterium caused a major **olive tree dieback** from **2013**. Millions of trees died, including centuries-old ones. It was the first major detection in Europe. In **California** the bacterium has been known since the 19th century. There it causes **Pierce's disease** in grapevines, in which the vines wilt and die.

In Switzerland, Xylella fastidiosa is a **priority quarantine organism**. These are especially dangerous pests whose introduction has to be prevented. Even a **suspicion** has to be reported to the cantonal plant protection service. Infected plants cannot be cured in the field. If the pathogen is discovered, infected plants and **host plants** in a zone around them are **removed**.

The name **Xylella** refers to the xylem in which the bacterium lives. The Latin **“fastidiosa”** means **demanding** or fussy. The name alludes to the fact that the bacterium is hard to grow in the laboratory. It needs special culture media and grows very slowly.

gewusst: The meadow spittlebug is the reason for “cuckoo spit”: its larvae live in small heaps of foam on plant stems.
Besides olives and vines, Xylella can also attack almond trees, oleander and lavender, for example.

teile.einleitung: Almost every plant and animal cell has a cell nucleus. It is the control centre of the cell. In the nucleus lies the genetic information with the blueprints for everything the cell needs.
wichtigste: The cell nucleus contains the genetic information in the form of DNA.
A double nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus.
Substances get in and out through nuclear pores.
In the nucleolus, building blocks for ribosomes arise.
Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 in orchid cells.
An ordinary plant cell has exactly one nucleus.
Sieve tube cells lose their nucleus as they mature.

abschnitte.text: In the **cell nucleus** lies the **genetic information** in the form of **DNA**. It contains the blueprints for all the **proteins** of the cell. From here, what happens in the cell is steered. An ordinary plant cell has **exactly one** nucleus. Bacteria, on the other hand, have no nucleus, and their genetic information lies loose in the cell.

The cell nucleus is surrounded by a **nuclear envelope** of **two membranes**. It separates the genetic material from the rest of the cell contents, the **cytoplasm**. The nuclear envelope is perforated by many **nuclear pores**. Through these openings, substances and messenger molecules travel back and forth between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. In this way the blueprints get to the places where proteins are built.

In the cell nucleus you often see a dark **nucleolus**. There, components of the **ribosomes** are made, that is, the protein factories of the cell. Between two cell divisions, the DNA lies loose as **chromatin** in the nucleus. Only before a division does it condense into clearly visible **chromosomes**.

The Scottish botanist **Robert Brown** described a round structure in orchid cells in **1831**. He called it the **“nucleus”**, that is, kernel. Brownian motion is also named after him. But there are living plant cells without a nucleus: the **sieve tube cells** carry sugar sap through the plant and lose their nucleus in doing so. They are looked after by neighbouring **companion cells**.

gewusst: If you unrolled the DNA from a single cell nucleus, it would be much longer than the cell itself.
Living things with a cell nucleus are called eukaryotes, which means roughly “with a true nucleus”.

teile.einleitung: Tropical rainforests grow close to the equator, where it is warm and damp all year round. They are the forests richest in species on Earth.
wichtigste: There are tropical rainforests in South America, Africa and South-East Asia.
It is warm there all year round, and it rains a great deal.
The forest has several storeys, and it is dark on the ground.
Typical animals are the sloth, toucan, jaguar and poison dart frogs.
The largest rainforest is the Amazon rainforest in South America.
Rainforests are being cleared, which threatens many animals and plants.

abschnitte.text: Tropical rainforests grow in a belt around the **equator**. There are large rainforests in South America, in Central Africa and in **South-East Asia**. The largest is the **Amazon rainforest**. It is warm there all year round. It rains almost every day, and the air is very damp. There is no winter as we have it.

The rainforest is built like a house with several storeys. At the very top, a few **giant emergent trees** stick out. Below them, the treetops form a dense **canopy**. Further down grow smaller trees and shrubs. On the **forest floor** it is darkest, because the leaves above block almost all the sunlight.

Many animals live high up in the trees. The **sloth** hangs upside down from the branches and moves very slowly. The **spider monkey** holds on with its long tail, as if it had a fifth hand. The **toucan** stands out with its huge, colourful beak. The beak looks heavy, but is very light.

The **jaguar** is the largest big cat in the Americas. It creeps through the rainforest and can even swim well. Very small but dangerous are the **poison dart frogs**. Their bright colours warn enemies: careful, I am poisonous! The poison is in their skin.

Very many different animals and plants live in the rainforest, many of them found nowhere else. Plants such as **cocoa**, vanilla and rubber originally come from rainforest regions. The trees store a lot of carbon and are important for the climate. Unfortunately, large areas are being **cleared**, for example for pastures, fields or timber.

gewusst: In a rainforest, hundreds of different insect species can live on a single large tree.
Because there is so much light at the top and so little below, some plants grow directly on the branches of other trees.

teile.einleitung: The bark of willows has been used as a remedy for a very long time. It contains the substance salicin, which helps against pain. From research into these substances came the well-known painkiller aspirin.
wichtigste: Willow bark contains salicin, a precursor of salicylic acid.
The name salicin comes from Salix, the Latin name of the willow.
The bark of young twigs is used.
Tea made from willow bark tastes bitter and sharp.
Felix Hoffmann made pure acetylsalicylic acid at Bayer in 1897.
From 1899 it came on the market as aspirin.
Willow bark is not recommended for children and young people under 18.

abschnitte.text: Willows form the plant genus **Salix**. For the remedy, the **bark of young twigs** is used. It is stripped in spring from twigs two to three years old, because they contain a lot of active substance. The bark also contains **tannins** and bitter substances. A tea made from it therefore tastes **bitter and sharp** and puckers the mouth a little.

The most important active substance is called **salicin**. Its name derives from Salix, as does the name **salicylic acid**. Salicin is a **precursor**. Only in the gut and in the liver is it converted into the active salicylic acid. This takes time. That is why willow bark tea works **more slowly** than a painkiller tablet.

In the 19th century, chemists studied the substances from willow bark more closely. The chemist **Felix Hoffmann** made pure **acetylsalicylic acid** for the first time in **1897** at the company Bayer. From **1899** it came on the market as **aspirin**. In the name sits the syllable “spir” from **Spiraea**, the old name of **meadowsweet**. Salicylic acid was also obtained from this plant in the past. The “A” stands for acetyl.

In **herbal medicine**, willow bark is used today mainly for mild **back and joint pain**. It is weaker than modern painkillers. Because it contains similar substances to aspirin, people who **cannot tolerate aspirin** should avoid it. The **European Medicines Agency** does not recommend medicines made from willow bark for children and young people under 18. For them, sufficient safety data are lacking.

gewusst: Aspirin is among the best-known and most widely used medicines in the world.
Meadowsweet, a meadow plant with fragrant white flowers, also contains salicylic-type substances.

teile.einleitung: A dead tree is not simply rubbish. **Deadwood** is an important habitat in the forest. Many beetles, fungi, birds and other animals need it to live.
wichtigste: Deadwood means dead trees and branches.
Fungi break down deadwood especially strongly.
The stag beetle spends its larval stage in rotting oak wood.
Woodpeckers find plenty of food in rotting wood.
Hedgehogs like to hibernate in heaps of branches and leaves.
Foresters leave some dead trees standing as habitat.

abschnitte.text: **Deadwood** is the name for **dead trees and branches**. There is standing deadwood, that is, dead trees that are still upright. And there is lying deadwood, for example fallen trunks or branches on the ground. The **tree stump** that stays in the ground after felling also counts. Depending on the type of wood and the moisture, it takes many years to decades until deadwood has disappeared completely.

**Fungi** break down deadwood most strongly. Their fine threads grow deep into the wood and make it soft and rotten. After that, beetles, woodlice, worms and bacteria help. In the end, **humus** is produced, fertile soil. The nutrients from the wood in this way benefit the living trees again.

Many beetles lay their eggs in the wood, and their larvae eat their way through it. **Many small bore holes** in a dead trunk often show that **beetles live** there. The **stag beetle**, the largest beetle in Europe, spends its larval stage of several years in **rotting oak wood**. Because there are fewer old oaks and less deadwood, it has become rare.

**Woodpeckers** find many beetle larvae in rotting wood. They also hack holes in dead trees. Later, tits, bats or dormice move in there. On the ground, heaps of branches and leaves provide a good winter home, for example for the **hedgehog**. That is why **foresters** deliberately leave some dead trees standing or lying. In Swiss forests there is meant to be more deadwood again today than in the past, so that biodiversity increases.

gewusst: The tinder fungus is a fungus on dead beeches. In the past it was used to make fire.
A dead tree can be almost as valuable to nature as a living one.

teile.einleitung: Ultraviolet radiation, UV radiation for short, is an invisible part of sunlight. In the mountains it is especially strong, and plants and people alike have to protect themselves from it.
wichtigste: UV radiation is invisible to our eyes.
It increases by about 10 per cent for every 1000 metres of altitude.
Fresh snow reflects a large part of the UV radiation.
Many Alpine plants produce red and purple pigments, the anthocyanins, as protection.
Too much UV can damage genetic material and chlorophyll in the cells.
People protect themselves with sun cream, sunglasses and a hat.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight does not consist only of the colours we see. It also contains **ultraviolet radiation**, which is invisible to our eyes. A distinction is made between **UV-A, UV-B and UV-C**. The atmosphere and especially the **ozone layer** block a large part of it. What arrives on the ground can cause sunburn in people and damage plants.

At great height, more UV radiation arrives on the ground than in the valley. The reason: the **layer of air above is thinner** and filters less. For every **1000 metres of altitude**, UV radiation increases by about **10 per cent**. On a **snowfield** the exposure is especially high. Fresh snow reflects a large part of the rays, so you receive them from above and in addition from below.

Too much UV radiation can damage the **genetic material** and the **chlorophyll** in plant cells. High-mountain plants therefore have special protective substances. Many produce **anthocyanins**, pigments that colour leaves and flowers red, purple or blue. In the outer layers of cells they act like a **sun cream**. That is why the flowers of many mountain flowers are so strongly coloured, which also attracts the few pollinators in the mountains.

The radiation first hits the **epidermis** of the leaf. It contains protective substances and is often covered with a **layer of wax**. In this way it blocks a large part of the UV rays before they reach the inside of the leaf. Some Alpine plants are also densely hairy, which also protects.

People too need protection at altitude. Most important are **sun cream, sunglasses and a hat**. They prevent sunburn and damage to the eyes. On glaciers and snowfields it is best to wear good glacier glasses. How strong the radiation is at any moment is shown by the **UV index**, which is given in the weather forecast, for example.

gewusst: Bees can see UV light. Some flowers have patterns that are visible only in UV light and show the insects the way to the nectar.
Even when the sky is cloudy, a large part of the UV radiation gets through.

teile.einleitung: The hawthorn is a thorny shrub or small tree. In spring it is full of white flowers, and in autumn it bears small red fruits. It is a well-known medicinal plant and important for many animals.
wichtigste: The hawthorn has sharp thorns on its twigs.
It flowers white in spring, mostly in May.
In autumn it bears small red fruits that look like tiny apples.
Like the apple and the rose, it belongs to the rose family.
Insects visit its flowers and pollinate them.
Birds eat its fruits in winter.
As a medicinal plant it is traditionally used for the heart.

abschnitte.text: The **hawthorn** flowers in spring, mostly in **May**. Then the shrub is full of **white flowers**. Each flower has **five petals**. Like the apple and the rose, the hawthorn belongs to the **rose family**. You often find it at forest edges, in hedges and on pastures.

The flowers attract many **insects**. Bees, flies and beetles fetch **nectar** and pollen. In doing so they carry the pollen from flower to flower and so **pollinate** them. After that the fruits can form.

In autumn the hawthorn bears small, **red fruits**. They look like tiny apples. The fruits stay on the shrub for a long time. That is why **thrushes** and other birds still find food there even in **winter**. With their droppings, the birds spread the seeds, and so young hawthorns grow in new places.

The hawthorn has **sharp thorns**. They protect it from being eaten by animals. For **birds**, the thorny twigs are a good place for a **nest**. Cats and martens find it hard to get through. In this way nests and young birds are well protected. In the past, hawthorn was also planted as a hedge around fields and pastures.

The hawthorn is a well-known **medicinal plant**. From its leaves and flowers, remedies are made that are traditionally used for the **heart**. Such remedies exist, for example, as tea or drops. They should be taken only on the advice of an expert.

gewusst: A hawthorn can live for several hundred years.
The scientific name of the hawthorn is Crataegus, from a Greek word for “strong” or “hard”, because of its hard wood.

teile.einleitung: The forest edge is the place where the forest stops and meadows or fields begin. Here two habitats meet. That is why especially many plants and animals live at the forest edge.
wichtigste: At the forest edge, the forest turns into meadow or field.
Animals find food here from forest and meadow, and hiding places too.
A good forest edge is built in steps like a staircase.
Right at the outside lies the herb fringe with grasses and flowers.
The thorny blackthorn often grows at the forest edge.
A dense forest edge slows the wind in a storm.
The south side is usually the warmest.

abschnitte.text: At the **forest edge** the forest stops, and meadows or fields begin. Here two habitats mix. Animals find food from the forest and from the meadow. Shrubs also offer **hiding places** and spots for nests. That is why especially many animal and plant species live at the forest edge.

A good forest edge is built in **steps**. Right at the outside lies the **herb fringe** with grasses and flowers. Then follows the **shrub belt** with bushes. Only after that come the tall trees. In this way many different habitats arise side by side. A forest edge that stops straight like a wall offers much less room for life.

At the forest edge grow many **shrubs**. Typical is the **blackthorn**, also called sloe. It flowers white in spring and later bears blue, sour fruits. Hawthorn, elder and wild roses are also common. Their flowers attract insects, and their fruits are food for birds.

The **common buzzard** likes to sit on branches or posts at the forest edge. From there it watches for mice on the meadow. In the herb fringe live butterflies, beetles and grasshoppers. Hedgehogs, lizards and many birds use the shrubs as shelter. Deer often come out of the forest in the evening to feed on the meadow.

A dense forest edge with shrubs and low branches **slows the wind**. In this way fewer trees are blown over in a storm. The **south side** of a forest gets the most sun in Switzerland. There live many **warmth-loving** animals and plants. Foresters today often look after forest edges deliberately so that they stay stepped and rich in species.

gewusst: A stepped forest edge can be home to many more species than the inside of a dense forest.
The fruits of the blackthorn become somewhat milder in taste only after the first frost.

teile.einleitung: Many plants can make new plants without any seeds at all. A daughter plant grows from a part of the mother plant. This is called **vegetative propagation**.
wichtigste: In vegetative propagation, new plants arise without fertilisation.
The offspring are clones of the mother plant, and their genetic material is the same.
Strawberries reproduce by runners.
Potatoes are propagated with stem tubers.
Ginger forms a rhizome, an underground shoot.
The kalanchoe forms little plantlets along the edges of its leaves.
Low genetic diversity can be dangerous, as the Irish famine shows.

abschnitte.text: In vegetative propagation, new plants grow from body cells of the mother plant. No flower and no **fertilisation** is needed. That is why the offspring have exactly the same genetic material as the mother plant. Such offspring are called **clones**. This is handy for gardeners, because a good variety is kept exactly as it is.

The garden strawberry forms **runners** above the ground. At their nodes, new daughter plants take root. The potato is a **stem tuber**, that is, a thickened underground stem. New plants sprout from its eyes, the buds. Ginger forms a **rhizome**, a horizontally growing underground shoot. If you divide it, new plants arise.

In the **kalanchoe**, finished little plants with roots arise in the notches of the leaf edge. When they fall off, they keep growing on their own. Gardeners also use **layering**: a shoot is bent into the soil and stays connected to the mother plant until it has roots of its own. Only then is it separated.

With **meristem culture**, you grow very many clones from a little tissue. For this, tiny pieces of the shoot tip are placed on a nutrient medium. The tip is often free of viruses. In this way, healthy, virus-free young plants arise in large numbers.

If all plants are the same, they are also equally prone to disease. In the 19th century, only a few vegetatively propagated potato varieties were grown in Ireland. From 1845, **potato blight** destroyed the harvests almost everywhere. The great **Irish famine** followed.

gewusst: From a single leaf, the kalanchoe can form dozens of new little plants.
Many varieties of fruit and potatoes that we eat have been passed on as clones for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Plants lose water when they open their stomata to take in carbon dioxide. Water use efficiency states how much biomass a plant forms per amount of water used. It is very important for agriculture in dry regions.
wichtigste: Water use efficiency is the biomass formed per amount of water used.
It is given, for example, in grams of dry mass per kilogram of water.
A typical C3 plant transpires about 500 grams of water per gram of dry mass.
C4 plants such as maize need about half of that.
CAM plants generally reach the highest efficiency.
More CO2 in the air usually increases the efficiency.
Drip irrigation greatly improves it in agriculture.

abschnitte.text: **Water use efficiency** relates the production of a plant to its water consumption. It is given, for example, in **grams of dry mass per kilogram of water**. An example: a plant forms 2 kg of dry mass and uses 600 kg of water. That is 2,000 g divided by 600 kg, so about **3.3 g per kg of water**. The other way round, it needs 300 kg of water per kg of dry mass.

For one gram of dry mass, a typical **C3 plant** such as wheat transpires about 500 grams of water. **C4 plants** such as maize need about half of that. Their enzyme **PEP carboxylase** binds CO2 very well and does not react with oxygen. So it is enough to open the stomata less widely. **CAM plants** such as many cacti open their stomata at night, when it is cool, and store CO2 as malic acid. They generally reach the highest efficiency.

Plants of dry sites often have special leaves. In some, the **stomata lie sunk in pits**. In these hollows, a calm, damp layer of air stays put. This slows water loss more than CO2 uptake. Thick layers of wax and hairs on the leaves also help to save water.

If the **CO2 concentration** of the air rises, more CO2 gets into the leaf per time that the stomata are open. Plants then often narrow their stomata and lose less water. Their efficiency usually rises. In C3 plants, the efficiency is often estimated from the **carbon isotope ratio (δ13C)**. The enzyme Rubisco prefers the light isotope 12C. If the stomata are narrower, more 13C is built in.

Water is scarce in many regions. That is why agriculture tries to harvest a lot with as little water as possible. Especially effective is **drip irrigation**. In it, the water reaches the root precisely. **Evaporation** and seepage of unused water stay low. The choice of suitable varieties also plays a part.

gewusst: For a single kilogram of wheat grain, depending on the climate, often over a thousand litres of water are needed.
The pineapple is a CAM plant and therefore gets by with little water.

teile.einleitung: Violets are small flowers that often bloom early in the year. The well-known **sweet violet** has a fine, sweet scent. Even a colour is named after the violet.
wichtigste: The colour violet is named after the violet.
The sweet violet smells strongly and is therefore also called the scented violet.
The sweet violet flowers in March and April.
A violet has five petals.
The pansy is closely related to the violet.
Ants carry the seeds of the violet away.

abschnitte.titel: A flower gives the colour its name
abschnitte.text: The word **violet** comes from the Latin name of the violet, viola. Many violets bloom in this blue-purple. But there are also white and yellow violets. Closely related to the violet is the **pansy**, a popular garden flower. Both belong to the same group of plants.
A violet has **five petals**. The lowest petal is larger than the others. At the back it has a small bulge, the **spur**. Nectar for insects collects in it. The flowers stand singly on thin stalks.

The **sweet violet** flowers in March and in April. It is one of the first scented flowers of the year. That is why it is also called the **scented violet**. It likes to grow at woodland edges, by hedges and in gardens. It especially likes half-shady places.

On the seeds of the violet hangs a small, nutritious **appendage**. Ants like it very much. They carry the seeds into their nest and eat the appendage. They leave the seed lying. In this way the **ants** help to spread the violet.
The fine scent of violets has been popular for a long time. It is used for **perfume** and soap. Sweets are sometimes flavoured with violets too.

gewusst: Because ants carry the seeds away, violets sometimes turn up in entirely new places in the garden.
The pansy is actually a violet too.

teile.einleitung: Plants are everywhere: in the forest, on the meadow, in the water and even on rocks high up in the Alps. They make their food themselves and in doing so supply the oxygen that humans and animals need for breathing. Without plants there would be no life on Earth as we know it.
wichtigste: Plants need light, water and air to make food themselves.
This process is called photosynthesis, and oxygen is produced in it.
Plants stand at the beginning of almost every food chain.
In Switzerland about 3,000 different species of ferns and flowering plants grow.
Around a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest.
The main cause of today’s climate change is greenhouse gases from human activities, above all from burning coal, oil and gas.
Climate change is altering where plants and animals can live.

abschnitte.text: Plants are living things that mostly grow fixed in one place. With their **roots** they take up water and minerals from the soil. The stem or trunk carries the water upwards into the leaves. Many plants form flowers from which fruits and seeds develop.

Plants need light, water and air to make their food. In the green leaves is the pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures sunlight. From water and the gas carbon dioxide from the air, they build up sugar. This process is called **photosynthesis**, and oxygen is produced as a waste product.

abschnitte.titel: The variety of the plant world
abschnitte.text: Plants include huge trees such as spruces and beeches, but also tiny mosses. Ferns do not reproduce with seeds but with fine **spores**. Flowering plants attract insects such as bees with colours and scent, and these carry the pollen onwards. Fungi sometimes look similar, but do not belong to the plants and form a kingdom of their own.

In Switzerland there are many different habitats, from warm Ticino to the glaciers. The higher you climb, the shorter the summer becomes and the smaller the plants get. Above the **tree line**, only dwarf shrubs, grasses and alpine flowers such as gentian and edelweiss still grow. The Swiss National Park in the Engadin was founded in 1914 and is the oldest national park in the Alps.

The main cause of today’s climate change is **greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide, which arise above all when coal, oil and gas are burned. They hold heat back in the Earth’s atmosphere, like a glass roof on a greenhouse. In Switzerland, the glaciers are therefore melting, and many alpine plants are moving to higher altitudes. Forests and moors help, because they take up and store carbon dioxide.

Many plants and animals have become rare today because their habitat is disappearing. That is why some species are under **nature protection** and must not be picked. Everyone can help, for example with a strip of flowers in the garden or on the balcony. Staying on paths and not leaving litter behind also protects nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: How plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen from water and air.
The green pigment in the leaves that captures the light.
Gases such as carbon dioxide that warm the Earth like a blanket.
A habitat with all the plants and animals that live together there.
The height in the mountains above which no forests grow any more.

gewusst: On a hot summer day, a large broadleaved tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water through its leaves.
The oxygen we breathe comes to a large extent from tiny algae in the sea.
Some lichens and mosses in the Alps still grow at heights of over 4,000 metres.

teile.einleitung: Some plants grow only where the soil has certain properties. Whoever knows them can “read” the soil without needing a laboratory. Such plants are called indicator plants.
wichtigste: An indicator plant shows certain properties of the soil.
Many stinging nettles indicate a lot of nitrogen in the soil.
The Blacke, the broad-leaved dock, indicates over-fertilised meadows.
Heather indicates acidic, nutrient-poor soil.
Rushes and field horsetail indicate wet or compacted soil.
Heinz Ellenberg developed the well-known indicator values for Central Europe.

abschnitte.text: Every plant has its favourite conditions. An **indicator plant** grows preferably where the soil has quite particular properties. Whoever knows it can draw conclusions about the **wetness**, **acidity** or **richness in nutrients** of the soil. Farmers, gardeners and researchers use this knowledge. The hint is most reliable when a species grows in a dense **stand**.

abschnitte.titel: Indicators of a lot of fertiliser
abschnitte.text: The **stinging nettle** grows lushly where there is a lot of **nitrogen** in the soil, for example at manure heaps or on fertilised edges. The **broad-leaved dock**, called **Blacke** in Switzerland, spreads on heavily fertilised meadows, often with a lot of slurry. Farmers fight it as a weed. A lot of **dandelion** also indicates nutrient-rich soil. Yellow dandelion meadows in spring are mostly intensively used **fertilised meadows**.

**Rushes** grow on wet, often compacted soils. Where they are common on a pasture, water stands in the soil. The **field horsetail** likes to grow where water is held up in the subsoil. It is regarded as a sign of **soil compaction** and **waterlogging**. Such soils are poorly aerated, and many crops grow less well there.

The **heather**, also called ling, grows on **acidic, lean** soils. You find it, for example, on silicate rock or in bogs. On **limestone** it is mostly absent. Lean means: there are few nutrients in the soil. Such sites are often especially rich in rare plants.

The German botanist **Heinz Ellenberg** assigned **numbers** to many plants of Central Europe. These **indicator values** describe, for example, how much light, moisture or nitrogen a species needs. From the plants on an area you can in this way describe the site quite precisely. The Ellenberg indicator values are still used today.

gewusst: Stinging nettles in one spot in the forest can reveal that a farm or a stable used to stand there.
The word “Blacke” is known mainly in Switzerland, while in the rest of the German-speaking world people mostly say Ampfer.

teile.einleitung: In the past, peat was extracted from many bogs, in Switzerland too. It was used for heating and later for garden compost. Today we know that **peat extraction** destroys bogs and harms the climate.
wichtigste: Cutting peat out with a spade is called peat cutting.
Fresh peat blocks had to dry in the air for a long time.
In Switzerland, a lot of peat was extracted mainly during the two world wars.
During extraction, stored carbon is released into the air as CO2.
In 2012 the Federal Council approved a plan to reduce peat consumption.
Most peat in Switzerland today comes from abroad.
A bog that has been mined takes centuries to millennia to recover.

abschnitte.text: In **peat cutting**, people cut the peat into blocks with a special **spade**. First the bog was drained with ditches. The freshly cut **peat blocks** were heavy and wet. They had to **dry in the air for a long time**, often the whole summer, before they would burn. Then they were used to heat living rooms and stoves.

Switzerland had hardly any coal. Especially **during the two world wars** fuel was scarce, because hardly any coal came from abroad. That is why a great deal of peat was extracted from many bogs at that time. As a result, a large part of Swiss bogs disappeared. In 1987 the people accepted the **Rothenthurm Initiative**. Since then, bogs of special beauty and national importance have been protected by the Federal Constitution.

Peat contains a lot of **carbon**, which plants once took in from the air. When a bog is drained and mined, the peat comes into contact with the air and decomposes. In the process the carbon is released into the atmosphere as **CO2** and makes climate change worse. In addition, **the plants and animals of the bog lose their habitat**, such as sundew, dragonflies and rare butterflies. A bog that has been mined needs **many centuries to millennia** before a thick layer of peat forms again.

Hardly any peat is extracted in Switzerland today. The peat in potting compost comes **mostly from abroad**, for example from Northern and Eastern Europe. In 2012 the **Federal Council** approved a **plan to reduce peat consumption**. Trade and nurseries are to switch step by step to peat-free compost. Substitutes include compost, wood fibre or bark humus.

gewusst: In Switzerland, since the Rothenthurm Initiative of 1987, part of the bogs have been protected in the Federal Constitution.
Peat blocks used to be piled up in stacks to dry, much like firewood.

teile.einleitung: Plants cannot walk. For them to settle new places, their seeds and fruits have to travel. Some use water for this: rivers, rain or ocean currents carry them away.
wichtigste: The spreading of seeds by water is called hydrochory.
The Greek word “hydor” means water.
The coconut can drift for a long time in the sea and germinate on distant coasts.
Tissue containing air helps fruits and seeds to float.
Streams and rivers carry seeds mainly downstream.
In mangroves, the seeds germinate already on the tree.
In rain-ballist plants, raindrops fling the seeds out of the fruit.

abschnitte.text: Plants often reproduce by seeds. For these to reach new places, some plants use **water**. Experts call this **hydrochory**. The word comes from the Greek “hydor” for water. Seeds are carried away by rivers, rain or ocean currents.

Many floating fruits contain **tissue filled with air**. The hollow spaces make them lighter than water. A **waxy surface** also stops them from soaking up water. For long journeys at sea, a seed needs a **waterproof shell**. It protects the embryo from the salt water until it is washed up on land.

The **coconut** is a famous example. Its husk is thick, fibrous and full of air. So it floats and can drift across the sea for weeks to months. If it reaches a beach, it can **germinate** there. That is why coconut palms are found on many tropical coasts.

Flowing water carries everything **downstream** with the current. That is why bank plants are often found along a whole river course. The **black alder** grows on stream banks. Its small nutlets contain tissue filled with air and float on the water. In this way the alder settles new spots on the bank.

In **mangroves**, the seeds germinate already on the mother plant. The rod-shaped seedlings come away from the tree, fall into the water and **drift** off. If they reach shallow mud, they take root quickly. **Rain-ballist plants** work quite differently: their fruit acts like a cup or a seesaw. When a raindrop hits, the seeds spray out.

gewusst: Some seeds are still able to germinate after months in sea water.
Water lilies and many marsh plants also spread their seeds with the water.

teile.einleitung: Under our feet in the forest lies a hidden world. In the **forest floor** live countless animals, fungi and bacteria. It turns old leaves into new soil and stores and cleans water.
wichtigste: Earthworms pull leaves into their burrows and turn them into soil.
Fungal threads grow as a fine web in the soil.
Many fungi swap water and nutrients with tree roots for sugar.
Most small living things live in the topmost layer of soil.
The forest floor soaks up rain like a sponge.
It filters the water, which is why spring water from the forest is usually clean.

abschnitte.text: The **earthworm** pulls fallen leaves into its burrows and eats them. Its droppings are very good, loose soil. **Millipedes** and woodlice also eat dead parts of plants. Most small living things live in the **topmost layer of soil**. There is a lot of food and air there.

A fungus consists mainly of fine **fungal threads** in the soil. What we see and call a mushroom is only its **fruiting body**. Many fungi grow closely along the **tree roots**. They give the tree water and nutrients. In return they get sugar from the tree. In this way both gain an advantage.

The loose forest floor **soaks up water** like a sponge. In heavy rain it stores a lot of it. In this way the forest helps to prevent **floods**. The water trickles slowly through the soil. In doing so, the soil acts like a **filter**. That is why water from forest springs is usually very clean, and many municipalities in Switzerland get their drinking water from forest areas.

The **badger** digs large **setts** with many tunnels into the forest floor with its strong claws. Earthworms are among its favourite food. Foxes and mice also use holes in the ground. For many animals the forest floor is a safe home.

gewusst: Under a single footprint in the forest floor live more tiny living things than can be counted.
The mushroom that you see in autumn is only a small part of a much larger web in the soil.

teile.einleitung: Wheat is one of the most important cereals in the world. From its grains, flour is made for bread, Zopf and cake. Durum wheat is used to make spaghetti and other pasta.
wichtigste: Wheat is a cereal like barley, rye and oats.
The grains sit at the top of the stalk in the ear.
In an ear there are usually about 30 to 50 grains.
From wheat you make mainly flour for bread.
For pasta, durum wheat is mostly used.
Most wheat is winter wheat and is sown in autumn.
In the mill the grains are ground into flour.

abschnitte.text: **Wheat** is a **cereal**, like barley, rye and oats. Cereals are **grasses** with edible grains. In wheat the grains sit close together in the **ear**. The ear grows at the top of the **stalk**. In an ear there are usually about 30 to 50 grains. A whole field bears millions of them.

Most wheat is **winter wheat**. It is sown in **autumn**, grows a little and spends the winter in the field. In spring it keeps growing and turns golden yellow in summer. Then it is ripe. A **combine harvester** cuts the stalks and separates the grains from the straw.

The grains go to the **mill**. There, rollers crush the grains into fine **flour**. In the past, water or wind turned the mill wheels. Depending on how much of the whole grain stays in the flour, pale white flour or dark **wholemeal flour** arises. Wholemeal flour contains more dietary fibre.

From wheat flour you bake **bread**, cakes and biscuits. The **Sunday Zopf**, a plaited loaf, is also baked from wheat flour, together with milk, butter and yeast. Wheat flour makes the dough nicely fine and airy. The reason is the **gluten** in wheat, which makes the dough elastic.

For **spaghetti** and other pasta, **durum wheat** is mostly used. It is ground into **semolina**, that is, a somewhat coarser flour. From this, firm pasta arises that does not fall apart in cooking. Durum wheat grows mainly in warm, dry regions.

gewusst: Together with maize and rice, wheat is one of the three cereals that supply the most food worldwide.
Spelt, a cereal popular in Switzerland, is a close relative of wheat.

teile.einleitung: **Wholemeal bread** is baked from flour for which the whole grain of cereal was ground. That is why it contains more vitamins, minerals and dietary fibre than white bread. It also keeps you full for longer.
wichtigste: For wholemeal flour the whole grain is ground, with husk and germ.
In the husk and germ there are many vitamins and minerals.
Wholemeal bread keeps you full for longer than white bread.
You can often recognise it by small dark bits of husk.
The Swiss food pyramid recommends preferring wholegrain.

abschnitte.text: A grain of cereal consists of three parts: the **husk**, the **germ** and the **endosperm**. For white flour, mainly the pale endosperm is used. For **wholemeal flour**, the whole grain is ground, with husk and germ. In the bread you therefore often see small dark particles. These are pieces of the grain husk.

The outer layers and the germ are especially rich in **vitamins** and **minerals**. In wholemeal bread they are kept. In addition there is a lot of **dietary fibre**, also called roughage. The body digests it slowly. That is why after wholemeal bread you stay **full for longer** than after white bread.

The **Swiss food pyramid** shows how to eat a balanced diet. It advises preferring **wholegrain** for cereal products. This applies to bread, but also to pasta, rice or flakes. Wholegrain contains more valuable substances than pale products. But a dark bread is not always a wholemeal bread: sometimes it is only coloured, and a look at the ingredients helps.

gewusst: A dark bread is not automatically a wholemeal bread.
The germ is the part of the grain from which a new cereal plant would grow.

teile.einleitung: In the forest, young trees are constantly growing up. But roe deer, red deer and chamois like to eat their buds and shoots. This feeding is called browsing damage. If it is too strong, the forest can no longer renew itself properly.
wichtigste: In browsing damage, game eats the buds and shoots of young trees.
On the Central Plateau, the roe deer causes the most browsing.
In mountain forests, it is above all the red deer that eats a lot.
The silver fir suffers especially strongly from browsing in Switzerland.
If the leader shoot is eaten, the little tree hardly grows any more in height.
Wire cages and tree shelters protect single young trees.
The cantons regulate game numbers by hunting.

abschnitte.text: In **browsing damage**, animals nibble off the tips and buds of young trees. Especially in winter they otherwise find little food. On the Central Plateau the **roe deer** is very common and causes the most browsing. In the mountain forests it is mainly **red deer** and **chamois**. In winter red deer even eat bark, for example in Graubünden, where their numbers are large.

The **leader shoot** is the top shoot of a little tree. It lets the tree grow upwards. If it is eaten again and again, the little tree stays small and bushy. Sometimes it dies altogether. It can take many years until a young tree has grown out of reach of the animals’ mouths.

Game likes to eat certain tree species more than others. The young **silver fir** is eaten especially gladly, as are maple and oak. The spruce is less popular. What is left are the less popular species, and the forest becomes **more uniform**. In some forests hardly any young firs grow up any more. This is a problem in the mountains, because many forests there protect villages and roads from avalanches and rockfall.

Single young trees are protected with **wire cages** or **tree shelters**. When the tree is big enough, they are removed again. Sometimes whole areas are also fenced. The **cantons** regulate game numbers by **hunting**. In doing so, hunting planning also pays attention to how the young forest is doing. The aim is a **balance between forest and game**.

gewusst: Foresters count on sample plots how many young trees have been nibbled, in order to measure browsing.
The lynx can also help: where it hunts, roe deer are more careful and stay less long in one place.

teile.einleitung: The greenhouse effect makes sure that the Earth is a warm planet that can be lived on. Certain gases in the air hold back some of the heat, much like the glass of a greenhouse. Since humans have been releasing additional greenhouse gases, this effect has become stronger, and the Earth is warming.
wichtigste: Greenhouse gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane hold heat back in the atmosphere.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, it would be far too cold on Earth, about minus 18 degrees on average.
Thanks to it, the average temperature is about plus 15 degrees.
Burning coal, oil and natural gas releases additional carbon dioxide into the air.
This greenhouse effect strengthened by humans causes climate change.
Since measurements began, Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the world average.
Scientists were already studying the greenhouse effect in the 19th century.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground and the seas. The warm Earth gives the energy off again as invisible **heat radiation**. **Greenhouse gases** in the air swallow part of this radiation and send some of it back to Earth. That way more heat stays near the Earth’s surface, as if under a blanket.

The greenhouse effect is in itself a good thing and vital for life. Without it, the average temperature of the Earth would be about minus 18 degrees, and everything would be frozen. Thanks to water vapour, carbon dioxide and other gases, it is about plus 15 degrees. The most important natural greenhouse gas is **water vapour**.

Since industrialisation, people have burned large amounts of coal, oil and natural gas. This produces **carbon dioxide**, whose share in the air has risen from about 280 ppm before 1850 to over 420 ppm (as of 2024). Cattle farming, rice fields and landfill sites also release the strong greenhouse gas **methane**. Cutting down forests strengthens the effect further.

The French researcher Joseph Fourier suspected as early as the 1820s that the atmosphere warms the Earth. The Irishman John Tyndall showed in the laboratory around 1859 that carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb heat radiation. The Swede **Svante Arrhenius** calculated in 1896 that more carbon dioxide would warm the Earth. Today the IPCC summarises the knowledge on this in large reports.

Switzerland is warming faster than the world average, because land heats up faster than seas. The **glaciers** in the Alps are melting strongly and have lost a large part of their ice since 1850. Hot summers, drought and heavy rain are becoming more frequent. In winter, rain rather than snow falls more and more often at low altitudes.

To slow climate change, fewer greenhouse gases must be released. This includes renewable energies such as sun, wind and hydropower instead of oil and gas. Everyone can help, for example by cycling and taking the train, eating less meat and saving energy. In the **Paris Agreement**, countries have set common goals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat radiation
A gas produced by burning and by breathing out, chemically CO2
Short for parts per million, that is, how many out of one million air particles
A long-term change in the climate, today mainly a warming

gewusst: On Venus there is an extreme greenhouse effect, and it is over 400 degrees hot there.
A real greenhouse warms mainly because the glass does not let the warm air escape, so it works somewhat differently from the atmosphere.
Cows release methane when they digest, and it is a much stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

teile.einleitung: **Peat mosses** are small, soft mosses that can build up whole bogs. They soak up water like a sponge. Over a very long time, peat forms from their dead parts.
wichtigste: Peat mosses belong to the genus Sphagnum.
They grow especially often in bogs.
Peat moss stores more than 30 times its dry weight in water.
It keeps growing at the top, while below it dies and turns into peat.
Peat moss makes the water in the bog acidic.
It can be green, red or brown.

abschnitte.text: Peat mosses make up the genus **Sphagnum**. There are many species worldwide, and several occur in Switzerland. They are coloured **green, red or brown**. Peat mosses have no roots. They **keep growing upwards** while the lower parts die off. Over a very long time, **peat** forms from these dead parts.

The little leaves of peat moss have large, empty cells with small holes. The moss stores water in them. Peat moss can take up **more than 30 times its dry weight** in water. If you step on a carpet of peat moss, it feels **wet and spongy**, and water wells up. In the past, dried peat moss was used **as a wound dressing**, because it soaks up a lot of liquid.

Peat moss takes up mineral substances from the water and gives off acid in return. In this way **peat moss makes the water acidic**. In the acidic, wet bog, only a few other plants can grow. Bacteria and fungi also hardly work there, which is why dead moss does not rot properly. That is how peat moss creates its own habitat: the **raised bog**.

Raised bogs made of peat moss have become **rare** in Switzerland. In the past many were drained or mined for peat. Yet they are **valuable for animals and plants**, for example for sundew, cotton grass and dragonflies. Since the **Rothenthurm Initiative** was accepted in 1987, important bogs have been protected by the Federal Constitution. Well-known bog landscapes are found, for example, at Rothenthurm in the canton of Schwyz and in the Entlebuch.

gewusst: A raised bog is fed only by rainwater, and the peat moss gets all its nutrients from it.
Because peat moss inhibits bacteria, it was collected in large quantities for dressings in the First World War.

teile.einleitung: A trophic level shows at which step of the food chain a living thing stands. The word comes from the Greek “trophe”, which means nourishment.
wichtigste: A trophic level is a feeding step in the food chain.
On the first level stand the producers, mostly green plants.
Plant eaters form the second level, meat eaters the third and higher.
Omnivores such as the fox belong to several levels at the same time.
At the very top stand apex predators, which have hardly any natural enemies.
A lot of energy is lost from level to level.

abschnitte.text: At the start of every food chain stand the **producers**. These are mainly green plants and algae. They make their own food with sunlight through **photosynthesis**. All other living things depend on them directly or indirectly. That is why the producers form the **first trophic level**.

Whoever eats plants stands on the **second level**. These animals are also called primary consumers, for example red deer, roe deer or grasshoppers. Animals that eat plant eaters stand on the **third level**. A wolf that eats a red deer therefore belongs to the third level. In the chain grass, grasshopper, shrew, tawny owl, the tawny owl stands on the fourth.

In nature there are not only simple chains but a whole **food web**. Many animals eat different things. An **omnivore** such as the fox eats berries and mice. That puts it on the second and the third level at the same time. Humans are omnivores too.

Animals on the highest level are called **apex predators**. Examples are the orca, the eagle or the wolf. Adult animals are hardly hunted by others. Even so they are not independent: if there is less prey, they too do worse.

Every living thing needs energy for living, moving and keeping warm. Only a small part of the energy of one level reaches the next. As a rule of thumb it is about **10 per cent**. That is why there are far more plants than plant eaters and only a few large predators. This is often shown as a **pyramid**.

gewusst: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead living things are called decomposers. They bring the nutrients back into the soil.
Because of the loss of energy, food chains are usually only a few steps long.

teile.einleitung: In **livestock farming**, farmers keep farm animals such as cows, goats, sheep or pigs. They supply milk, meat and wool. In Switzerland, dairy farming in particular is very important.
wichtigste: Cows are ruminants with four sections of the stomach.
A cow gives milk after she has had a calf.
Dairy cows are usually milked twice a day.
Brown Swiss, Simmental and Eringer are Swiss breeds of cattle.
The Saanen goat from the Bernese Oberland is widespread worldwide as a dairy goat.
Every head of cattle wears ear tags and is recorded in the animal movement database.

abschnitte.text: A cow has **four sections of the stomach**: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. In the **rumen**, bacteria break down the grass. Then the cow brings the food back up and chews it again. That is why she is called a **ruminant**. In this way she can use grass that we humans cannot digest.

Like all mammals, a cow makes milk for her young. For her to give milk, she must first have had a **calf**. Dairy cows are usually milked **twice a day**, in the morning and in the evening. With **milking robots**, the cows go to be milked by themselves, sometimes more often.

The **Brown Swiss** comes from central and eastern Switzerland and is well adapted to mountain regions. The red and white spotted **Simmental** is named after the Simmental valley in the Bernese Oberland and is kept all over the world. The **Eringer** from the Valais are small, strong and mostly dark. In the cow fights they measure their strength, and the winner becomes “queen”.

The white **Saanen goat** comes from the Saanenland in the Bernese Oberland. It gives especially much milk and is therefore kept worldwide. A castrated male bovine is called an **ox**. An uncastrated one is called a bull. Oxen are calmer and used to be harnessed as draught animals to carts and ploughs.

In Switzerland, cattle wear **ear tags** with a number. Every animal is thus recorded in the **animal movement database**. In this way you know at any time where it was born and where it lives. This is especially important in **animal disease outbreaks**, so that people can act quickly.

gewusst: The Saanen goat from a small Bernese valley is one of the most widespread dairy goats in the world.
The cow fights go back to natural behaviour: even on the alp, Eringer cows settle the pecking order in the herd among themselves.

teile.einleitung: Plants do not sweat as we do, but they constantly give off water into the air. This release of water vapour through the leaves is called transpiration. It makes sure that water gets from the roots up to the highest treetop.
wichtigste: Transpiration is the release of water vapour through the leaves.
The water escapes mainly through tiny stomata on the underside of the leaf.
The evaporation creates a pull that draws water up from the roots.
Most of the water taken up, often over 90 per cent, evaporates again.
Transpiration cools the leaves on hot days.
In drought, plants close their stomata to save water.
Heat, wind, light and dry air increase transpiration.

abschnitte.text: **Transpiration** is the evaporation of water from the above-ground parts of a plant, mainly from the leaves. The water leaves the leaf as invisible water vapour. The main route is through the **stomata**, tiny pores that can open and close. A small part also evaporates directly through the wax layer on the surface of the leaf.

A stoma consists of two bean-shaped **guard cells** that form a gap between them. On a single leaf there are thousands of them, mostly on the underside. Through the openings, carbon dioxide also gets into the leaf, which the plant needs for photosynthesis. So the plant has to weigh up taking in carbon dioxide against saving water.

When water evaporates from the leaf, more water is drawn up from the fine pipes. Because water molecules stick to each other, a continuous thread of water forms all the way to the root. In this way the **transpiration pull** draws the water upwards in the vessels, without any pump. Together with the water, minerals from the soil travel to the leaves.

On hot, sunny and windy days, much more water evaporates than on cool, damp days. A large broadleaved tree can give off several hundred litres of water on a hot summer day. When the water in the soil becomes scarce, the plant closes its stomata, and the leaves begin to **wilt**. Cacti save water by having spines instead of leaves and a thick layer of wax.

Through transpiration, plants cool themselves and their surroundings. That is why it is more pleasant in the shade of a tree or in a park than in a car park. Forests give off so much water vapour that new clouds and rain can form from it. In the Amazon rainforest, a large part of the rain comes from the **evaporation** of the trees themselves.

On a sunny day, put a transparent plastic bag over a leafy twig and tie it shut. After a few hours you can see small drops on the inside. This is water vapour from the leaves that has **condensed** into water on the plastic skin. The experiment shows how much water a plant constantly gives off.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny opening in the leaf through which gases and water vapour flow
Two cells that open and close a stoma
The conducting tissue in which water flows upwards from the root
The change from liquid water to water vapour

gewusst: A maize plant evaporates more than a hundred litres of water during its life.
Without transpiration, tall trees could not carry their water up to the crown.
Many plants open their stomata in the morning and partly close them in the midday heat.

teile.einleitung: Ferns and mosses do not grow from seeds but from tiny **spores**. From a spore a small **prothallus** arises first. Only from it later grows the well-known plant.
wichtigste: The prothallus of ferns is called the prothallium.
The thread-like prothallus of mosses is called the protonema.
The fern prothallus is often heart-shaped and only a few millimetres across.
It is green and carries out photosynthesis itself.
On the fern prothallus, the sex cells arise in archegonia and antheridia.
When the young fern plant has leaves and roots of its own, the prothallus dies.

abschnitte.text: If a fern spore falls on damp ground, a flat, green little plate grows from it. This is the prothallus, in technical language the **prothallium**. In many ferns it is **heart-shaped**. It is usually only a few millimetres to about a centimetre across and lies close to the ground. That is why it is easily overlooked in nature.

abschnitte.titel: A small plant of its own
abschnitte.text: The prothallus is green, because it contains **chlorophyll**. With light it can make sugar itself, that is, carry out **photosynthesis**. So it is an independent little plant. But it needs a lot of moisture, because it has no real roots and no protective skin.

abschnitte.titel: Sex cells in a film of water
abschnitte.text: On the underside of the prothallus the **sex cells** arise. In flask-shaped **archegonia**, egg cells form. In the **antheridia**, mobile sex cells with flagella arise. They swim in a thin **film of water** to the egg cells. That is why ferns need damp places. From this, a young fern plant then grows. As soon as it has leaves and roots of its own, the **prothallus dies**.

Mosses also have a prothallus. From a moss spore, a green, branched **web of threads** grows first. It is called the **protonema**. Only from this web do the little moss plants grow. A moss cushion can thus arise from a single spore.

gewusst: The big fern in the woods and its tiny heart-shaped prothallus do not look at all alike.
Without water, the sex cells of ferns cannot swim to each other.

teile.einleitung: The welwitschia is one of the strangest plants in the world. It grows only in the Namib, a coastal desert in the south-west of Africa. All its life it has only two leaves, and it can be over 1,000 years old.
wichtigste: The welwitschia forms only two leaves in its whole life.
It grows in the Namib in the south-west of Africa.
Many plants are hundreds of years old, the oldest perhaps about 2,000 years.
It gets water from fog and from the ground.
The leaves keep growing at the base and fray at the ends.
Instead of colourful flowers it bears small cones.
It is named after the Austrian botanist Friedrich Welwitsch.

abschnitte.text: The **welwitschia** grows only in the **Namib**, a coastal desert in the south-west of Africa. It rains very rarely there. But from the sea, **fog** often drifts over the desert. Together with water deep in the ground, the plant can survive in this way. It has a short, thick trunk that hardly sticks out of the sand.

The welwitschia forms only **two leaves** in its whole life. But these keep growing all the time, like a **conveyor belt** from the base by the trunk. At the front they wear away. **Wind and sun** tear the leaves into many strips, and the ends dry up. That is why an old welwitschia looks like a heap of tangled ribbons.

Welwitschias grow very slowly and become **very old**. Many plants are hundreds of years old. The oldest are perhaps about **2,000 years** old. This makes the welwitschia one of the **longest-lived plants** on Earth.

The welwitschia bears no colourful flowers but small **cones**. It is distantly related to the **conifers**. It is named after **Friedrich Welwitsch**, a botanist from Austria. He discovered it in **1859**. A botanist is a person who studies plants.

gewusst: The welwitschia is shown on the coat of arms of Namibia.
Its scientific name is Welwitschia mirabilis, and “mirabilis” means “wonderful” in Latin.

teile.einleitung: The **tractor** is the most important vehicle on the farm. It pulls machines across the field, transports loads and lifts heavy things. In Switzerland you see it on fields, meadows and mountain roads.
wichtigste: On the field, a tractor pulls machines such as a plough, harrow or seed drill.
Most tractors run on diesel.
On many tractors the rear wheels are especially large.
With the front loader you can lift heavy things.
On modern tractors the driver sits in a cab.
In Switzerland, with a category G licence you may drive a small tractor from the age of 14.

abschnitte.text: A tractor has a powerful engine that usually runs on **diesel**. On many tractors the **rear wheels** are especially large. Their coarse treads grip well in soft ground so that the tractor does not spin. On modern tractors the driver sits in a closed **cab**, which protects against weather, noise and dust. At the back the tractor has a **power take-off**, a rotating shaft that drives attached machines.

For arable farming, the tractor pulls a **plough**, which turns the soil over. Then the **harrow** breaks up the coarse clods. With the **seed drill**, the seeds are put into the ground in even rows. To spread manure on the field, the farmer attaches a **manure spreader**. That way a single vehicle can do many different jobs.

At the front, many tractors have a **front loader**. This is a bucket or fork on two arms that can be raised and lowered hydraulically. It is used to load manure, soil or heavy **hay bales**. On trailers, the tractor transports fodder, wood or harvest. In winter, some farmers also use it to clear snow in their municipality.

In Switzerland, with a driving licence of **category G** you may drive a small agricultural tractor from the age of **14**. A test is needed for this. On steep mountain meadows, farmers often use special, low vehicles that do not tip over so easily. In the past there were also Swiss tractor firms, for example **Hürlimann** from Wil in the canton of St Gallen. Before there were tractors, horses and oxen pulled the plough.

gewusst: The first tractors were driven by steam and were huge and heavy.
Modern tractors can be steered by satellite and follow their track across the field to the centimetre.

teile.einleitung: How does the water get from the root to the top of a tall tree? For this the plant has a plumbing system of its own, the xylem. In German it is called Holzteil, the wood part, because wood is made of it.
wichtigste: The xylem carries water and minerals up from the root.
In German the xylem is called Holzteil.
The conducting cells are dead and form hollow tubes.
Lignin strengthens the cell walls and makes wood hard.
Evaporation at the leaves pulls the water upwards.
Conifers carry water in tracheids, flowering plants also in tracheae.
The inner part of the trunk, the heartwood, no longer carries water.

abschnitte.text: The **xylem** or **wood part** carries water with dissolved **minerals** from the root to the leaves. The transport always goes **upwards**. The cells that carry the water are **dead**. Their contents have disappeared, and hollow tubes are left. **Lignin** is deposited in the cell walls. It makes them firm and resistant to pressure, and this process is called **lignification**.

**Conifers** carry water almost only in long, spindle-shaped cells with thickened walls. These **tracheids** make up most of the softwood. In **flowering plants** there are also **tracheae**, also called vessels. They arise from cells lying one above another whose cross walls dissolve. In this way they form long tubes through which the water flows quickly.

The tree has no pump. At the leaves, water **evaporates** through the **stomata**. This creates a **pull** that draws the water in the xylem after it. The water molecules hold firmly together, like a chain. In this way the water is pulled up into the crown, even in very tall trees.

In spring the tree needs a lot of water and forms wide, thin-walled cells. This **earlywood** is lighter. In late summer, narrow, thick-walled cells arise, the darker **latewood**. This is how **annual rings** arise. In many trees such as oak or larch, only the outer part, the **sapwood**, still carries water. The inner part becomes **heartwood**, which is often darker and especially durable.

gewusst: The sugar from the leaves is not transported in the xylem but in a second plumbing system, the phloem.
From the annual rings of a tree stump you can read off how old the tree was.

teile.einleitung: Some plants only flower once they have been through a winter. This promotion of flowering by a longer period of cold is called **vernalisation**. The word comes from the Latin ver for spring.
wichtigste: Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by a longer period of cold.
Most effective is usually about 0 to 10 °C over several weeks.
Winter wheat is sown in autumn because it needs the winter cold.
Biennial plants such as the sugar beet flower only after the winter.
The cold is sensed mainly in the shoot meristem.
In thale cress, cold switches off the gene FLC.
Every new generation has to experience a winter itself.

abschnitte.text: Many plants need several weeks of cold before they can flower. In this way they make sure they do not flower already in autumn but only in spring. Most effective are usually cool temperatures of about **0 to 10 °C**. Hard frost is not needed for this. The cold is sensed mainly in the shoot tip, in the **shoot meristem**. This is a tissue from which new shoots grow.

**Winter wheat** is sown as early as autumn. It germinates, spends the winter as a small plant and forms ears the following year. If it is sown only in spring, it often stays stuck at the leaf stage. It then forms hardly any ears. Spring cereals, on the other hand, need no cold and are sown in spring.

The **sugar beet** is biennial. In the first year it stores sugar in the beet. After the winter it shoots up and flowers. It is similar with carrots or cabbage. Because we harvest the beets already in the first year, we rarely see their flowers.

In **thale cress**, a small experimental plant, the process is known exactly. The gene **FLC** inhibits flowering. Long cold silences this gene permanently, through changes to the **chromatin**, the packaging of the genetic material. In this way the plant remembers the winter. During seed formation, however, this is reset. Every new generation has to experience a winter itself.

abschnitte.titel: A wrong turn in the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: In the Soviet Union, **Trofim Lysenko** promoted the cold treatment of seed. He called it **yarovisation**, after the Russian word for spring cereal. Lysenko promised exaggerated harvest successes. He combined the method with false theories of heredity that have been scientifically disproved.

gewusst: The plant “remembers” the winter for weeks, although it has no brain.
The acquired state of cold is not passed on to the seeds.

teile.einleitung: The Big Bang is the beginning of our universe. According to the Big Bang theory, the universe arose about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state. Since then it has been expanding and has produced stars, galaxies and planets.
wichtigste: The universe arose about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state.
The Big Bang was not an explosion in a space, but space itself began to expand.
To this day the universe continues to expand.
The Belgian researcher Georges Lemaître developed the idea in the 1920s.
Edwin Hubble observed in 1929 that distant galaxies are moving away from us.
The cosmic background radiation is regarded as the afterglow of the Big Bang.
In the first minutes, the atomic nuclei of hydrogen and helium formed.

abschnitte.text: The **Big Bang** describes the beginning of space, time and matter. At that time everything was unimaginably hot and squeezed together into a tiny space. Since then the universe has been expanding and cooling down as it does so. What was before the Big Bang, or whether there was a “before” at all, science cannot answer to this day.

In the first minutes, the atomic nuclei of the lightest elements formed, mainly **hydrogen** and helium. For about 380,000 years the universe was a hot, opaque fog. Then it became cool enough for atoms to form, and light could travel freely. After a few hundred million years, the first stars lit up.

abschnitte.titel: How did people come up with it?
abschnitte.text: The Belgian priest and physicist **Georges Lemaître** proposed in 1927 that the universe is expanding. The American **Edwin Hubble** showed in 1929 that galaxies move away faster the further away they are. If you run this movement backwards, everything was once together at one point.
