The name “Big Bang” comes from the astronomer Fred Hoyle, who in 1949 called the theory that, rather mockingly.

In 1964, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson by chance discovered a faint noise coming from all directions of the sky. It is the **cosmic background radiation**, the cooled-down light from the early days of the universe. The amounts of hydrogen and helium in space also fit the calculations exactly. Space telescopes such as the James Webb Telescope see galaxies whose light has been travelling for over 13 billion years.

abschnitte.titel: From the Big Bang to us
abschnitte.text: Stars and galaxies such as our Milky Way formed from clouds of gas. In stars, heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron were made. About 4.6 billion years ago the Sun and the Earth formed. So the substances we are made of were once produced in stars.

At **CERN** near Geneva, researchers smash tiny particles together with enormous energy. For a moment this creates conditions like those shortly after the Big Bang. In this way they hope to understand what the early universe was made of. Swiss universities also take part in large space missions.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything that exists, that is, space, time, stars and galaxies together
A huge collection of billions of stars, for example the Milky Way
Faint radiation from all directions, the afterglow of the Big Bang
The distance that light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres

gewusst: A small part of the hiss on old tube televisions came from the cosmic background radiation.
When we observe distant galaxies, we are looking into the past, because their light has been travelling for so long.
The Big Bang was silent, because in empty space there is no air that could carry sound.

teile.einleitung: Environmental DNA, eDNA for short, is genetic material that living things release into their surroundings. From a sample of water or soil, you can find out which species live in a place.
wichtigste: Living things constantly lose cells, mucus, hair or droppings, and with them DNA.
This DNA can be obtained from samples of water, soil or air.
In this way species are detected without seeing or catching them.
With metabarcoding, many species in one sample are identified at the same time.
With quantitative PCR, you search specifically for a single species.
eDNA breaks down quickly in water and mostly shows only the recent presence of a species.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing leaves traces. Fish lose mucus and scales, mammals hair, and all of them excrete droppings. In these is their **DNA**, their genetic material. These traces in the environment are called **environmental DNA** or **eDNA**. Researchers filter water, for example, and examine which DNA is in it.

The great advantage: you **neither have to see nor catch** the animals. A water sample can show that a shy fish or a rare newt lives in the water. The animals are not disturbed in the process. **Non-native species** can also be discovered early in this way. In Switzerland, experts at **Eawag**, the federal water research institute, for example, are researching with this method.

If you want to detect **a single species**, you usually use **quantitative PCR**. In this, species-specific primers copy only the DNA of the species being sought. The measurement shows whether and how much of it is present. In **metabarcoding**, by contrast, you copy a typical stretch of DNA from all the organisms in the sample and read it out. A comparison with a **reference database** shows which species are present. If a species is missing from the database, it goes undetected.

abschnitte.titel: What eDNA reveals and what it does not
abschnitte.text: Free DNA is broken down in water by **UV light, heat and microbes**, often within days to weeks. A detection therefore usually means that the species was there a short time ago. In a river, the DNA is also carried **with the current** downstream. A sample can therefore contain DNA from animals that live further upstream.

Even tiny traces of DNA can be detected. That is why equipment or hands can easily **contaminate** a sample. Researchers wear gloves and take **blank samples** of clean water with them. If a blank sample shows DNA, the measurement is doubtful and has to be repeated.

gewusst: With eDNA from the air, researchers in zoos were able to show which animals live nearby.
A few litres of water from a lake can contain DNA from dozens of fish species.

teile.einleitung: Truffles are fungi whose tuber-like fruiting bodies grow underground. Because of their strong aroma, they are among the most expensive foods in the world.
wichtigste: Truffles grow underground and cannot be seen from outside.
They live in a partnership with tree roots, for example of oak, beech and hazel.
Today truffles are mostly searched for with trained dogs.
The white Alba truffle from Piedmont is regarded as the most expensive.
In Switzerland the Burgundy truffle grows most often.
In the kitchen, truffles are usually shaved raw into thin slices.

abschnitte.text: Truffles are **fungi**. The part that is eaten is their **fruiting body**. It looks like a small tuber and grows in the ground. That is why you cannot see truffles from outside. Ripe truffles give off a very strong scent. It attracts animals such as **wild boar**, which dig them up and eat them. With their droppings they spread the spores in other places.

Truffles cannot grow alone. They form a **mycorrhiza**, a partnership with the roots of broadleaved trees such as **oaks, beeches and hazel bushes**. The fungus helps the tree to take up water and nutrients. In return it gets sugar from the tree. For **truffle plantations**, young trees are planted whose roots have been inoculated with truffle fungus. It often takes many years until the first harvest.

Because truffles lie hidden in the ground, you need a good nose. Today people mostly work with trained **truffle dogs**. They smell the ripe tubers and show the spot. In the past, **pigs** were also used. But they like to eat the truffles themselves.

The most expensive kind is the **white Alba truffle** from Piedmont in Italy. It can hardly be cultivated and is collected almost only in the wild. For one kilogram, you often pay several thousand francs. Also well known is the **black Périgord truffle**, named after a region in south-west France. It is harvested in winter. In Switzerland the **Burgundy truffle** grows most often, for example in the Jura and the Central Plateau, and it is harvested in autumn.

Truffles have a very strong aroma that is lost with long cooking. That is why they are usually shaved **raw into thin slices** over a finished dish, for example over pasta, risotto or scrambled eggs. A few grams are enough for a plate.

gewusst: The Burgundy truffle and the summer truffle are now mostly regarded as one and the same species.
Because wild boar love truffles, their tracks are sometimes a clue for collectors.

teile.einleitung: When leaves, branches or food scraps slowly break down, this is called **rotting**. Many small animals, fungi and bacteria help with it. In the end, new soil arises from it.
wichtigste: In rotting, leaves slowly break down into soil.
Soil animals such as woodlice, millipedes and worms shred the leaves.
Fungi and bacteria break down the remains further.
The decomposers need moisture.
In the cold, leaves rot only slowly.
Oak leaves rot especially slowly.
Glass does not rot in nature.

abschnitte.text: In autumn many leaves fall to the ground. They do not stay lying there for ever. In **rotting**, they break down into tiny pieces. In the end, new, dark **soil** arises from them. In this way the nutrients from the leaves come back into the ground. The trees can use them again later.

First come **soil animals** such as woodlice, millipedes and earthworms. They eat the soft leaf tissue and shred the leaves. That is why on old leaves you often see only the fine **network of veins**, because the hard veins last longer. After that, **fungi** and **bacteria** break down the remains further.

The small decomposers need **water** to live. In dry leaves, rotting goes only slowly. **Warmth** helps too. In the cold the living things hardly work, so leaves rot very slowly in winter. In the damp, mild spring, on the other hand, it goes faster.

Not everything rots equally fast. **Oak leaves** are hard and contain a lot of **tannins**. That is why it takes a long time for them to break down. A banana skin in the **compost**, on the other hand, soon turns brown and falls apart. A **glass bottle** does not rot at all. Glass is not broken down by bacteria and fungi and stays in nature for a very long time.

gewusst: Without rotting, more and more old leaves would pile up in the forest year after year.
In the compost at home the same thing happens as in the forest, only faster.

teile.einleitung: The meadow clary is a meadow flower with bright blue-violet blossoms. It is related to the culinary sage and smells spicy. Its flowers have a clever trick to dust bumblebees with pollen.
wichtigste: The flowers of the meadow clary are mostly blue-violet.
They stand in storeys one above another on the stem.
The stem is square, typical of the mint family.
The flower has an upper and a lower lip like an open mouth.
A lever in the flower dabs pollen onto the back of bumblebees.
It likes to grow on dry, sunny meadows.
Most leaves lie as a rosette at the bottom on the ground.

abschnitte.text: The **meadow clary** has bright **blue-violet** flowers. They stand in **storeys** one above another on the stem. Each single flower has an **upper lip** and a **lower lip**. It recalls an **open mouth**. That is why clary belongs to the **mint family**, the lipped flowers.

The clary flower has a clever **lever**. When a **bumblebee** crawls into the flower, it pushes with its head against this lever. Then the **stamens** swing down and dab **pollen** onto its back. When the bumblebee flies to the next flower, it rubs the pollen off there. In this way the flower is pollinated. This mechanism is also called a **barrier**.

The stem of the meadow clary is **square**. This is typical of the family of the mint family. Most **leaves** lie at the bottom on the ground. They are big, wrinkled and form a **rosette**. On the stem there are only a few small leaves. If you rub a leaf, it smells **spicy**, because scented substances are contained in the leaves.

The meadow clary loves **sun and warmth**. You find it on **dry meadows** and on sunny banks. It is related to the **culinary sage** from the garden, because both belong to the same genus. On heavily fertilised meadows it becomes rarer, because other plants crowd it out there.

gewusst: The name sage comes from the Latin “salvia”, which is related to “salvus”, meaning “healthy”.
A meadow full of meadow clary can shimmer entirely blue from afar in early summer.

teile.einleitung: Plant cells often have a large space filled with liquid: the **central vacuole**. It is surrounded by a membrane of its own, the **tonoplast**. This envelope decides which substances get in and out.
wichtigste: The tonoplast is the membrane of the central vacuole.
It is a simple lipid bilayer.
The liquid in the vacuole is called cell sap.
The V-ATPase pumps protons into the vacuole.
That is why the cell sap is usually more acidic than the cytoplasm.
Aquaporins let water pass easily through the tonoplast.

abschnitte.text: The tonoplast is a **simple lipid bilayer**, that is, a membrane made of two layers of fat molecules. In it are many **proteins** that work as pumps, channels and transporters. It separates the **cell sap** in the vacuole from the **cytoplasm** of the cell. In fully grown plant cells, the vacuole can fill most of the cell.

An important pump is the **V-ATPase**. It uses the energy from ATP and pumps **protons**, that is, positively charged hydrogen particles, into the vacuole. That is why the cell sap is usually **more acidic** than the cytoplasm. This creates a **proton gradient**, a difference in the amount of protons. **Proton antiporters** use this difference: they let one proton out and bring another substance in instead.

In the tonoplast sit **aquaporins**. These are channel proteins that let water through quickly. When the vacuole takes up water, it presses from the inside against the cell wall. This pressure is called **turgor** and keeps leaves and stems firm. When water is lacking, the turgor drops and the plant wilts.

The tonoplast is **selectively permeable**, which means it lets only certain substances through. That is why the vacuole can store substances separately from the cytoplasm, for example **tannins**, sugars, salts or pigments. Some of these substances would harm the cytoplasm. The red and blue pigments of many flowers and of beetroot are also found in the cell sap.

gewusst: The name tonoplast comes from the Greek “tonos” for tension, which fits the cell pressure.
The red colour of beetroot comes from the cell sap in the vacuoles.

teile.einleitung: The root is the part of the plant that is usually in the soil. It takes up water and nutrients from the ground and holds the plant firm. Some roots, like the carrot, we even eat as vegetables.
wichtigste: The root takes up water from the soil.
With the water, minerals also get into the plant.
Roots are mostly in the soil.
Besides drinking, roots also serve to hold on.
Fine root hairs enlarge the surface of the root enormously.
Some plants store nutrients in thick roots.
The carrot is a root that we eat.

abschnitte.text: Besides the shoot and the leaf, the **root** is one of the three basic organs of seed plants. It mostly grows downwards into the soil, drawn by gravity and by water. At the tip, a **root cap** protects the delicate, growing cells. When a seed germinates, the seedling root appears first.

Behind the root tip grow countless fine **root hairs**. They are only a few millimetres long but enlarge the surface of the root many times over. Through them, the plant takes up water and dissolved minerals such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Through channels inside, the water gets into the stem and up to the leaves.

Roots anchor the plant so that wind and rain cannot knock it over or wash it away. The silver fir and the dandelion have a long **taproot** that grows vertically into the depths. The spruce, on the other hand, forms shallow roots and is more easily blown over in a storm. Grasses have many fine fibrous roots that hold the soil together and protect it from erosion.

Some plants store sugar and starch for the next year in thick **storage roots**. The carrot, the parsnip and salsify are such edible roots. In beetroot, too, we eat a thickened part of the root. The potato, on the other hand, is not a root but a tuber, that is, a thickened underground shoot.

Ivy climbs walls and trees with **clinging roots**. Mangroves on tropical coasts stand on stilt roots in the salt water. Many orchids in rainforests have aerial roots that take up moisture from the air. Almost all trees also work together with fungi that are connected with their roots and supply them with water.

The root system of a plant is often much bigger than you think. In a tree, the roots often reach further sideways than the crown. A single rye plant can form several hundred kilometres of roots altogether. In the forest there is therefore almost as much life under the ground as above it.

begriffe.erklaerung: tiny little hairs on the root that take up water
a thick main root that grows vertically into the depths
nutrients from the soil that the plant needs to grow
a protective cap at the root tip

gewusst: A fig tree in South Africa has roots that reach over a hundred metres deep into a cave.
The carrot used not to be orange but mostly purple or yellow.
Roots keep growing in winter too, as long as the ground is not frozen.

teile.einleitung: When it does not rain for a long time and it is hot, plants come under **drought stress**. They get too little water and have to save it. This shows, for example, in brown leaves in the middle of summer.
wichtigste: In drought, many plants first close their stomata.
Then little carbon dioxide gets into the leaf, and the plant hardly grows.
Heat increases drought stress, because more water evaporates.
Loamy soil rich in humus stores water best.
Spruces with shallow roots suffer especially and are often attacked by the spruce bark beetle.
The sessile oak usually survives drought well thanks to its taproot.

abschnitte.text: Plants lose water mainly through the **stomata** in the leaves. In drought they **close** these openings first to save water. But **carbon dioxide** also gets into the leaf through the stomata, and the plant needs it for photosynthesis. If they stay closed, it hardly gets any building material and **hardly grows**. In **heat**, even more water evaporates, so the stress becomes greater.

In extreme drought, the pull in the water pipes of a tree becomes very strong. Then **air bubbles** can form that interrupt the transport of water. Experts call this **embolism**. Parts of the crown then get no more water and die off. In broadleaved trees, strong drought stress can often be recognised by the **leaves turning brown as early as high summer**.

The **spruce** has **shallow roots**. It cannot reach water from deeper layers of soil and therefore suffers especially badly. Weakened spruces are readily attacked by the **spruce bark beetle**, a small bark beetle. Its larvae feed under the bark and can kill the tree. The **sessile oak**, on the other hand, forms a strong **taproot** that reaches deep into the ground. It therefore usually survives drought well.

How much a plant suffers also depends on the **soil**. **Loamy soil rich in humus** stores water like a sponge and releases it slowly. Sandy soil, on the other hand, dries out quickly. With climate change, hot, dry summers are becoming more frequent in Switzerland, for example in 2018. Foresters are therefore planting more tree species that tolerate drought better.

gewusst: In the hot summer of 2018, many beeches in parts of Switzerland turned brown as early as summer.
Some plants in deserts open their stomata only in the cool night to save water.

teile.einleitung: Cellular respiration is the process by which cells gain energy from nutrients such as sugar. In it, sugar is broken down with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water. It takes place in almost all living things, in humans, animals and also in plants.
wichtigste: In cellular respiration, glucose is broken down with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water.
The energy gained is stored in the molecule ATP.
Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, and its end product is pyruvate.
In glycolysis, the cell gains a net 2 ATP from one glucose molecule.
The citric acid cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
At the end of the respiratory chain, oxygen takes up the electrons.
The cellular respiration of plants goes on day and night.

abschnitte.text: Every cell constantly needs energy, for growing, moving and repairing. It gains this energy in **cellular respiration** by breaking down sugar such as **glucose**. As waste, carbon dioxide and water arise, and we breathe out the carbon dioxide. The energy is temporarily stored in the molecule **ATP**, which acts like a small battery of the cell.

In the first step, a glucose molecule is split into two parts in the **cytoplasm** of the cell. In this, two molecules of **pyruvate** arise. The cell gains a net 2 ATP in this step. Glycolysis needs no oxygen yet and occurs in almost all living things.

The pyruvate moves into the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell. In their inner space, the matrix, it is broken down step by step in the **citric acid cycle**. In this, carbon dioxide is released, and energy-rich electrons are loaded onto carrier molecules. The cycle was described in 1937 by Hans Krebs and is therefore also called the Krebs cycle.

At the inner membrane of the mitochondria, the carrier molecules pass their electrons on to the **respiratory chain**. The energy of the electrons is used to pump protons to one side of the membrane. This **proton gradient** drives ATP synthase, a tiny rotary machine that makes ATP. At the end, oxygen takes up the electrons, and water arises.

Plants breathe too, day and night in all living cells. In light they also carry out **photosynthesis** and so make more sugar and oxygen than they use. At night plants only release carbon dioxide, because photosynthesis rests. Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are thus like two sides of a cycle.

If oxygen is lacking, some cells can still gain a little energy from glycolysis. Yeasts make alcohol and carbon dioxide from it, which is used in baking bread and brewing beer. Our muscles form **lactic acid** during great exertion. But fermentation yields much less energy than cellular respiration, which gains about 30 ATP in total from one glucose molecule.

begriffe.erklaerung: the energy carrier of the cell, like a rechargeable battery
a part of the cell in which cellular respiration mostly takes place
grape sugar, the most important fuel of the cell
the liquid inside of the cell
a difference in the amount of protons on the two sides of a membrane

gewusst: Every day a human makes about as much ATP as he or she weighs.
Mitochondria have their own genetic material, because a very long time ago they were probably independent bacteria.
For the discovery of the citric acid cycle, Hans Krebs received the Nobel Prize in 1953.

teile.einleitung: Emergent trees are the tallest trees in the tropical rainforest. They stick out far above the canopy and are often very old.
wichtigste: Emergent trees are very tall, often old trees in the rainforest.
Broad buttress roots give them a hold on the ground.
On their branches grow orchids and other epiphytes.
The Brazil nut tree and the kapok tree are well-known emergent trees.
The harpy eagle builds its nest high up in their crowns.
When an emergent tree falls, young plants get light.

abschnitte.text: In the rainforest, the treetops form a dense **canopy**. But some trees stick out far above it. They are called **emergent trees**. They can grow to 50 metres and more. At the very top they are especially exposed to sun, wind and rain. Many of these trees are hundreds of years old.

The soil in the rainforest is often not deep. That is why many emergent trees have no deep taproots. Instead they support themselves with **buttress roots**. These are broad, flat roots that stand out from the trunk like walls. They give the tall tree a hold, much like buttresses on a wall. Some buttress roots are so large that a person can hide behind them.

On the branches of emergent trees grow many other plants. They are called **epiphytes**. They include many **orchids**, ferns and bromeliads. They do not grow in the ground but on the tree, because up there they get **more light**. They usually do not harm the tree but only use it as a support.

A well-known emergent tree is the **Brazil nut tree** from the Amazon region. It grows to about 50 metres tall. Its nuts grow in hard capsules. Another giant is the **kapok tree**. Its fruits contain soft fibres called **kapok**. In the past it was used to stuff cushions and mattresses.

In the crowns of emergent trees, the **harpy eagle** builds its nest. It is a mighty bird of prey of the rainforest. When an emergent tree falls, a **gap in the canopy** is created. Sunlight falls on the ground, and young trees can now grow quickly. That is how the forest renews itself.

gewusst: The capsules of the Brazil nut tree are so hard that mainly agoutis, a kind of rodent, can open them.
A single emergent tree can be a habitat for hundreds of different animal and plant species.

teile.einleitung: Water potential describes how strongly water in a place “wants to flow on”. With it you can explain how water gets from the soil through the plant into the air. It is usually measured in megapascals (MPa).
wichtigste: Pure, free water at normal pressure has, by definition, a water potential of 0 MPa.
Water flows by itself from higher to lower water potential.
Water potential is the sum of several components.
Dissolved substances lower it, and this is the osmotic potential.
Binding to surfaces such as soil particles gives the matric potential.
For every metre of height, the gravitational component rises by about 0.01 MPa.
In the field it is measured with the Scholander pressure chamber.

abschnitte.text: The reference point is **pure, free water** at normal pressure and the same height. By definition it has a **water potential of 0 MPa**. Almost all values in plants and soils are smaller than zero, that is, negative. The more negative the value, the more strongly the water is held. Water always flows passively **from higher to lower** water potential.

Water potential is the **sum** of several parts. The **osmotic potential** arises from dissolved substances and is negative. The **pressure potential** arises from the pressure in the cell and is usually positive. The **matric potential** arises because water sticks to surfaces such as soil particles and cell walls. In addition there is the **gravitational component**. An example: a cell with an osmotic potential of minus 0.8 MPa and a pressure potential of 0.5 MPa has a total of minus 0.3 MPa.

The osmotic potential is calculated according to **van 't Hoff**: Ψs = −c · R · T. For a sucrose solution of 0.1 mol/L at 293 K, this gives about minus 0.24 MPa. The **gravitational component** is ρ · g · h. Per metre of height, that is about 9,800 Pa, so about **0.01 MPa**. For air, Ψ = (R · T / Vw) · ln(RH) applies. At 50 per cent relative humidity and 20 °C this gives about **minus 94 MPa**.

abschnitte.titel: From the soil into the air
abschnitte.text: Water potential falls from the soil through the root, the stem and the leaf into the **atmosphere**. The gradient from the leaf to the dry air is especially large. That is why water is pulled upwards through the plant. If you water with **very salty water**, the soil water becomes very negative. If it is lower than in the root, the plant can no longer take up water and **wilts**.

In the field, water potential is often measured with the **Scholander pressure chamber**. You put a cut twig or leaf into the chamber so that the cut surface sticks out. Then you build up **gas pressure** until sap comes out at the cut surface. This pressure corresponds to the negative water potential in the **xylem**, that is, in the water pipes of the plant.

gewusst: The unit megapascal is large: 1 MPa corresponds roughly to ten times normal air pressure.
Dry air has such a low water potential that it can pull water up in tall trees over many metres.

teile.einleitung: A dry meadow is a poor, sunny meadow on dry ground. It is one of the habitats richest in species in Switzerland, but it has become rare.
wichtigste: Dry meadows grow mainly on sunny, steep south-facing slopes, for example in the Valais or the Jura.
The soil is mostly shallow, poor in nutrients and lets rainwater drain away quickly.
Many plants have small, hairy or leathery leaves that lose little water.
Grasshoppers, butterflies and lizards such as the European green lizard live here.
Since 1900, more than 95 per cent of dry meadows and pastures in Switzerland have disappeared.
The federal inventory “TWW” has protected the most valuable areas since 2010.

abschnitte.text: Dry meadows form where the ground dries out quickly. This is often the case on steep **south-facing slopes** that get a lot of sun. The soil is thin, stony and **poor in nutrients**. Because hardly any fertiliser is used here, fast-growing grasses cannot push out the other plants. That way many rare, small plants find room.

In summer it gets very hot and dry on dry meadows. Many plants protect themselves with **small, hairy or leathery leaves** that lose less water. Others have deep roots. Typical is **wild thyme**, a low subshrub with strongly scented leaves. Sage, orchids and many grasses also grow here.

Dry meadows are a paradise for animals that love warmth. Especially rich in species are the **grasshoppers**, whose chirping can be heard everywhere in summer. In addition there are many butterflies, wild bees and beetles. On warm slopes in the Valais and Ticino lives the bright green **European green lizard**, the largest lizard in Switzerland.

Most dry meadows were created by people. They stay open only if they are mown or grazed by animals. Without use, shrubs come up first and later trees, which is called **scrub encroachment**. Then the plants that love light disappear. That is why dry meadows are usually mown late in the year and without fertiliser.

Since 1900, more than **95 per cent** of the dry meadows and pastures in Switzerland have disappeared. The reasons are mainly fertilising, building and scrub encroachment. The federal government has therefore created the inventory of **dry meadows and pastures of national importance**, TWW for short. It has been in force since 2010. Farmers who look after such areas receive payments for doing so.

gewusst: Very many different plant species can grow on a single dry meadow, often clearly more than on a fertilised meadow.
Wild thyme is related to the culinary thyme from the kitchen.

teile.einleitung: Every living cell is surrounded by a wafer-thin skin, the cell membrane. It separates the inside of the cell from its surroundings. Like a doorman, it decides which substances may go in and out.
wichtigste: The cell membrane lets only certain substances through, and it is semipermeable.
It consists mainly of a double layer of fatty substances.
Built-in proteins serve as channels and pumps.
A cell membrane is only a few nanometres thick.
Plant cells, animal cells and bacteria all have a cell membrane.
In plant cells it lies closely against the cell wall on the inside.
In a strong salt solution it comes away from the cell wall, which is called plasmolysis.

abschnitte.text: The **cell membrane** encloses the **cytoplasm**, that is, the contents of the cell. Every living cell has one, whether **plant, animal or bacterium**. In plant cells it lies close against the inside of the firm **cell wall**. A cell wall of cellulose, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, on the other hand, exist only in plants.

The cell membrane is a very thin **double layer of lipids**, that is, fatty substances. It is only **a few nanometres** thick, which is a few millionths of a millimetre. That is why it cannot be made out on its own in a light microscope. Built into the fatty layer are **proteins**. Some form **channels**, others **pump** substances through the membrane in a targeted way.

The cell membrane lets only **certain substances** through. This is called **semipermeable** or selectively permeable. In this way the cell can take up nutrients and release waste substances. At the same time it holds on to what it needs. Water can cross the membrane well. If water moves through a semipermeable membrane to the side with more dissolved substances, this is called **osmosis**.

If you put plant cells in a **strong salt solution**, the vacuole loses water through osmosis. The cell contents shrink, and the cell membrane **comes away from the cell wall**. This process is called **plasmolysis**. Under the microscope you can observe it well, for example in red onion cells. If you then add pure water again, the cell contents expand again.

gewusst: The cell membrane is not rigid but flexible like a thin film of oil.
Without a cell membrane there could be no life, because only it makes a cell a separate space.

teile.einleitung: The castor oil plant, also called the miracle tree, is a striking plant with large, often reddish leaves. It is beautiful to look at, but its seeds are among the most poisonous things that nature produces. At the same time, the well-known castor oil is pressed from them.
wichtigste: The castor oil plant belongs to the spurge family.
Its seeds contain the very strong poison ricin.
The Latin word “ricinus” means tick.
Ricin paralyses the ribosomes that make proteins in the cells.
Castor oil is non-toxic, because the poison stays in the press residue.
In the past, castor oil was a well-known laxative.
In Switzerland you see the castor oil plant as an ornamental plant in gardens and parks.

abschnitte.text: The **castor oil plant**, called Wunderbaum in German, comes from warmer regions. There it can grow several metres tall. In Switzerland it cannot stand frost and is mostly planted as an annual **ornamental plant** in gardens and parks. People like it for its large, hand-shaped, often **reddish leaves**. It belongs to the **spurge family**. Many plants of this family have poisonous sap or seeds.

The seeds of the castor oil plant are shiny and speckled. They look like **ticks** that have sucked their fill. That is where the plant gets its name: the Latin word **“ricinus”** means tick. The seeds sit in spiny capsules. They are pretty but must never be eaten.

In the seeds there is **ricin**. It is among the most poisonous natural substances. Ricin paralyses the **ribosomes** in the body’s cells. These are the tiny components that make **proteins**. Without new proteins, the cells die. The hard **seed coat** holds back part of the poison. But if a seed is **chewed**, the ricin gets into the body much more easily. If poisoning is suspected, Tox Info Suisse helps in Switzerland on the number 145.

From the seeds, **castor oil** is pressed. Surprisingly, the oil is **non-toxic**. Ricin does not dissolve in the oil but stays behind in the **press cake**. Castor oil strongly stimulates the gut. In the past it was therefore often taken as a **laxative** against constipation. Today it is also used in industry, for example for lubricants and cosmetics.

gewusst: The castor oil plant can grow as tall as a man in a single summer.
Although the plant is called a tree, botanically it is more a large herb or a shrub.

teile.einleitung: In **anaerobic digestion**, microorganisms break down green waste, slurry or food scraps without oxygen. This produces **biogas**, which consists mainly of methane. What is left is a valuable fertiliser.
wichtigste: Digestion takes place in several steps and begins with hydrolysis.
Then come acidification, acetic acid formation (acetogenesis) and methane formation.
The methane is made by methanogenic archaea.
Mesophilic plants run at about 37 °C, thermophilic ones at about 55 °C.
Methane formers work best at a pH of around 7.
Unlike composting, you also gain energy as biogas.

abschnitte.text: First comes **hydrolysis**: enzymes split large molecules such as proteins, fats and carbohydrates into small building blocks. In **acidification**, organic acids arise from them. In **acetogenesis**, bacteria convert these mainly into **acetic acid**, hydrogen and carbon dioxide. In the last step, **methane formation**, methane is produced.

The methane is made by **methanogenic archaea**. Archaea are tiny single-celled organisms and form a domain of their own among living things, next to bacteria and all the others. They make methane mainly from acetic acid or from hydrogen and carbon dioxide. They are sensitive to acid and work best at an almost **neutral pH** of around 7.

**Mesophilic** plants run at about 37 °C, **thermophilic** ones at about 55 °C. The higher temperature speeds up the breakdown and kills disease germs. In **wet digestion**, the material can be pumped like slurry. In **dry digestion**, it has more dry matter and is stackable or pasty.

If a **digester**, that is the fermentation tank, gets too much easily degradable material, it goes out of balance. The acid-forming bacteria work faster than the methane formers. The acids pile up, the **pH falls**, and methane formation collapses. That is why a plant has to be fed evenly.

In composting, the energy in green waste is lost as heat. In digestion it stays stored in the **methane**. The biogas can supply electricity and heat or serve as fuel. The digestate is spread on the fields as **fertiliser**. In Switzerland there are many such plants on farms and in municipalities.

gewusst: Methane-forming archaea also live in the rumen of cows.
A digester can turn “sour” from too much feed alone and stop making gas.

teile.einleitung: The courgette is mostly called Zucchetti in Switzerland. It is a vegetable of the gourd family and grows in many gardens in summer. A single plant bears so many fruits that a few are often enough.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people mostly say Zucchetti instead of Zucchini.
Most courgettes are dark green.
The Italian word means “little pumpkins”.
The plant grows as a large bush with huge leaves.
You can also eat the flowers.
If you do not harvest in time, the fruits become very large.

abschnitte.text: The **courgette** is closely related to the pumpkin and belongs to the **gourd family**. The Italian word “zucchini” means **little pumpkins**. In Switzerland people mostly say Zucchetti, in Germany Zucchini. Most fruits are **dark green**, but there are also yellow, light green and round varieties. They are harvested young, when they are still tender.

A courgette plant usually grows as a **large bush** with **huge leaves**. It needs a lot of space, sun, warmth and water. From early summer it forms large yellow flowers. From the flowers the fruits grow, and very quickly: often you can harvest every few days. Because **each plant bears very many fruits**, a few plants are usually enough for a family.

If you leave a courgette hanging too long, **it becomes very large**, almost like a pumpkin. Its skin then becomes hard, and large seeds form inside. Young fruits therefore taste better. Important to know: if a courgette tastes clearly **bitter**, you should not eat it. It may then contain bitter substances that cause stomach ache and nausea.

Courgettes can be fried, grilled, steamed, stuffed or eaten raw in salads. The **flowers** are also edible. In Italy they are gladly stuffed or fried in batter. A well-known dish from France is **ratatouille**, a vegetable stew with courgettes, tomatoes, peppers, aubergines and onions. Courgettes consist for the most part of water and have few calories.

gewusst: On a warm summer day, courgettes can grow several centimetres.
The ancestors of all pumpkins and courgettes come from America.

teile.einleitung: In a vegetation survey, you note down all the plant species on a marked-off area and estimate how much area each covers. This makes it possible to describe and compare plant communities.
wichtigste: In a vegetation survey, you note all the plant species of an area.
For each species the degree of cover is estimated.
The well-known method comes from the Grisons botanist Josias Braun-Blanquet.
His scale runs from r and + through 1 to 5.
In a forest, the tree, shrub, herb and moss layers are estimated separately.
The area should be at least as large as the minimum area.

abschnitte.text: In a **vegetation survey**, you choose a marked-off area, for example in a meadow or in a forest. You mark it out precisely, for example with **string and pegs**. Then you note **all the plant species** that grow in it. Species outside the area are not counted. Only with a clear boundary can different surveys be compared with each other.

The well-known method was developed by **Josias Braun-Blanquet** (1884 to 1980). He came from **Chur** and is regarded as the founder of **phytosociology**. This science studies which plants regularly grow together. Such groups are called **plant communities**. His scale for estimating cover is still used in many countries today.

For each species you estimate the **degree of cover**. It states what share of the area the plants of one species cover when seen from above. The usual scale runs from **r** and **+** through 1 to 5. “r” stands for “rare”: the species occurs with only one or very few individuals. Level **5** means that the species covers **more than three quarters** of the area. That way you can quickly see which species dominate.

In a forest, plants grow at different heights. From top to bottom, a distinction is made between the **tree layer, shrub layer, herb layer** and **moss layer**. For each layer, the cover is estimated separately. The moss layer is the lowest, lying directly on the ground.

abschnitte.titel: How large the area must be
abschnitte.text: The area must not be too small. Otherwise typical species are missing. Experts speak of the **minimum area**: this is the smallest area on which almost all the typical species of a plant community occur. If you enlarge the area beyond this, hardly any new species are added. In a forest this area is much larger than in a meadow.

gewusst: Braun-Blanquet worked for a long time in Montpellier in southern France.
From many vegetation surveys you can see how meadows and forests change over the years.

teile.einleitung: A **forest fire** is a fire that spreads in a forest. In Switzerland, most forest fires are caused by carelessness. Fires are especially frequent in Ticino.
wichtigste: Most forest fires in Switzerland are caused by careless people.
A lightning strike can start a fire without any human involvement.
Most forest fires occur in the canton of Ticino.
There it burns mainly in late winter and in spring.
In 2003, about 300 hectares of forest burned above Leuk in the Valais.
The forest fire danger is given in five levels.
When the danger is great, a ban on fires in the forest often applies.

abschnitte.text: Most forest fires are caused by **careless people**. Cigarettes thrown away, unattended fires or sparks from machines can set dry leaves alight. A fire arises entirely without people, for example, from a **lightning strike**. If lightning strikes a tree, dry wood can catch fire. Such fires occur mainly in summer thunderstorms.

In the canton of **Ticino** there are the most forest fires in Switzerland. On the southern side of the Alps the climate is mild, but there are again and again long **dry spells**. The danger is especially high in **late winter** and **early spring**. Before the leaves come out, a lot of dry leaf litter lies on the ground. Often a dry north wind, the **north foehn**, blows then and fans the fire.

Many slopes are steep and hard to reach. That is why **helicopters** help with firefighting. They fill a **water container on a cable** in a lake or river. Then they release the water precisely over the fire. On the ground, the fire brigades work at the same time.

On **13 August 2003**, about 300 hectares of forest burned above **Leuk** in the Valais. It was one of the largest forest fires in Switzerland in recent decades. The burned area has been studied since then, to see how the forest recovers. On steep slopes a fire is especially problematic. There the forest protects against **rockfall**, avalanches and debris flows. It takes decades until a new **protective forest** has grown back.

In Switzerland, the forest fire danger is given in **five levels**, from level 1, low danger, to level 5, very great danger. In dry weather, a single spark can start a fire. Then the authorities often order a **fire ban**. It applies in the forest and near forests, often also to permanent fireplaces.

gewusst: In Ticino it does not burn most often in high summer, but in late winter and spring.
After a fire, plants that need a lot of light often grow first on the area.

teile.einleitung: If you want to know which plants and animals live in a place, you cannot count every single one. That is why experts work with samples. A tried and tested method is the **transect**, a line or a strip along which species are recorded.
wichtigste: A transect is a line or a strip along which species are recorded.
Transects are suited to changes along an environmental gradient.
A belt transect is a strip of a set width.
In the line-point method you note the plant touched at fixed intervals.
Butterflies are often counted on fixed routes in suitable weather.
The Swiss Biodiversity Monitoring uses fixed routes in square kilometres.

abschnitte.text: With a **line transect**, you stretch a measuring tape through an area, for example. Then you note which species occur along this line. A **belt transect**, on the other hand, is a **strip of a set width**, for example one metre. That way you record more area. In the **line-point method**, you look at **fixed intervals**, for example every 10 centimetres, to see which plant touches the tape.

Transects are especially suited to showing changes along an **environmental gradient**. A gradient is a gradual transition, for example from wet to dry or from warm to cold. In the **Alps**, transects are often laid from the valley up to the **summit region**. That way you study the **change of species with altitude**. If the survey is repeated after some years, you can see whether plants are moving higher up because of warming.

Animals too are recorded with transects. **Butterflies** are often counted on **fixed routes in suitable weather**, that is, in sun, warmth and little wind. In **distance sampling**, you also measure the distance of each animal sighted from the line. Animals far away are more easily overlooked. With the distances, the **probability of detection** can be estimated and so the real number of animals can be calculated.

The **Swiss Biodiversity Monitoring** has been observing the diversity of species across the whole country since the early 2000s. For this, experts walk fixed routes in **square kilometres** that are spread across the whole of Switzerland. They record, among other things, **butterflies**, **breeding birds** and plants. Because the same routes are always studied using the same method, changes over the years can be compared well.

gewusst: The word transect comes from the Latin “transsecare”, which means to cut through.
Even a school playground or the edge of a forest is suitable for a simple transect with string and a notepad.

teile.einleitung: Not the same plants grow everywhere on Earth. Large areas with a similar plant life are called **vegetation zones**. They are closely linked to the climate.
wichtigste: A vegetation zone is a large area with a similar plant life.
Above all the climate, that is temperature and rainfall, determines the vegetation zones.
The zones run like belts around the Earth, roughly along the lines of latitude.
The tropical rainforest grows at the equator.
Beyond the boreal coniferous forest, towards the poles, comes the treeless tundra.
On mountains, plant life changes in altitudinal belts.
Above the tree line, closed forests no longer grow.

abschnitte.text: The Sun shines most strongly at the equator, and it gets cooler towards the poles. That is why the vegetation zones run like **belts** around the Earth. They largely follow the **climate zones**. But mountains, seas and winds make the borders uneven. On a map, the zones therefore do not look like straight stripes.

At the equator it is hot and very humid all year round. There grows the evergreen **tropical rainforest** with giant trees. A little further away lies the **savanna**. There the rainy season and the dry season alternate, and mainly grasses grow, with single trees such as acacias or baobabs. In the **desert**, often less than 250 millimetres of rain falls in a year, and only specially adapted plants such as cacti survive.

In the temperate latitudes, where Switzerland lies too, **deciduous and mixed forests** grow naturally. Further north follows the **boreal coniferous forest**, a huge belt of spruces, pines and larches. Even further north it becomes too cold for trees. There lies the treeless **tundra** with mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs.

On a mountain, too, it gets cooler as you go up. That is why plant life changes step by step, which is called **altitudinal belts**. In the Alps, deciduous forest, coniferous forest, alpine meadows and rock follow one another, for example. The **tree line** is the line above which closed forests no longer grow. In the Swiss Alps it lies, depending on the region, at roughly 1,800 to 2,400 metres.

gewusst: If you climb a few hundred metres in the Alps, you experience a change in plants similar to a long journey towards the north.
The boreal coniferous forest is one of the largest continuous areas of forest on Earth.
